def_1_4_4_infinite_limit_to_plus_infinit.motivation_md: This formal definition allows us to rigorously prove that a function's output can be made arbitrarily large by keeping its input sufficiently close to $a$, which is essential for understanding vertical asymptotes and function behavior near singularities.
def_1_4_4_infinite_limit_to_plus_infinit.recap_md: - $f(x)$ must be defined in an open interval containing $a$, except possibly at $a$ itself. - For any positive $M$, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)>M$ when $0<|x-a|<\delta$.

def_1_4_5_infinite_limit_to_minus_infini.title: Infinite Limit as x approaches a (to -Infinity)
def_1_4_5_infinite_limit_to_minus_infini.one_liner: The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$ means that for any negative $M$, there is a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<M$ whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
def_1_4_5_infinite_limit_to_minus_infini.content: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing $a$, except that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$ if given any negative number $M$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)$ satisfies $f(x)<M$ if $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
def_1_4_5_infinite_limit_to_minus_infini.motivation_md: This definition provides a formal way to describe how a function's output can be made arbitrarily small (large negative) by keeping its input sufficiently close to $a$, which is crucial for analyzing vertical asymptotes where a function dives downwards.
def_1_4_5_infinite_limit_to_minus_infini.recap_md: - $f(x)$ must be defined in an open interval containing $a$, except possibly at $a$ itself. - For any negative $M$, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<M$ when $0<|x-a|<\delta$.

idea_1_5_continuity_intro.title: Introduction to Continuity
idea_1_5_continuity_intro.one_liner: Continuity translates the intuitive idea of an 'unbroken curve' into a precise mathematical formulation, like the trajectory of a baseball.
idea_1_5_continuity_intro.content: [FIGURE:08058e9f1dd66e94 | A hand is reaching upwards towards a baseball suspended in mid-air against a cloudy blue sky. This image likely serves as a decorative or introductory visual, as its direct relevance to the...] Joseph Helfenberger/iStockphoto A thrown baseball cannot vanish at some point and reappear someplace else to continue its motion. Thus, we perceive the path of the ball as an unbroken curve. In this section, we translate "unbroken curve" into a precise mathematical formulation called continuity.
idea_1_5_continuity_intro.motivation_md: The concept of continuity is fundamental in calculus, allowing us to describe functions whose graphs have no breaks, jumps, or holes. This property is essential for many theorems and applications, such as the Intermediate Value Theorem.
idea_1_5_continuity_intro.recap_md: - Continuity mathematically defines an 'unbroken curve'. - It describes functions whose graphs have no sudden jumps or gaps. - The path of a thrown baseball is an intuitive example of continuous motion.

idea_1_5_conditions_for_discontinuity.title: Conditions for discontinuity
idea_1_5_conditions_for_discontinuity.one_liner: A function has a discontinuity at $x=c$ if it is undefined at $c$, its limit does not exist at $c$, or its function value and limit at $c$ are different.
idea_1_5_conditions_for_discontinuity.content: Intuitively, the graph of a function can be described as a "continuous curve" if it has no breaks or holes. To make this idea more precise, we need to understand what properties of a function can cause breaks or holes. Referring to Figure 1.5.1, we see that the graph of a function has a break or hole if any of the following conditions occur: - The function $f$ is undefined at $c$ (Figure 1.5.1a). - The limit of $f(x)$ does not exist as $x$ approaches $c$ (Figures 1.5.1b, 1.5.1c). - The value of the function and the value of the limit at $c$ are different (Figure 1.5.1d). If one or more of these conditions fails to hold, then we say that $f$ has a discontinuity at $x=c$. Each function drawn in Figure 1.5.1 illustrates a discontinuity at $x=c$. In Figure 1.5.1a, the function is not defined at $c$, violating the first condition of Definition 1.5.1. In Figure 1.5.1b, the one-sided limits of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ both exist but are not equal, so $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, violating the second condition of Definition 1.5.1. A function like this has a jump discontinuity at $c$. In Figure 1.5.1c, the one-sided limits of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ are infinite, so $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, violating the second condition of Definition 1.5.1. A function like this has an infinite discontinuity at $c$. In Figure 1.5.1d, the function is defined at $c$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists, but these two values are not equal, violating the third condition of Definition 1.5.1. A function like this has a removable discontinuity at $c$. Exercises 33 and 34 help to explain why discontinuities of this type are given this name.
idea_1_5_conditions_for_discontinuity.motivation_md: Identifying the conditions for discontinuity helps us understand precisely where and why a function's graph might have breaks or holes. This clarity is vital for analyzing function behavior, ensuring mathematical rigor, and applying theorems that rely on continuity.
idea_1_5_conditions_for_discontinuity.recap_md: - A discontinuity occurs if $f(c)$ is undefined, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, or $f(c) \neq \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$. - Jump discontinuities happen when one-sided limits exist but are unequal. - Infinite discontinuities occur when one-sided limits are infinite. - Removable discontinuities occur when the limit exists but doesn't match $f(c)$ or $f(c)$ is undefined.

thm_1_6_1_continuity_trig_functions.title: Theorem 1.6.1: Continuity of Trigonometric Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

thm_1_6_1_continuity_trig_functions.one_liner: If $c$ is any number in the natural domain of a trigonometric function, then the limit of the function as $x$ approaches $c$ is equal to the function evaluated at $c$.
thm_1_6_1_continuity_trig_functions.content: If $c$ is any number in the natural domain of the stated trigonometric function, then the limit of the function as $x$ approaches $c$ is equal to the function evaluated at $c$. This means that all six trigonometric functions are continuous on their natural domains:$$ \begin{array}{lll} \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \tan x=\tan c \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \csc x=\csc c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sec x=\sec c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cot x=\cot c \end{array} $$
thm_1_6_1_continuity_trig_functions.motivation_md: This theorem formally establishes that trigonometric functions are continuous wherever they are defined. This property is crucial because it allows for direct substitution to evaluate limits of trigonometric expressions, simplifying calculations and enabling further analysis in calculus.
thm_1_6_1_continuity_trig_functions.recap_md: - Trigonometric functions are continuous on their natural domains.- For any trigonometric function $f(x)$, if $c$ is in its domain, then $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$.

idea_continuity_inverse_functions.title: Continuity of Inverse Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

idea_continuity_inverse_functions.one_liner: Geometrically, if a one-to-one function has no breaks or holes, its inverse also has no breaks, suggesting that the inverse of a continuous function is continuous.
idea_continuity_inverse_functions.content: Since the graphs of a one-to-one function $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are reflections of one another about the line $y=x$, it is geometrically clear that if the graph of $f$ has no breaks or holes in it, then neither does the graph of $f^{-1}$. This observation, combined with the fact that the range of $f$ is the domain of $f^{-1}$, suggests that the inverse of a continuous function is continuous. This result is stated without formal proof.
idea_continuity_inverse_functions.motivation_md: This concept provides the intuitive geometric basis for understanding why the inverse of a continuous function must also be continuous. By relating the graphical properties of a function and its inverse, it builds a foundation for the formal theorem on the continuity of inverse functions.
idea_continuity_inverse_functions.recap_md: - The graphs of a one-to-one function $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are reflections across the line $y=x$.- If $f$ is continuous (has no breaks or holes), its reflection $f^{-1}$ will also be continuous.- This suggests that the inverse of a continuous function is continuous.

thm_1_6_2_inverse_continuous_function.title: Theorem 1.6.2: Continuity of Inverse Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

thm_1_6_2_inverse_continuous_function.one_liner: If a one-to-one function $f$ is continuous at each point of its domain, then its inverse function $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point of its domain.
thm_1_6_2_inverse_continuous_function.content: If $f$ is a one-to-one function that is continuous at each point of its domain, then its inverse function $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point of its domain. This means $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point in the range of $f$.
thm_1_6_2_inverse_continuous_function.motivation_md: This theorem formally establishes that the property of continuity is preserved under the operation of taking an inverse for one-to-one functions. This is crucial for analyzing the continuity of inverse trigonometric and logarithmic functions, which are fundamental in higher-level calculus.
thm_1_6_2_inverse_continuous_function.recap_md: - If $f$ is a one-to-one function that is continuous on its domain, then $f^{-1}$ is also continuous.- The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$.

thm_1_6_3_continuity_exp_log.title: Theorem 1.6.3: Continuity of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

thm_1_6_3_continuity_exp_log.one_liner: Exponential functions $b^x$ are continuous on $(-\infty, \infty)$ and logarithmic functions $\log_b x$ are continuous on $(0, \infty)$.
thm_1_6_3_continuity_exp_log.content: Let $b>0, b \neq 1$. (a) The function $b^{x}$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$. (b) The function $\log _{b} x$ is continuous on $(0,+\infty)$.
thm_1_6_3_continuity_exp_log.motivation_md: This theorem provides fundamental continuity properties for exponential and logarithmic functions, which are essential building blocks for calculus and modeling natural phenomena. Knowing they are continuous allows for direct substitution when evaluating limits within their domains.
thm_1_6_3_continuity_exp_log.recap_md: - Exponential functions $b^x$ (for $b>0, b \neq 1$) are continuous on $(-\infty, \infty)$.- Logarithmic functions $\log_b x$ (for $b>0, b \neq 1$) are continuous on $(0, \infty)$.

technique_obtaining_limits_by_squeezing.title: Obtaining Limits by Squeezing

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

technique_obtaining_limits_by_squeezing.one_liner: The method of squeezing proves a limit $f(x) \rightarrow L$ by trapping $f$ between two functions, $g$ and $h$, whose limits are known to be $L$.
technique_obtaining_limits_by_squeezing.content: In Section 1.1, numerical evidence was used to conjecture that $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$. However, this limit is not easy to establish with certainty because it is an indeterminate form of type $0/0$, and no simple algebraic manipulation can obtain the limit. While general methods for finding limits of indeterminate forms will be developed later, in this particular case, a technique called squeezing can be used. The method of squeezing is used to prove that $f(x) \rightarrow L$ as $x \rightarrow c$ by "trapping" or "squeezing" $f$ between two functions, $g$ and $h$, whose limits as $x \rightarrow c$ are known with certainty to be $L$. As illustrated in Figure 1.6.2, this forces $f$ to also have a limit of $L$ as $x \rightarrow c$. This is the idea behind the following theorem, which is stated without proof.
technique_obtaining_limits_by_squeezing.motivation_md: Some limits, like $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}$, are indeterminate forms that cannot be solved by algebraic manipulation. The squeezing technique provides a powerful geometric and analytical method to determine such limits by bounding the function between two others with known limits.
technique_obtaining_limits_by_squeezing.recap_md: - The squeezing method is used for limits that are hard to find algebraically, especially indeterminate forms.- It involves "trapping" a function $f(x)$ between two functions, $g(x)$ and $h(x)$.- If $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to c} g(x) = \lim_{x \to c} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$.

thm_1_6_4_squeezing_theorem.title: Theorem 1.6.4: The Squeezing Theorem

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

thm_1_6_4_squeezing_theorem.one_liner: The Squeezing Theorem states that if a function $f(x)$ is bounded between two functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ that converge to the same limit $L$, then $f(x)$ also converges to $L$.
thm_1_6_4_squeezing_theorem.content: The Squeezing Theorem states: Let $f, g$, and $h$ be functions satisfying $g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)$ for all $x$ in some open interval containing the number $c$, with the possible exception that the inequalities need not hold at $c$. If $g$ and $h$ have the same limit as $x$ approaches $c$, say $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow c} h(x)=L$, then $f$ also has this limit as $x$ approaches $c$, that is, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=L$.
thm_1_6_4_squeezing_theorem.motivation_md: This theorem provides a rigorous mathematical tool to determine the limit of a function when direct evaluation or algebraic manipulation is not feasible. It is particularly useful for functions that oscillate or are defined in complex ways, by bounding them between simpler functions whose limits are known.
thm_1_6_4_squeezing_theorem.recap_md: - If $g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)$ for $x$ near $c$ (but not necessarily at $c$).- If $\lim_{x \to c} g(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to c} h(x) = L$.- Then $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$.

thm_1_6_5_special_trig_limits.title: Theorem 1.6.5: Special Trigonometric Limits

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

thm_1_6_5_special_trig_limits.one_liner: This theorem states two special trigonometric limits: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ and $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0$.
thm_1_6_5_special_trig_limits.content: This theorem presents two special trigonometric limits:(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0$
thm_1_6_5_special_trig_limits.motivation_md: These two special trigonometric limits are fundamental in calculus, especially for deriving the derivatives of trigonometric functions. They resolve indeterminate forms ($0/0$) that cannot be found by direct substitution or simple algebraic methods, often proven using the Squeezing Theorem.

idea_1_making_connections_secant_circles.title: Secant circles and tangent circles (osculating circle)

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

idea_1_making_connections_secant_circles.one_liner: This concept introduces the idea of a 'tangent circle' or 'osculating circle' as the limiting position of 'secant circles', analogous to how a tangent line is the limit of secant lines.
idea_1_making_connections_secant_circles.content: In Section 1.1, the notion of a tangent line to a graph at a given point was developed by considering it as a limiting position of secant lines through that point (Figure 1.1.4a). In these exercises, an analogous idea will be developed where secant lines are replaced by "secant circles" and the tangent line is replaced by a "tangent circle" (called the osculating circle). This exploration begins with the graph of $y=x^{2}$.
idea_1_making_connections_secant_circles.motivation_md: This concept extends the fundamental idea of a tangent line (as a limit of secant lines) to higher dimensions by introducing "secant circles" and "tangent circles" (osculating circles). This analogy helps build intuition for more complex geometric concepts in calculus and differential geometry.
idea_1_making_connections_secant_circles.recap_md: - A tangent line is the limiting position of secant lines.- An analogous idea replaces secant lines with "secant circles."- The "tangent circle" is called the osculating circle.

def_1_5_continuous_from_right.title: Continuous from the right
def_1_5_continuous_from_right.one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous from the right at $c$ if the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ from the right equals $f(c)$.
def_1_5_continuous_from_right.content: A function $f$ is continuous from the right at a point $c$ if the following condition holds: $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}} f(x)=f(c) $$
def_1_5_continuous_from_right.motivation_md: This definition is crucial for extending the concept of continuity to closed intervals, where a function cannot be approached from both sides at the endpoints. It allows for a precise description of behavior at boundaries.
def_1_5_continuous_from_right.recap_md: - A function is continuous from the right at $c$ if its right-hand limit at $c$ equals its value at $c$. - This is expressed by the formula $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}} f(x)=f(c)$.

def_1_5_2_continuity_on_closed_interval.title: Continuity on a closed interval
def_1_5_2_continuity_on_closed_interval.one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ if it is continuous on the open interval $(a, b)$, continuous from the right at $a$, and continuous from the left at $b$.
def_1_5_2_continuity_on_closed_interval.content: A function $f$ is defined as continuous on a closed interval $[\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b}]$ if it satisfies the following three conditions: 1. $f$ is continuous on the open interval $(a, b)$. 2. $f$ is continuous from the right at $a$. 3. $f$ is continuous from the left at $b$.
def_1_5_2_continuity_on_closed_interval.motivation_md: This definition extends the concept of continuity from a single point or an open interval to a closed interval, addressing the specific behavior required at the endpoints where a two-sided limit cannot be taken.
def_1_5_2_continuity_on_closed_interval.recap_md: - For continuity on $[a, b]$, the function must be continuous on the open interval $(a, b)$. - It must be continuous from the right at the left endpoint $a$. - It must be continuous from the left at the right endpoint $b$.

thm_1_5_3_properties_continuous_function.title: Properties of continuous functions
thm_1_5_3_properties_continuous_function.one_liner: If two functions $f$ and $g$ are continuous at a point $c$, then their sum, difference, product, and quotient (provided the denominator is not zero) are also continuous at $c$.
thm_1_5_3_properties_continuous_function.content: **THEOREM 1.5.3** If the functions $f$ and $g$ are continuous at a point $c$, then the following properties hold: (a) The sum $f+g$ is continuous at $c$. (b) The difference $f-g$ is continuous at $c$. (c) The product $f g$ is continuous at $c$. (d) The quotient $f / g$ is continuous at $c$ if $g(c) \neq 0$, and it has a discontinuity at $c$ if $g(c)=0$.
thm_1_5_3_properties_continuous_function.motivation_md: These properties are fundamental for determining the continuity of more complex functions built from simpler continuous functions. They allow us to combine known continuous functions (like polynomials) through arithmetic operations and maintain continuity, simplifying analysis.
thm_1_5_3_properties_continuous_function.recap_md: - The sum and difference of continuous functions are continuous. - The product of continuous functions is continuous. - The quotient of continuous functions is continuous, provided the denominator is not zero.

idea_1_5_continuity_polynomials_rational.title: Continuity of polynomials and rational functions
idea_1_5_continuity_polynomials_rational.one_liner: To show a function is continuous everywhere, one can prove it is continuous at an arbitrary point, which demonstrates that polynomials are continuous everywhere and rational functions are continuous where their denominator is nonzero.
idea_1_5_continuity_polynomials_rational.content: To demonstrate that a function is continuous everywhere, the general procedure involves showing it is continuous at an arbitrary point. For instance, according to Theorem 1.2.3, if $p(x)$ is a polynomial and $a$ is any real number, then $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=p(a) $$ This directly implies that polynomials are continuous everywhere. Furthermore, because rational functions are defined as ratios of polynomials, it can be deduced from part (d) of Theorem 1.5.3 that rational functions are continuous at all points except for the zeros of their denominator, where they exhibit discontinuities. This leads to a specific result regarding their continuity.
idea_1_5_continuity_polynomials_rational.motivation_md: This section provides a practical method for establishing the continuity of entire classes of functions, specifically polynomials and rational functions. By leveraging prior theorems, it simplifies the process of identifying where these common functions are continuous or discontinuous.
idea_1_5_continuity_polynomials_rational.recap_md: - To prove a function is continuous everywhere, show it is continuous at an arbitrary point. - Polynomials are continuous everywhere because $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=p(a)$ for any $a$. - Rational functions are continuous everywhere except at points where their denominator is zero.

thm_1_5_4_continuity_polynomials_rationa.title: Continuity of polynomials and rational functions
thm_1_5_4_continuity_polynomials_rationa.one_liner: Polynomials are continuous everywhere, while rational functions are continuous at all points where their denominator is not zero, having discontinuities where the denominator is zero.
thm_1_5_4_continuity_polynomials_rationa.content: **THEOREM 1.5.4** This theorem states the following regarding the continuity of polynomials and rational functions: (a) A polynomial function is continuous everywhere. (b) A rational function is continuous at every point where its denominator is nonzero, and it has discontinuities at the points where the denominator is zero.
thm_1_5_4_continuity_polynomials_rationa.motivation_md: This theorem provides a definitive statement about the continuity of two fundamental classes of functions, polynomials and rational functions. It allows for quick determination of their continuity without needing to apply the limit definition at every point.
thm_1_5_4_continuity_polynomials_rationa.recap_md: - Polynomials are continuous across their entire domain. - Rational functions are continuous everywhere except where their denominator is zero. - Discontinuities for rational functions occur precisely at the zeros of their denominator.

thm_1_5_5_limit_composite_function.title: Limit of a composite function
thm_1_5_5_limit_composite_function.one_liner: If the limit of $g(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ is $L$, and $f$ is continuous at $L$, then the limit of the composite function $f(g(x))$ as $x$ approaches $c$ is $f(L)$, meaning the limit can be "moved inside" the continuous function.
thm_1_5_5_limit_composite_function.content: **THEOREM 1.5.5** If the limit of $g(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ is $L$, i.e., $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$, and if the function $f$ is continuous at $L$, then the limit of the composite function $f(g(x))$ as $x$ approaches $c$ is $f(L)$. This can be expressed as: $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)\right) $$ This equality also holds if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c}$ is replaced by any of the one-sided limits ($\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}}$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}}$) or limits at infinity ($\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}$).
thm_1_5_5_limit_composite_function.motivation_md: This theorem is incredibly useful for evaluating limits of composite functions, especially when the outer function is continuous. It allows us to simplify the limit calculation by first finding the limit of the inner function and then applying the outer function.
thm_1_5_5_limit_composite_function.recap_md: - If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and $f$ is continuous at $L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f(L)$. - The limit operator can be "moved inside" a continuous function: $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)\right)$. - This property applies to two-sided, one-sided, and infinite limits.

thm_1_5_6_continuity_compositions.title: Continuity of compositions
thm_1_5_6_continuity_compositions.one_liner: If $g$ is continuous at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then their composition $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$; if both $f$ and $g$ are continuous everywhere, then $f \circ g$ is also continuous everywhere.
thm_1_5_6_continuity_compositions.content: **THEOREM 1.5.6** This theorem describes the continuity of composite functions: (a) If the function $g$ is continuous at a point $c$, and the function $f$ is continuous at the value $g(c)$, then their composition, denoted as $f \circ g$, is continuous at $c$. (b) More generally, if both the function $g$ is continuous everywhere and the function $f$ is continuous everywhere, then their composition $f \circ g$ is also continuous everywhere.
thm_1_5_6_continuity_compositions.motivation_md: This theorem is a powerful tool for determining the continuity of composite functions without having to apply the definition of continuity directly. It allows us to deduce the continuity of complex functions by analyzing the continuity of their simpler component functions.
thm_1_5_6_continuity_compositions.recap_md: - If $g$ is continuous at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$. - If both $f$ and $g$ are continuous everywhere, then their composition $f \circ g$ is continuous everywhere.

idea_1_5_absolute_value_continuous_funct.title: Absolute value of a continuous function
idea_1_5_absolute_value_continuous_funct.one_liner: The absolute value of a continuous function is always continuous, meaning if $g(x)$ is continuous, then $|g(x)|$ is also continuous.
idea_1_5_absolute_value_continuous_funct.content: It is known from Example 4 that the absolute value function, $|x|$, is continuous everywhere. Consequently, if a function $g(x)$ is continuous at a point $c$, then by applying part (a) of Theorem 1.5.6 (Continuity of Compositions), the function $|g(x)|$ must also be continuous at $c$. More broadly, if $g(x)$ is continuous everywhere, then $|g(x)|$ is also continuous everywhere. Informally, this means: The absolute value of a continuous function is continuous. For example, since the polynomial $g(x)=4-x^{2}$ is continuous everywhere, it follows that the function $\left|4-x^{2}\right|$ is also continuous everywhere (Figure 1.5.7).
idea_1_5_absolute_value_continuous_funct.motivation_md: This idea provides a useful shortcut for determining the continuity of functions involving absolute values. By recognizing that the absolute value function itself is continuous, and applying the theorem on continuity of compositions, we can quickly ascertain the continuity of $|g(x)|$ if $g(x)$ is known to be continuous.
idea_1_5_absolute_value_continuous_funct.recap_md: - The function $|x|$ is continuous everywhere. - If $g(x)$ is continuous at $c$, then $|g(x)|$ is continuous at $c$ (by Theorem 1.5.6). - The absolute value of any continuous function is itself continuous.

idea_terminal_velocity.title: Terminal velocity
idea_terminal_velocity.one_liner: Air resistance causes a skydiver's velocity to approach a maximum limit, known as "terminal velocity."
idea_terminal_velocity.content: Air resistance prevents a skydiver's velocity from increasing indefinitely. Instead, the velocity approaches a specific limit, which is called the "terminal velocity."
idea_terminal_velocity.motivation_md: This concept explains a real-world phenomenon where a physical quantity, velocity, doesn't increase infinitely but reaches a maximum due to opposing forces. It introduces the idea of a "limit" in a tangible context, setting the stage for its mathematical definition in calculus.
idea_terminal_velocity.recap_md: - Air resistance limits the speed of falling objects. - This maximum speed is called terminal velocity. - Terminal velocity is an example of a physical limit.

idea_intro_limits_calculus.title: Introduction to limits in calculus
idea_intro_limits_calculus.one_liner: Calculus, developed by Newton and Leibniz, provided the understanding of instantaneous rates of change, with the concept of a "limit" serving as its fundamental building block.
idea_intro_limits_calculus.content: The development of calculus in the seventeenth century by Newton and Leibniz gave scientists their first true understanding of "instantaneous rate of change," including concepts like velocity and acceleration. Once this idea was conceptually grasped, efficient computational methods emerged, leading to a significant advancement in science. The fundamental building block for understanding rates of change is the concept of a "limit," an idea so crucial that all other calculus concepts are now based upon it.
idea_intro_limits_calculus.motivation_md: Calculus was developed to understand instantaneous rates of change, a concept previously elusive. The "limit" provides the foundational mathematical tool to precisely define and compute these rates, enabling breakthroughs in physics and engineering. It's the core idea that underpins the entire subject.
idea_intro_limits_calculus.recap_md: - Calculus, by Newton and Leibniz, explained instantaneous rates of change. - The concept of a "limit" is the fundamental building block of calculus. - All other calculus concepts are based on limits.

idea_intuitive_approach_limits.title: Intuitive approach to limits
idea_intuitive_approach_limits.one_liner: The concept of a "limit" is the fundamental building block of calculus, and this section aims to develop an intuitive feel for its basic ideas informally.
idea_intuitive_approach_limits.content: The concept of a "limit" serves as the fundamental building block for all calculus concepts. This section will explore limits informally, aiming to develop an intuitive understanding of the basic ideas. Subsequent sections will then focus on computational methods and precise definitions.
idea_intuitive_approach_limits.motivation_md: Before diving into rigorous definitions and computations, it's crucial to build an intuitive understanding of what a limit represents. This informal approach helps learners grasp the core idea, making the formal definitions and methods more accessible and meaningful later on.
idea_intuitive_approach_limits.recap_md: - Limits are the fundamental building block of calculus. - This section focuses on an informal, intuitive understanding of limits. - Formal definitions and computational methods will be covered later.

idea_geometric_origins_calculus.title: Geometric origins of calculus: Tangent Line and Area Problems
idea_geometric_origins_calculus.one_liner: Many calculus ideas originated from two geometric problems: finding the tangent line to a graph at a point, and calculating the area between a function's graph and the x-axis.
idea_geometric_origins_calculus.content: Many core ideas of calculus originated from two fundamental geometric problems:THE TANGENT LINE PROBLEM: Given a function $f$ and a point $P\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ on its graph, the goal is to find an equation for the line that is tangent to the graph at point $P$ (Figure 1.1.1).THE AREA PROBLEM: Given a function $f$, the objective is to find the area located between the graph of $f$ and an interval $[a, b]$ on the $x$-axis (Figure 1.1.2).
idea_geometric_origins_calculus.motivation_md: These two geometric problems, the tangent line and area problems, were historically significant challenges that calculus was developed to solve. They provide concrete, visual contexts for understanding the core concepts of differentiation (tangent lines) and integration (areas), which are central to calculus.
idea_geometric_origins_calculus.recap_md: - Calculus ideas originated from the Tangent Line Problem and the Area Problem. - The Tangent Line Problem involves finding the line tangent to a graph at a point. - The Area Problem involves finding the area under a function's graph over an interval.

idea_limitations_tangent_definition.title: Limitations of traditional tangent line definition
idea_limitations_tangent_definition.one_liner: The traditional definition of a tangent line for circles, meeting at one point, is insufficient for general curves as it can misidentify non-tangent lines or exclude true tangents.
idea_limitations_tangent_definition.content: In plane geometry, a line is defined as tangent to a circle if it intersects the circle at precisely one point (Figure 1.1.3a). However, this definition, while suitable for circles, is not appropriate for more general curves. For instance, in Figure 1.1.3b, a line meets the curve only once but is clearly not what would be considered a tangent line. Conversely, in Figure 1.1.3c, a line appears tangent to the curve, yet it intersects the curve more than once.
idea_limitations_tangent_definition.motivation_md: The traditional definition of a tangent line, based on a single point of intersection, works only for circles. To extend the concept of tangency to more complex curves, a more robust and general definition is needed. This highlights the necessity for a calculus-based approach using limits.
idea_limitations_tangent_definition.recap_md: - The geometric definition of a tangent line for circles requires it to meet at exactly one point. - This definition fails for general curves, as a line can intersect once without being tangent. - It also fails if a tangent line intersects a general curve at more than one point.

definition_tangent_line_secant_limit.title: Tangent line as a limit of secant lines
definition_tangent_line_secant_limit.one_liner: A tangent line to a curve at point $P$ is defined as the limiting position of secant lines formed by $P$ and another point $Q$ as $Q$ approaches $P$ along the curve.
definition_tangent_line_secant_limit.content: To define a tangent line applicable to curves beyond circles, a different perspective is needed. Consider a point $P$ on a curve in the $xy$-plane where we want to find the tangent line. Let $Q$ be any other point on the curve, distinct from $P$. The line passing through both $P$ and $Q$ is known as a secant line for the curve at $P$. Intuitively, as point $Q$ moves along the curve closer and closer to $P$, the secant line will rotate and approach a specific limiting position. This line, in its limiting position, is defined as the tangent line at $P$ (Figure 1.1.4a). This new definition of a tangent line aligns with the traditional definition when applied to circles, as shown in Figure 1.1.4b.
definition_tangent_line_secant_limit.motivation_md: The limitations of the traditional tangent definition for general curves necessitate a more robust approach. By defining the tangent line as the limit of secant lines, we can precisely capture the "direction" of the curve at a single point, which is crucial for understanding instantaneous rates of change and local behavior.
definition_tangent_line_secant_limit.recap_md: - A secant line passes through two points, $P$ and $Q$, on a curve. - As point $Q$ approaches point $P$ along the curve, the secant line rotates. - The limiting position of this secant line defines the tangent line at $P$.

idea_area_as_limit_approximations.title: Area as a limit of approximations
idea_area_as_limit_approximations.one_liner: The area of regions with curved boundaries can be defined as the limiting value of approximations made by summing the areas of an increasing number of inscribed rectangles.
idea_area_as_limit_approximations.content: Similar to how the general concept of a tangent line leads to the idea of a limit, so does the general concept of area. For plane regions bounded by straight lines, areas can often be computed by dividing the region into rectangles or triangles and summing their individual areas (Figure 1.1.6). However, for regions with curved boundaries, like the one shown in Figure 1.1.7a, a more general method is required. One such method involves approximating the region's area by inscribing several rectangles of equal width under the curve and adding their areas (Figure 1.1.7b). Intuition suggests that if this approximation process is repeated with an increasing number of rectangles, they will progressively fill the gaps beneath the curve, causing the approximations to converge closer and closer to the exact area under the curve (Figure 1.1.7c). This implies that the area under the curve can be defined as the limiting value of these approximations. While this idea will be explored in detail later, it highlights another instance where the concept of a limit is essential.
idea_area_as_limit_approximations.motivation_md: Calculating areas of irregular shapes with curved boundaries is a complex problem that traditional geometry cannot solve directly. By using limits, we can approximate these areas with simpler shapes (rectangles) and then refine the approximation indefinitely, providing a precise definition for the area under a curve. This forms the basis of integral calculus.
idea_area_as_limit_approximations.recap_md: - Areas of regions with curved boundaries require a general approach. - Approximating area with more and more inscribed rectangles improves accuracy. - The exact area under a curve is defined as the limiting value of these approximations.

idea_decimals_as_limits.title: Decimals as limits of finite sums
idea_decimals_as_limits.one_liner: Decimal expansions, like that of $\frac{1}{3}$, represent limits of finite sums, where adding more terms brings the sum closer to the exact value.
idea_decimals_as_limits.content: Limits also appear in the familiar context of decimals. For instance, the decimal expansion of the fraction $\frac{1}{3}$ is given by:$$ \frac{1}{3}=0.33333 \ldots \tag{3} $$Here, the dots signify that the digit 3 repeats indefinitely. While perhaps not typically considered this way, equation (3) can be expressed as:$$ \frac{1}{3}=0.33333 \ldots=0.3+0.03+0.003+0.0003+0.00003+\cdots \tag{4} $$This is a sum containing "infinitely many" terms. As will be discussed further later, equation (4) is interpreted to mean that the sequence of finite sums:$$ 0.3, \quad 0.3+0.03, \quad 0.3+0.03+0.003, \quad 0.3+0.03+0.003+0.0003, \ldots $$approaches a limiting value of $\frac{1}{3}$ as more terms are progressively included. Therefore, limits are present even in the common context of decimal representations of real numbers.
idea_decimals_as_limits.motivation_md: This concept demonstrates that limits are not just abstract calculus ideas but are embedded in familiar mathematical concepts like decimal representations. Understanding decimals as limits of finite sums provides a concrete, accessible example of an infinite process converging to a finite value, reinforcing the intuitive understanding of limits.
idea_decimals_as_limits.recap_md: - Decimal expansions, such as $0.333\ldots$, can be written as infinite sums. - These infinite sums are interpreted as the limit of a sequence of finite sums. - As more terms are added, the finite sums approach the exact decimal value.

definition_limits_informal_view.title: Limits (An Informal View)
definition_limits_informal_view.one_liner: If $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $L$ by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but not equal to $a$), then $L$ is the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$.
definition_limits_informal_view.content: If the values of $f(x)$ can be made as close as we like to $L$ by taking values of $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but not equal to $a$), then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$. This is read as "the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ is $L$" or "$f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$." This expression can also be written as $f(x) \rightarrow L \quad \text { as } \quad x \rightarrow a$.
definition_limits_informal_view.motivation_md: The concept of a limit is fundamental to calculus, allowing us to analyze the behavior of functions near specific points, even if the function is undefined at that exact point. It forms the basis for understanding continuity, derivatives, and integrals.
definition_limits_informal_view.recap_md: - An informal limit describes $f(x)$ getting arbitrarily close to $L$ as $x$ gets arbitrarily close to $a$ (but $x \neq a$).- The notation for a limit is $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ or $f(x) \rightarrow L \quad \text { as } \quad x \rightarrow a$.

idea_sampling_pitfalls_limits.title: Sampling pitfalls in numerical limit estimation
idea_sampling_pitfalls_limits.one_liner: Numerical evidence can lead to incorrect limit conclusions due to roundoff error or unrepresentative sample values, highlighting the need for alternative corroboration methods.
idea_sampling_pitfalls_limits.content: Numerical evidence can sometimes lead to incorrect conclusions about limits because of roundoff error or because the sample values chosen do not reveal the true limiting behavior. For example, one might incorrectly conclude that $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{x}\right)=0$. The fact that this is not correct is evidenced by the graph of $f$ in Figure 1.1.11. The graph reveals that the values of $f$ oscillate between -1 and 1 with increasing rapidity as $x \rightarrow 0$ and hence do not approach a limit. The data in the table deceived us because the $x$-values selected all happened to be $x$-intercepts for $f(x)$. This points out the need for having alternative methods for corroborating limits conjectured from numerical evidence.
idea_sampling_pitfalls_limits.motivation_md: To prevent misinterpretations when estimating limits, it's crucial to understand that numerical sampling alone can be misleading, necessitating more robust analytical techniques to confirm true limiting behavior.
idea_sampling_pitfalls_limits.recap_md: - Numerical sampling can yield incorrect limit conclusions due to roundoff errors or biased sample points.- For example, sampling $x$-intercepts can falsely suggest a limit of zero for an oscillating function.- Always corroborate numerical limit conjectures with alternative methods.

definition_one_sided_limits_informal_vie.title: One-Sided Limits (An Informal View)
definition_one_sided_limits_informal_vie.one_liner: One-sided limits describe the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from either the right ($x>a$) or the left ($x<a$) independently.
definition_one_sided_limits_informal_vie.content: If the values of $f(x)$ can be made as close as we like to $L$ by taking values of $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but greater than $a$), then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$. If the values of $f(x)$ can be made as close as we like to $L$ by taking values of $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but less than $a$), then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$. The expression $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$ is read "the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right is $L$" or "$f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right." Similarly, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$ is read "the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left is $L$" or "$f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left."
definition_one_sided_limits_informal_vie.motivation_md: One-sided limits are essential for analyzing function behavior at points where a two-sided limit might not exist, such as at discontinuities or endpoints of domains, by considering approach from only one direction.
definition_one_sided_limits_informal_vie.recap_md: - A right-hand limit, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$, means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from values greater than $a$.- A left-hand limit, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$, means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from values less than $a$.

idea_when_limits_do_not_exist.title: When limits do not exist
idea_when_limits_do_not_exist.one_liner: A limit does not exist if the function's values do not approach a single real number $L$ as $x$ approaches a point, whether from both sides or from a single side.
idea_when_limits_do_not_exist.content: In general, there is no guarantee that a function $f$ will have a two-sided limit at a given point $a$; that is, the values of $f(x)$ may not get closer and closer to any single real number $L$ as $x \rightarrow a$. In this case we say that $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x) \text { does not exist }$. Similarly, the values of $f(x)$ may not get closer and closer to a single real number $L$ as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$or as $x \rightarrow a^{-}$. In these cases we say that $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x) \text { does not exist }$ or that $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x) \text { does not exist }$.
idea_when_limits_do_not_exist.motivation_md: Understanding when limits do not exist is crucial for identifying points of discontinuity, vertical asymptotes, or oscillatory behavior where a function's behavior is not well-defined by a single limiting value.
idea_when_limits_do_not_exist.recap_md: - A two-sided limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ does not exist if $f(x)$ does not approach a single real number $L$ as $x \rightarrow a$.- One-sided limits $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)$ do not exist if $f(x)$ does not approach a single real number $L$ from that specific direction.

theorem_relationship_one_two_sided_limit.title: Relationship between One-Sided and Two-Sided Limits
theorem_relationship_one_two_sided_limit.one_liner: A two-sided limit exists at a point if and only if both one-sided limits exist at that point and are equal to the same value.
theorem_relationship_one_two_sided_limit.content: The two-sided limit of a function $f(x)$ exists at $a$ if and only if both of the one-sided limits exist at $a$ and have the same value; that is, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L \quad \text { if and only if } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$.
theorem_relationship_one_two_sided_limit.motivation_md: This theorem provides a fundamental criterion for determining the existence of a two-sided limit, allowing us to break down a complex limit problem into two simpler one-sided limit problems, which can be easier to evaluate.
theorem_relationship_one_two_sided_limit.recap_md: - For $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ to exist, $f(x)$ must approach the same value $L$ from both the left and the right.- This means $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$ must both be true for the two-sided limit to be $L$.

infinite_limits_informal_view.title: Infinite Limits (An Informal View)
infinite_limits_informal_view.one_liner: Infinite limits describe situations where $f(x)$ increases or decreases without bound as $x$ approaches a point $a$ from the left, right, or both sides.
infinite_limits_informal_view.content: The expressions $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$ denote that $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively. If both are true, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$. Similarly, the expressions $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty$ denote that $f(x)$ decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively. If both are true, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$.
infinite_limits_informal_view.motivation_md: Infinite limits help describe the behavior of functions that grow or shrink without bound near certain points, which is crucial for identifying vertical asymptotes and understanding function behavior at discontinuities.
infinite_limits_informal_view.recap_md: - $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$ means $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both sides.- $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$ means $f(x)$ decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both sides.- One-sided infinite limits describe this unbounded behavior from either the left ($x \rightarrow a^{-}$) or the right ($x \rightarrow a^{+}$).

vertical_asymptotes_definition.title: Vertical Asymptotes
vertical_asymptotes_definition.one_liner: A vertical asymptote is a vertical line $x=a$ that a function's graph approaches as $f(x)$ rises or falls without bound when $x$ approaches $a$.
vertical_asymptotes_definition.content: Figure 1.1.17 illustrates geometrically what happens when any of the following situations occur: $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty$. In each case the graph of $y=f(x)$ either rises or falls without bound, squeezing closer and closer to the vertical line $x=a$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the side indicated in the limit. The line $x=a$ is called a vertical asymptote of the curve $y=f(x)$ (from the Greek word asymptotos, meaning "nonintersecting").
vertical_asymptotes_definition.motivation_md: Vertical asymptotes help characterize the behavior of functions where they become unbounded, providing critical information about the function's domain, range, and graphical features, especially in rational functions.
vertical_asymptotes_definition.recap_md: - A vertical asymptote at $x=a$ occurs when $f(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from either side.- The graph of $y=f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to the vertical line $x=a$ but never touches or crosses it.

technique_computing_limits.title: Techniques for Computing Limits
technique_computing_limits.one_liner: This section introduces various techniques for computing limits of functions, building upon the informal limit concept previously discussed.
technique_computing_limits.content: In this section we will discuss techniques for computing limits of many functions. We base these results on the informal development of the limit concept discussed in the preceding section. A more formal derivation of these results is possible after Section 1.4.
technique_computing_limits.motivation_md: While informal definitions and numerical estimations provide intuition, formal techniques are necessary to accurately and reliably compute limits for a wide range of functions, ensuring precision in calculus and preparing for more advanced topics.
technique_computing_limits.recap_md: - This section focuses on practical methods for calculating limits.- The techniques build upon the intuitive understanding of limits established earlier.- More rigorous proofs for these techniques will be covered in later sections.

idea_instantaneous_velocity_intro.title: Introduction to Instantaneous Velocity

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_instantaneous_velocity_intro.one_liner: Instantaneous velocity describes a particle's behavior at a specific instant, found by taking the limit of average velocities over increasingly small time intervals.
idea_instantaneous_velocity_intro.content: For a particle in rectilinear motion, average velocity describes its behavior over an interval of time. However, we are interested in the particle's "instantaneous velocity," which describes its behavior at a specific instant in time. Formula (4) is not directly applicable for computing instantaneous velocity because the "time elapsed" at a specific instant is zero, making (4) undefined. To circumvent this problem, we compute average velocities for small time intervals between $t=t_{0}$ and $t=t_{0}+h$. These average velocities can be viewed as approximations to the instantaneous velocity of the particle at time $t_{0}$. If these average velocities have a limit as $h$ approaches zero, that limit can be taken as the instantaneous velocity of the particle at time $t_{0}$.
idea_instantaneous_velocity_intro.motivation_md: Average velocity is insufficient for precise analysis at a single moment. We need a method to describe motion *at* an instant, not *over* an interval, which leads to the concept of instantaneous velocity. This requires a way to handle division by zero when the time interval shrinks to nothing.
idea_instantaneous_velocity_intro.recap_md: - Instantaneous velocity describes motion at a specific moment, unlike average velocity over an interval. - Direct calculation using $\Delta t = 0$ is undefined. - It is approximated by average velocities over small intervals, then found by taking the limit as the interval approaches zero.

idea_velocity_geometric_interpretation.title: Geometric interpretation of velocity

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_velocity_geometric_interpretation.one_liner: Geometrically, average velocity is the slope of a secant line on a position-time curve, while instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent line at a specific point.
idea_velocity_geometric_interpretation.content: Geometrically, the average velocity $v_{\text {ave }}$ between $t=t_{0}$ and $t=t_{0}+h$ is the slope of the secant line passing through points $P\left(t_{0}, f\left(t_{0}\right)\right)$ and $Q\left(t_{0}+h, f\left(t_{0}+h\right)\right)$ on the position versus time curve. The instantaneous velocity $v_{\text {inst }}$ at time $t_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line to the position versus time curve at the point $P\left(t_{0}, f\left(t_{0}\right)\right)$ (Figure 2.1.7).
idea_velocity_geometric_interpretation.motivation_md: Visualizing velocity concepts on a graph helps build intuition. By connecting average and instantaneous velocity to secant and tangent lines, respectively, we can better understand their relationship and how instantaneous velocity emerges from the limit of average velocities.
idea_velocity_geometric_interpretation.recap_md: - Average velocity corresponds to the slope of a secant line on a position-time graph. - Instantaneous velocity corresponds to the slope of the tangent line at a specific point on the position-time graph.

idea_slopes_rates_of_change.title: Slopes and Rates of Change

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_slopes_rates_of_change.one_liner: Velocity is a rate of change, and this concept extends to various applications where the slope of a linear function $y=mx+b$ naturally measures the constant rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$.
idea_slopes_rates_of_change.content: Velocity can be viewed as a rate of change, specifically the rate of change of position with respect to time. Rates of change are fundamental and occur in many other applications. For example: A microbiologist might study the rate at which the number of bacteria in a colony changes with time. An engineer might be interested in the rate at which the length of a metal rod changes with temperature. An economist might examine the rate at which production cost changes with the quantity of a product manufactured. A medical researcher might investigate the rate at which the radius of an artery changes with the concentration of alcohol in the bloodstream. Our next objective is to precisely define the "rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$" when $y$ is a function of $x$. For a linear function $y=mx+b$, the slope $m$ is the natural measure of this rate of change. As Figure 2.1.8 illustrates, a 1-unit increase in $x$ anywhere along the line produces an $m$-unit change in $y$, indicating that $y$ changes at a constant rate with respect to $x$, and $m$ quantifies this rate.
idea_slopes_rates_of_change.motivation_md: The concept of rate of change is not exclusive to physics; it's a universal idea in many fields. Understanding how slopes of lines represent constant rates of change provides a foundational step towards defining rates of change for more complex, non-linear functions.
idea_slopes_rates_of_change.recap_md: - Velocity is a specific example of a rate of change (position with respect to time). - Rates of change are crucial in diverse fields like biology, engineering, economics, and medicine. - For linear functions $y=mx+b$, the slope $m$ represents the constant rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$.

idea_units_rates_of_change.title: Units and rates of change

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_units_rates_of_change.one_liner: In applied problems, units of measurement are essential when calculating slopes and describing rates of change, as changing units can alter the slope.
idea_units_rates_of_change.content: In applied problems, changing the units of measurement can change the slope of a line. Therefore, it is essential to include the units when calculating the slope and describing rates of change. The following example illustrates this.
idea_units_rates_of_change.motivation_md: Understanding the impact of units on rates of change is crucial for accurate and meaningful interpretation of real-world problems. It emphasizes the practical importance of dimensional analysis in calculus applications.
idea_units_rates_of_change.recap_md: - Units of measurement affect the numerical value of a slope. - Always include units when calculating and describing rates of change.

idea_avg_inst_rate_of_change_general.title: Average vs. instantaneous rate of change for general curves

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_avg_inst_rate_of_change_general.one_liner: Unlike linear functions, the rate of change for a general curve $y=f(x)$ is not constant, requiring a distinction between average and instantaneous rates of change.
idea_avg_inst_rate_of_change_general.content: While the rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ is constant along a nonvertical line $y=mx+b$, this is not true for a general curve $y=f(x)$. For instance, as shown in Figure 2.1.10, the change in $y$ resulting from a 1-unit increase in $x$ tends to have a greater magnitude in regions where the curve rises or falls rapidly compared to regions where it rises or falls slowly. Similar to how we treated velocity, we will distinguish between the average rate of change over an interval and the instantaneous rate of change at a specific point for general curves.
idea_avg_inst_rate_of_change_general.motivation_md: Linear functions provide a simple model for constant rates of change, but most real-world phenomena are non-linear. This concept introduces the necessity of extending the idea of rate of change to curves, leading to the distinction between average and instantaneous rates, which is fundamental to calculus.
idea_avg_inst_rate_of_change_general.recap_md: - The rate of change is constant for linear functions but varies for general curves $y=f(x)$. - For curves, the change in $y$ for a 1-unit change in $x$ depends on the steepness of the curve. - We differentiate between average rate of change over an interval and instantaneous rate of change at a point.

def_average_rate_of_change.title: Definition of Average Rate of Change

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

def_average_rate_of_change.one_liner: The average rate of change of $y=f(x)$ over an interval $[x_0, x_1]$ is defined as the ratio of the change in $y$ to the change in $x$.
def_average_rate_of_change.content: If $y=f(x)$, then we define the average rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ over the interval $\left[x_{0}, x_{1}\right]$ to be $$ r_{\mathrm{ave}}=\frac{f\left(x_{1}\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x_{1}-x_{0}} \tag{8} $$
def_average_rate_of_change.motivation_md: This definition formalizes the intuitive idea of how much a function's output changes relative to its input over a given range. It provides a measurable quantity for comparing changes across different intervals and serves as a foundation for understanding instantaneous rates of change.
def_average_rate_of_change.recap_md: - The average rate of change measures how much $y$ changes per unit change in $x$ over an interval. - It is calculated as the difference in function values divided by the difference in input values: $r_{\mathrm{ave}}=\frac{f\left(x_{1}\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$.

def_instantaneous_rate_of_change.title: Definition of Instantaneous Rate of Change

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

def_instantaneous_rate_of_change.one_liner: The instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ at a specific point $x_0$ is defined as the limit of the average rate of change as $x_1$ approaches $x_0$.
def_instantaneous_rate_of_change.content: We define the instantaneous rate of change of $\boldsymbol{y}$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{x}$ at $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{0}}$ to be $$ r_{\mathrm{inst}}=\lim _{x_{1} \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f\left(x_{1}\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x_{1}-x_{0}} \tag{9} $$
def_instantaneous_rate_of_change.motivation_md: This definition provides a precise mathematical way to quantify how a function changes at a single point, overcoming the limitations of average rates of change over intervals. It is a cornerstone of differential calculus, enabling the study of slopes of tangent lines and velocities at specific moments.
def_instantaneous_rate_of_change.recap_md: - The instantaneous rate of change describes how $y$ changes with respect to $x$ at a single point $x_0$. - It is defined as the limit of the average rate of change as the interval shrinks to $x_0$: $r_{\mathrm{inst}}=\lim _{x_{1} \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f\left(x_{1}\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$.

idea_rates_of_change_geometric_interpret.title: Geometric interpretation of rates of change

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_rates_of_change_geometric_interpret.one_liner: Geometrically, the average rate of change is the slope of a secant line, while the instantaneous rate of change is the slope of the tangent line, which is the limit of secant slopes.
idea_rates_of_change_geometric_interpret.content: Geometrically, the average rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ over the interval $\left[x_{0}, x_{1}\right]$ is the slope of the secant line passing through the points $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ and $Q\left(x_{1}, f\left(x_{1}\right)\right)$ (Figure 2.1.11). The instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ at $x_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line at the point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$, as it is the limit of the slopes of the secant lines through $P$.
idea_rates_of_change_geometric_interpret.motivation_md: Visualizing rates of change as slopes of lines on a graph provides a powerful intuitive understanding. Connecting average rate to secant lines and instantaneous rate to tangent lines helps solidify the concept of the derivative as a geometric property.
idea_rates_of_change_geometric_interpret.recap_md: - Average rate of change corresponds to the slope of the secant line connecting two points on a curve. - Instantaneous rate of change corresponds to the slope of the tangent line at a single point on the curve. - The tangent line's slope is the limit of the secant line slopes as the two points converge.

def_increment.title: Increment
def_increment.one_liner: An increment in a variable $w$, denoted by $\Delta w$, is the change from an initial value $w_0$ to a final value $w_1$, calculated as $w_1 - w_0$.
def_increment.content: If a variable $w$ changes from an initial value $w_0$ to a final value $w_1$, the difference $w_1 - w_0$ is called an increment in $w$ and is denoted by $\Delta w$. $$\Delta w=w_{1}-w_{0} \tag{8}$$ Increments can be positive or negative, depending on whether the final value is larger or smaller than the initial value. The symbol $\Delta w$ should not be interpreted as a product, but rather as a single symbol representing the change in the value of $w$.
def_increment.motivation_md: Increments provide a fundamental way to quantify change in a variable. This concept is crucial for understanding rates of change, slopes of secant lines, and ultimately, the definition of the derivative, where changes in variables approach zero.
def_increment.recap_md: - An increment $\Delta w$ represents the change in a variable $w$ from an initial value $w_0$ to a final value $w_1$. - It is calculated as $\Delta w = w_1 - w_0$. - $\Delta w$ is a single symbol, not a product, and can be positive or negative.

idea_derivative_in_terms_of_delta_x.title: Derivative in terms of Δx
idea_derivative_in_terms_of_delta_x.one_liner: The variable $h$ in the derivative formula is commonly regarded as an increment $\Delta x$ in $x$, leading to an alternative notation for the derivative.
idea_derivative_in_terms_of_delta_x.content: It is common to regard the variable $h$ in the derivative formula as an increment $\Delta x$ in $x$. The standard derivative formula: $$f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \tag{9}$$ can therefore be written using $\Delta x$ as: $$f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x} \tag{10}$$
idea_derivative_in_terms_of_delta_x.motivation_md: This alternative notation for the derivative emphasizes that the limit involves a 'change in x' approaching zero. It connects the derivative directly to the concept of increments, making the relationship between instantaneous rate of change and average rate of change more explicit.
idea_derivative_in_terms_of_delta_x.recap_md: - The variable $h$ in the derivative definition can be replaced by $\Delta x$. - This emphasizes that $h$ represents an increment in $x$. - The derivative can be written as $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x}$.

idea_derivative_notations_other_variable.title: Derivative Notations with Other Variables
idea_derivative_notations_other_variable.one_liner: Derivative notations must be adjusted when variables other than $x$ and $y$ are used, such as expressing velocity $v(t)$ as $\frac{ds}{dt}$ for a position function $s=f(t)$.
idea_derivative_notations_other_variable.content: When letters other than $x$ and $y$ are used for the independent and dependent variables, the derivative notations must be adjusted accordingly. For example, if $s=f(t)$ is the position function for a particle in rectilinear motion, then the velocity function $v(t)$ can be expressed as: $$v(t)=\frac{d s}{d t}=\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}=\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(t+\Delta t)-f(t)}{\Delta t} \tag{14}$$
idea_derivative_notations_other_variable.motivation_md: Understanding how to adapt derivative notation to different variables is essential for applying calculus to various real-world problems, especially in physics and engineering, where variables like time ($t$), position ($s$), and velocity ($v$) are common.
idea_derivative_notations_other_variable.recap_md: - Derivative notation changes to match the independent and dependent variables used. - For a function $s=f(t)$, the derivative is $\frac{ds}{dt}$. - This notation is common in physics, where $s$ is position and $t$ is time.

intro_to_techniques_of_differentiation.title: Introduction to Techniques of Differentiation
intro_to_techniques_of_differentiation.one_liner: This section introduces important theorems to calculate derivatives more efficiently, moving beyond the limit definition used previously.
intro_to_techniques_of_differentiation.content: In the previous section, the derivative of a function $f$ was defined as a limit, and that limit was used to calculate a few simple derivatives. This section will develop some important theorems that will enable us to calculate derivatives more efficiently.
intro_to_techniques_of_differentiation.motivation_md: Calculating derivatives directly from the limit definition can be tedious and time-consuming. This concept introduces a set of rules and theorems that streamline the differentiation process, making it much faster and more practical for complex functions.
intro_to_techniques_of_differentiation.recap_md: - The derivative was previously defined using limits. - This section focuses on developing theorems for more efficient derivative calculation. - These techniques simplify the process of finding derivatives.

thm_2_3_1_derivative_of_constant_functio.title: Theorem 2.3.1: Derivative of a Constant Function
thm_2_3_1_derivative_of_constant_functio.one_liner: Theorem 2.3.1 states that the derivative of any constant function is 0, meaning $\frac{d}{dx}[c]=0$ for any real number $c$.
thm_2_3_1_derivative_of_constant_functio.content: Theorem 2.3.1 states that the derivative of a constant function is 0. This means that if $c$ is any real number, then: $$\frac{d}{d x}[c]=0 \tag{1}$$
thm_2_3_1_derivative_of_constant_functio.motivation_md: This theorem provides the simplest differentiation rule, reflecting that a constant function has no change, and thus its instantaneous rate of change (derivative) is zero. It's a foundational rule for differentiating more complex functions.
thm_2_3_1_derivative_of_constant_functio.recap_md: - The derivative of any constant function is 0. - If $f(x) = c$, where $c$ is a real number, then $f'(x) = 0$. - This is expressed as $\frac{d}{dx}[c]=0$.

derivatives_of_power_functions.title: Derivatives of Power Functions
derivatives_of_power_functions.one_liner: This concept introduces the derivatives of simple power functions like $f(x)=x$, $f(x)=x^2$, and $f(x)=x^3$, showing a pattern for their derivatives.
derivatives_of_power_functions.content: The simplest power function is $f(x)=x$. Since its graph is a line with a slope of 1, its derivative is $f^{\prime}(x)=1$ for all $x$. This can be written as: $$\frac{d}{d x}[x]=1 \tag{2}$$ Previous examples show that the power function $f(x)=x^{2}$ has derivative $f^{\prime}(x)= 2 x$, and $f(x)=x^{3}$ has derivative $f^{\prime}(x)=3 x^{2}$. These are expressed as: $$\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{2}\right]=2 x \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{3}\right]=3 x^{2} \tag{3-4}$$
derivatives_of_power_functions.motivation_md: Understanding the derivatives of basic power functions is crucial because many polynomial and rational functions are built from these fundamental forms. Recognizing the pattern in these derivatives leads directly to the general Power Rule, a cornerstone of differentiation.
derivatives_of_power_functions.recap_md: - The derivative of $f(x)=x$ is $f'(x)=1$. - The derivative of $f(x)=x^2$ is $f'(x)=2x$. - The derivative of $f(x)=x^3$ is $f'(x)=3x^2$.

thm_2_3_2_the_power_rule.title: Theorem 2.3.2: The Power Rule (positive integer exponents)
thm_2_3_2_the_power_rule.one_liner: Theorem 2.3.2, known as The Power Rule, states that if $n$ is a positive integer, the derivative of $x^n$ is $nx^{n-1}$.
thm_2_3_2_the_power_rule.content: Theorem 2.3.2, known as The Power Rule, states that if $n$ is a positive integer, then: $$\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{n}\right]=n x^{n-1} \tag{5}$$ The proof involves using the definition of a derivative and the binomial formula for expanding $(x+h)^n$: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{n}\right] & =f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(x+h)^{n}-x^{n}}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\left[x^{n}+n x^{n-1} h+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{n-2} h^{2}+\cdots+n x h^{n-1}+h^{n}\right]-x^{n}}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{n x^{n-1} h+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{n-2} h^{2}+\cdots+n x h^{n-1}+h^{n}}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left[n x^{n-1}+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!} x^{n-2} h+\cdots+n x h^{n-2}+h^{n-1}\right] \\ & =n x^{n-1}+0+\cdots+0+0 \\ & =n x^{n-1} \end{aligned}$$
thm_2_3_2_the_power_rule.motivation_md: The Power Rule is one of the most fundamental and frequently used differentiation rules. It provides a direct and efficient method for finding the derivative of any power function $x^n$, significantly simplifying calculations compared to using the limit definition.
thm_2_3_2_the_power_rule.recap_md: - The Power Rule applies to functions of the form $x^n$ where $n$ is a positive integer. - The derivative of $x^n$ is $nx^{n-1}$. - This rule is derived using the limit definition of the derivative and the binomial theorem.

thm_2_3_3_extended_power_rule.title: Theorem 2.3.3: Extended Power Rule (any real exponent)
aliases: Derivative of Real Powers of x (Power Rule)
thm_2_3_3_extended_power_rule.one_liner: Theorem 2.3.3, the Extended Power Rule, generalizes the Power Rule to include any real number $r$ as an exponent, stating $\frac{d}{dx}[x^r] = rx^{r-1}$.
thm_2_3_3_extended_power_rule.content: Theorem 2.3.3, known as the Extended Power Rule, states that if $r$ is any real number, then: $$\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{r}\right]=r x^{r-1} \tag{7}$$
thm_2_3_3_extended_power_rule.motivation_md: The Extended Power Rule significantly broadens the applicability of the Power Rule, allowing differentiation of functions with fractional or negative exponents, such as square roots or terms in denominators. This makes it a versatile tool for a much wider range of algebraic functions.
thm_2_3_3_extended_power_rule.recap_md: - The Extended Power Rule applies to $x^r$ where $r$ is any real number. - The derivative of $x^r$ is $rx^{r-1}$. - This rule generalizes the Power Rule for positive integer exponents.

def_osculating_circle.title: Osculating Circle

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

def_osculating_circle.one_liner: The osculating circle to a curve $y=f(x)$ at $(0, f(0))$ is defined as the unique circle through $(0, f(0))$ with center $(0, L)$, provided $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} C(x)=L \neq f(0)$ exists.
def_osculating_circle.content: If $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} C(x)=L \neq f(0)$, then the osculating circle to the curve $y=f(x)$ at $(0, f(0))$ is defined as the unique circle passing through $(0, f(0))$ with its center at $(0, L)$. If $C(x)$ does not have a finite limit different from $f(0)$ as $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$, then the curve is said to have no osculating circle at $(0, f(0))$. (This definition assumes that $f(x) \neq f(0)$ for positive values of $x$ close to 0.)
def_osculating_circle.motivation_md: The osculating circle provides a way to approximate a curve's curvature at a specific point. It represents the circle that "best fits" the curve at that point, offering insights into how sharply the curve is bending. This concept is crucial in differential geometry for understanding local curve behavior.
def_osculating_circle.recap_md: - The osculating circle is a unique circle through a point $(0, f(0))$ on a curve $y=f(x)$.- Its center is $(0, L)$, where $L = \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} C(x)$ and $L \neq f(0)$.- If this limit does not exist or equals $f(0)$, the curve has no osculating circle at that point.

idea_chapter_2_intro_derivative.title: Introduction to The Derivative
idea_chapter_2_intro_derivative.one_liner: Calculus excels at capturing continuous motion mathematically, enabling instant-by-instant analysis of changing quantities, which is addressed by the concept of the derivative.
idea_chapter_2_intro_derivative.content: One of calculus's crowning achievements is its ability to mathematically capture continuous motion, allowing for instant-by-instant analysis. Many real-world phenomena involve changing quantities, such as the speed of a rocket, currency inflation, the number of bacteria in a culture, earthquake shock intensity, or the voltage of an electrical signal. This chapter will develop the "derivative" concept, a mathematical tool for studying the rate at which one quantity changes relative to another. The study of rates of change is closely related to the geometric concept of a tangent line to a curve, so this chapter will also discuss the general definition of a tangent line and methods for finding its slope and equation.
idea_chapter_2_intro_derivative.motivation_md: This chapter introduces the derivative, a fundamental concept in calculus. It provides the mathematical framework to analyze how quantities change, enabling the study of motion and rates of change in diverse real-world scenarios, from physics to economics.
idea_chapter_2_intro_derivative.recap_md: - Calculus can analyze continuous motion and changing quantities instant by instant.- The derivative is the mathematical tool for studying rates of change between quantities.- Rates of change are geometrically linked to the tangent line to a curve.

idea_2_1_intro.title: Introduction to Tangent Lines and Rates of Change

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_2_1_intro.one_liner: This section will discuss tangent lines, velocity, and rates of change, aiming to show how these seemingly unrelated ideas are closely linked.
idea_2_1_intro.content: This section will discuss three key ideas: tangent lines to curves, the velocity of an object moving along a line, and the rate at which one variable changes relative to another. The goal is to demonstrate how these seemingly unrelated concepts are, in actuality, closely linked.
idea_2_1_intro.motivation_md: This introduction sets the stage for understanding the interconnectedness of fundamental calculus concepts. By linking tangent lines, velocity, and general rates of change, it prepares the learner to see the derivative as a unifying mathematical tool.
idea_2_1_intro.recap_md: - This section introduces tangent lines to curves.- It also covers the velocity of an object moving along a line.- The goal is to connect these ideas with the general rate of change of one variable relative to another.

idea_tangent_lines_intuitive.title: Intuitive approach to tangent lines

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_tangent_lines_intuitive.one_liner: This concept explains the intuitive approach to tangent lines, using the limit of the slope of a secant line as a second point approaches the point of tangency.
idea_tangent_lines_intuitive.content: Previously, in Example 1 of Section 1.1, the notion of a limit was used informally to find a tangent line's equation. Now that limits are precisely defined, we can provide a mathematical definition for the tangent line to a curve $y=f(x)$ at a point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$. Consider a point $Q(x, f(x))$ on the curve distinct from $P$, as illustrated in Figure 2.1.1. The slope $m_{P Q}$ of the secant line through $P$ and $Q$ is given by: $$ m_{P Q}=\frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}} $$ As $x$ approaches $x_{0}$, point $Q$ moves along the curve towards $P$. If the secant line through $P$ and $Q$ approaches a limiting position as $x \rightarrow x_{0}$, this position is considered the tangent line at $P$. Equivalently, if the slope $m_{P Q}$ of the secant line approaches a limit as $x \rightarrow x_{0}$, this limit is defined as the slope $m_{\tan }$ of the tangent line at $P$. This leads to the formal definition.
idea_tangent_lines_intuitive.motivation_md: This section bridges the gap between an informal understanding of tangent lines and a rigorous mathematical definition.
