By showing how the slope of a secant line approaches the slope of a tangent line via a limit, it lays the groundwork for the derivative, which is fundamentally defined by this limiting process.
idea_tangent_lines_intuitive.recap_md: - The tangent line's slope is found by considering a secant line through two points $P$ and $Q$.- The slope of the secant line is $m_{P Q}=\frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}}$.- As $Q$ approaches $P$ (i.e., $x \rightarrow x_{0}$), the limit of $m_{P Q}$ defines the slope of the tangent line $m_{\tan }$.

def_tangent_line.title: Definition of Tangent Line to a Curve

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

def_tangent_line.one_liner: The tangent line to a curve $y=f(x)$ at $P(x_0, f(x_0))$ is defined by the equation $y-f(x_0)=m_{\tan}(x-x_0)$, where $m_{\tan}$ is the limit of the difference quotient as $x \rightarrow x_0$.
def_tangent_line.content: DEFINITION 2.1.1: Suppose that $x_{0}$ is in the domain of the function $f$. The tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at the point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ is the line with the equation: $$ y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=m_{\tan }\left(x-x_{0}\right) $$ where the slope $m_{\tan }$ is given by: $$ m_{\tan }=\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}} \tag{1} $$ This definition holds provided the limit exists. For simplicity, this is also referred to as the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x_{0}$.
def_tangent_line.motivation_md: This formal definition provides a precise mathematical way to describe the instantaneous direction of a curve at a specific point. It is fundamental for understanding rates of change, optimization problems, and the local behavior of functions, forming the bedrock of differential calculus.
def_tangent_line.recap_md: - The tangent line at $P(x_0, f(x_0))$ has the equation $y-f(x_0)=m_{\tan}(x-x_0)$.- The slope $m_{\tan}$ is defined as $\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}}$.- This definition applies only if the limit for $m_{\tan}$ exists.

idea_tangent_slope_formula_h.title: Alternative formula for tangent slope

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_tangent_slope_formula_h.one_liner: An alternative formula for the tangent slope $m_{\tan}$ uses a difference $h=x-x_0$, rewriting the limit as $h \rightarrow 0$ to get $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$.
idea_tangent_slope_formula_h.content: An alternative and commonly used way to express Formula (1) exists. If we let $h$ represent the difference $h=x-x_{0}$, then the condition $x \rightarrow x_{0}$ becomes equivalent to $h \rightarrow 0$. This allows us to rewrite Formula (1) in terms of $x_{0}$ and $h$ as: $$ m_{\tan }=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h} \tag{2} $$ Both Formula (1) and Formula (2) for $m_{\tan }$ typically result in indeterminate forms of type $0/0$. Therefore, algebraic simplifications or other limit evaluation methods are generally required to determine these limits.
idea_tangent_slope_formula_h.motivation_md: This alternative formula for the tangent slope, often called the difference quotient, simplifies calculations and is particularly useful for algebraic manipulation when evaluating limits. It is a foundational expression in the definition of the derivative, making it easier to apply calculus concepts to various functions.
idea_tangent_slope_formula_h.recap_md: - The difference $h=x-x_0$ allows for an alternative expression of the tangent slope.- As $x \rightarrow x_0$, $h \rightarrow 0$.- The alternative formula for $m_{\tan}$ is $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$.- Both formulas often lead to $0/0$ indeterminate forms, requiring algebraic simplification.

idea_velocity_intro.title: Introduction to Velocity

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

idea_velocity_intro.one_liner: Calculus studies motion, and to describe an object's motion completely, one must specify both its speed and direction, which together define its velocity.
idea_velocity_intro.content: The study of motion is one of the important themes in calculus. To completely describe an object's motion, one must specify both its speed (how fast it is going) and its direction of movement. The combination of speed and direction of motion is what constitutes the object's velocity. For instance, knowing an aircraft's speed is 500 $\mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$ indicates its pace but not its path. Conversely, knowing the aircraft's velocity is 500 $\mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$ due south precisely defines both its speed and its direction of motion.
idea_velocity_intro.motivation_md: This introduction establishes velocity as a key concept in calculus, highlighting its importance in describing motion comprehensively. By distinguishing velocity from mere speed, it sets the stage for understanding how calculus provides tools to analyze instantaneous rates of change in physical contexts.
idea_velocity_intro.recap_md: - Calculus is used to study motion.- Complete description of motion requires both speed and direction.- Velocity is the combination of an object's speed and its direction of motion.

def_displacement.title: Displacement of a particle

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

def_displacement.one_liner: The change in position, $f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)$, is defined as the displacement of a particle over the time interval between $t_{0}$ and $t_{0}+h$.
def_displacement.content: The change in position, expressed as $$ f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right) $$ is also known as the displacement of the particle over the time interval between $t_{0}$ and $t_{0}+h$.
def_displacement.motivation_md: Displacement is a fundamental concept in kinematics, representing the net change in an object's position regardless of the path taken. It is crucial for understanding motion and serves as a building block for defining velocity and acceleration in calculus.
def_displacement.recap_md: - Displacement is the change in an object's position.- It is calculated as $f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)$ for a position function $f(t)$.- This represents the displacement over the time interval from $t_0$ to $t_0+h$.

theorem_derivative_of_cos_x.title: Derivative of Cosine Function
theorem_derivative_of_cos_x.one_liner: The derivative of the cosine function with respect to $x$ is given by $\frac{d}{d x}[\cos x]=-\sin x$.
theorem_derivative_of_cos_x.content: The derivative of the cosine function with respect to $x$ is given by the formula:$$ \begin{equation*} \frac{d}{d x}[\cos x]=-\sin x \tag{4} \end{equation*} $$
theorem_derivative_of_cos_x.motivation_md: Knowing the derivative of basic trigonometric functions like cosine is fundamental for differentiating more complex functions involving trigonometry, and for solving problems in physics and engineering.
theorem_derivative_of_cos_x.recap_md: - The derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$.

idea_substitution_order_in_derivatives.title: Importance of Substitution Order in Derivatives
idea_substitution_order_in_derivatives.one_liner: When evaluating a derivative at a specific point, it is crucial to substitute the value of $x$ *after* the differentiation process is complete.
idea_substitution_order_in_derivatives.content: When finding the value of a derivative at a specific point, such as $x=x_{0}$, it is important to substitute $x_{0}$ only after the derivative has been obtained. For instance, in Example 3, the substitution $x=\pi / 4$ was made after $f^{\prime \prime}$ was calculated. Consider what would happen if one were to incorrectly substitute $x=\pi / 4$ into $f^{\prime}(x)$ before calculating $f^{\prime \prime}$.
idea_substitution_order_in_derivatives.motivation_md: Understanding the correct order of operations when evaluating derivatives is essential to avoid common errors and ensure accurate results. Substituting too early can lead to incorrect derivatives, as constants differentiate to zero.
idea_substitution_order_in_derivatives.recap_md: - Substitute the specific point $x_0$ only after the derivative is fully calculated.

theorem_derivatives_of_other_trig_functi.title: Derivatives of Tangent, Secant, Cotangent, and Cosecant
theorem_derivatives_of_other_trig_functi.one_liner: This concept provides the derivative formulas for the tangent, secant, cotangent, and cosecant functions.
theorem_derivatives_of_other_trig_functi.content: The derivatives of the tangent, secant, cotangent, and cosecant functions are given by the following formulas:$$ \begin{align*} \frac{d}{d x}[\tan x] & =\sec ^{2} x & \frac{d}{d x}[\sec x] & =\sec x \tan x \tag{5-6}\\ \frac{d}{d x}[\cot x] & =-\csc ^{2} x & \frac{d}{d x}[\csc x] & =-\csc x \cot x \tag{7-8} \end{align*} $$
theorem_derivatives_of_other_trig_functi.motivation_md: These formulas extend our ability to differentiate a wider range of trigonometric expressions, which are frequently encountered in calculus applications, physics, and engineering problems.

technique_derive_tan_x_quotient_rule.title: Deriving the Derivative of Tangent Function using Quotient Rule
technique_derive_tan_x_quotient_rule.one_liner: The derivatives of tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant functions can be derived efficiently using the quotient rule and their definitions in terms of sine and cosine.
technique_derive_tan_x_quotient_rule.content: While these derivatives can be obtained using the definition of the derivative, it is often easier to use the known derivatives of sine and cosine and apply the quotient rule to their fundamental trigonometric relationships. These relationships are:$$ \tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}, \quad \cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}, \quad \sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x}, \quad \csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x} $$For example, the derivative of $\tan x$ can be derived as follows:$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{d x}[\tan x] & =\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right]=\frac{\cos x \cdot \frac{d}{d x}[\sin x]-\sin x \cdot \frac{d}{d x}[\cos x]}{\cos ^{2} x} \\ & =\frac{\cos x \cdot \cos x-\sin x \cdot (-\sin x)}{\cos ^{2} x}=\frac{\cos ^{2} x+\sin ^{2} x}{\cos ^{2} x}=\frac{1}{\cos ^{2} x}=\sec ^{2} x \end{aligned} $$
technique_derive_tan_x_quotient_rule.motivation_md: Using the quotient rule simplifies the derivation of trigonometric derivatives, making it more efficient than using the limit definition, especially when the derivatives of sine and cosine are already known.
technique_derive_tan_x_quotient_rule.recap_md: - Express $\tan x$, $\cot x$, $\sec x$, $\csc x$ in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

idea_maximum_speed_mass_spring.title: Maximum Speed in a Mass-Spring System
idea_maximum_speed_mass_spring.one_liner: This concept explores why the maximum speed of a mass in a mass-spring system occurs at its rest position and how to calculate it.
idea_maximum_speed_mass_spring.content: In Example 5, the top of the mass in a mass-spring system has its maximum speed when it passes through its rest position. Why does this occur, and what is the value of that maximum speed?
idea_maximum_speed_mass_spring.motivation_md: Understanding the dynamics of oscillating systems, like a mass-spring, is crucial in physics and engineering. Identifying points of maximum speed helps analyze energy transformations and predict system behavior.
idea_maximum_speed_mass_spring.recap_md: - The maximum speed of a mass in a mass-spring system occurs at its rest position.

idea_chain_rule_introduction.title: Introduction to The Chain Rule
idea_chain_rule_introduction.one_liner: The Chain Rule provides a formula to express the derivative of a composite function $f \circ g$ in terms of the derivatives of $f$ and $g$.
idea_chain_rule_introduction.content: This section introduces a formula that expresses the derivative of a composite function, denoted as $f \circ g$, in terms of the derivatives of its individual components, $f$ and $g$. This formula is a powerful tool that enables us to differentiate complex functions by utilizing the known derivatives of simpler functions.
idea_chain_rule_introduction.motivation_md: The Chain Rule is essential for differentiating composite functions, which are very common in mathematics and its applications. It allows us to break down complex differentiation problems into simpler, manageable steps.
idea_chain_rule_introduction.recap_md: - The Chain Rule differentiates composite functions.

idea_chain_rule_motivation.title: Motivational Example for Derivatives of Compositions
idea_chain_rule_motivation.one_liner: This motivational example uses a car's mileage and fuel cost to intuitively demonstrate how rates of change multiply for composite functions, leading to the Chain Rule.
idea_chain_rule_motivation.content: Consider a scenario where you are traveling to school in a car that gets 20 miles per gallon of gasoline. The number of miles you can travel ($y$) is a function of the number of gallons of gas ($u$) you have initially, so $y=f(u)$. Additionally, your local service station sells gasoline for $4 per gallon, meaning the number of gallons of gas you have ($u$) is a function of the amount of money ($x$) you spend, so $u=g(x)$.The rate at which your mileage changes with respect to the amount of gasoline used is $f^{\prime}(u)=\frac{d y}{d u}=20 \text { miles per gallon }$. Similarly, since gasoline costs $4 per gallon, each dollar spent yields $1/4$ of a gallon, so $g^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d u}{d x}=\frac{1}{4} \text { gallons per dollar }$.The number of miles you can travel is also a function of the dollars spent on gasoline, expressed as the composition $y=f(u)=f(g(x))$. If you are interested in how many miles you can travel per dollar, which is $d y / d x$, intuition suggests that these rates of change multiply:$$ \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y}{d u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}=\frac{20 \text { miles }}{1 \text { gallon }} \cdot \frac{1 \text { gallons }}{4 \text { dollars }}=\frac{20 \text { miles }}{4 \text { dollars }}=5 \text { miles per dollar } $$
idea_chain_rule_motivation.motivation_md: This example provides an intuitive, real-world context for understanding how rates of change combine when one quantity depends on another, which in turn depends on a third. It illustrates the core idea behind the Chain Rule.
idea_chain_rule_motivation.recap_md: - The number of miles traveled depends on gallons, and gallons depend on dollars spent.

thm_2_6_1_the_chain_rule.title: The Chain Rule
thm_2_6_1_the_chain_rule.one_liner: The Chain Rule states that if $g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$, then the composite function $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $x$, and its derivative is $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y}{d u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
thm_2_6_1_the_chain_rule.content: 2.6.1 THEOREM (The Chain Rule) If $g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$, then the composition $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $x$. Moreover, if $y=f(g(x))$ and $u=g(x)$, then $y=f(u)$ and the derivative is given by:$$ \begin{equation*} \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y}{d u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x} \tag{1} \end{equation*} $$
thm_2_6_1_the_chain_rule.motivation_md: This theorem provides the formal mathematical statement and formula for the Chain Rule, allowing us to rigorously differentiate any composite function, which is a cornerstone technique in calculus.
thm_2_6_1_the_chain_rule.recap_md: - If $y=f(g(x))$ and $u=g(x)$, then $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y}{d u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.

end_behavior_trig_exp_log_functions.title: End Behavior of Trigonometric, Exponential, and Logarithmic Functions

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

end_behavior_trig_exp_log_functions.one_liner: Trigonometric functions generally do not have limits as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$ due to their periodicity, while exponential and logarithmic functions approach specific values or $\pm \infty$.
end_behavior_trig_exp_log_functions.content: Consider the function $f(x)=\sin x$ that is graphed in Figure 1.3.7. For this function, the limits as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ fail to exist, not because $f(x)$ increases or decreases without bound, but because its values vary between -1 and 1 without approaching a specific real number. In general, trigonometric functions fail to have limits as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ because of their periodicity. There is no specific notation to denote this kind of behavior. In Section 0.5, we showed that the functions $e^{x}$ and $\ln x$ both increase without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ (Figures 0.5.8 and 0.5.9). Thus, in limit notation we have $$\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \ln x=+\infty \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} e^{x}=+\infty$$ For reference, the following limits are consistent with the graphs in Figure 1.3.8: $$\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} e^{x}=0 \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \ln x=-\infty$$ [FIGURE:59eb0cfd3b50c508 | A Cartesian coordinate system displays the graphs of two functions and a dashed line representing $y=x$. The blue curve, labeled $y=e^x$, passes through $(0,1)$ and increases exponentially. The...] Finally, the following limits can be deduced by noting that the graph of $y=e^{-x}$ is the reflection about the $y$-axis of the graph of $y=e^{x}$ (Figure 1.3.9). [FIGURE:9888c8985ac81517 | A graph displays two exponential functions, $y=e^x$ (blue) and $y=e^{-x}$ (purple), on a Cartesian coordinate system. The curve $y=e^x$ increases exponentially from left to right, while $y=e^{-x}$...] $$\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} e^{-x}=0 \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} e^{-x}=+\infty$$
end_behavior_trig_exp_log_functions.motivation_md: Understanding how functions behave at the extremes of their domains is crucial for analyzing their overall shape and predicting long-term trends. This concept provides a foundational understanding of limits at infinity for common function types, which is essential for curve sketching and solving real-world problems involving growth or decay.
end_behavior_trig_exp_log_functions.recap_md: - Trigonometric functions like $\sin x$ do not have limits as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$ due to their periodic oscillation. - Exponential functions like $e^x$ tend to $+\infty$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and $0$ as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. - Logarithmic functions like $\ln x$ tend to $+\infty$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and $-\infty$ as $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$.

substitution_principle_limits.title: Substitution Principle for Evaluating Limits

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

substitution_principle_limits.one_liner: The substitution principle allows evaluating limits of composite functions $f[g(x)]$ by setting $t=g(x)$ and finding the limit of $f(t)$ as $t$ approaches the limit of $g(x)$.
substitution_principle_limits.content: This principle, a useful tool for evaluating limits, states that we can evaluate $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} e^{x^{2}}$ by making the substitution $t=x^{2}$ and writing $$\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} e^{x^{2}}=\lim _{t \rightarrow+\infty} e^{t}=+\infty$$ More generally, if $g(x) \rightarrow+\infty$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$, then for any function $f(x)$, we can evaluate $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f[g(x)]$ by substituting $t=g(x)$ and writing $$\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f[g(x)]=\lim _{t \rightarrow+\infty} f(t)$$ This "equality" means that either both limits exist and are equal, or both limits fail to exist. This result remains valid if $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}$ is replaced by $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c}$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}}$, or $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}}$. Similarly, if $g(x) \rightarrow-\infty$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$, we can evaluate $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f[g(x)]$ by substituting $t=g(x)$ and writing $$\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f[g(x)]=\lim _{t \rightarrow-\infty} f(t)$$ This also holds for other limit types.
substitution_principle_limits.motivation_md: Evaluating limits of composite functions can be complex. The substitution principle simplifies this process by transforming the limit into a more familiar form, often reducing it to a known basic limit, making calculations more straightforward and intuitive.
substitution_principle_limits.recap_md: - To evaluate $\lim_{x \rightarrow A} f[g(x)]$, substitute $t=g(x)$. - Find the limit of $g(x)$ as $x \rightarrow A$, say $B$, then evaluate $\lim_{t \rightarrow B} f(t)$. - This principle applies to limits as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$, $x \rightarrow c$, $x \rightarrow c^{-}$, or $x \rightarrow c^{+}$.

asymptotic_curves.title: Asymptotic Curves

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

asymptotic_curves.one_liner: Curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are asymptotic as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ if the limit of their difference, $f(x)-g(x)$, is zero as $x \rightarrow+\infty$.
asymptotic_curves.content: The notion of an asymptote can be extended to include curves as well as lines. Specifically, we say that curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are asymptotic as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ provided $$\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0$$ and are asymptotic as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ provided $$\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0$$
asymptotic_curves.motivation_md: While vertical and horizontal asymptotes describe linear behavior, this definition extends the concept to more complex functions. It allows us to describe when two curves "approach" each other as $x$ tends to infinity, providing a powerful tool for analyzing the long-term behavior of functions that are not necessarily linear.
asymptotic_curves.recap_md: - Two curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are asymptotic as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0$. - They are asymptotic as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0$. - This extends the concept of asymptotes beyond just lines to include other curves.

idea_1_4_limits_rigorously.title: Limits (Discussed More Rigorously)
idea_1_4_limits_rigorously.one_liner: This section aims to define the notion of a limit precisely, enabling certain establishment of limits and proof of theorems, and offering a deeper understanding of function properties.
idea_1_4_limits_rigorously.content: In the previous sections of this chapter, we focused on discovering limit values, either by sampling $x$-values or by applying limit theorems stated without proof. The main goal in this section is to define the notion of a limit precisely. This will make it possible to establish limits with certainty and to prove theorems about them. It will also provide a deeper understanding of some of the more subtle properties of functions.
idea_1_4_limits_rigorously.motivation_md: Informal definitions of limits, while intuitive, lack the mathematical rigor needed for proofs and certainty. This rigorous discussion provides the precise framework necessary to formally define limits, prove their properties, and build the entire edifice of calculus on a solid foundation.
idea_1_4_limits_rigorously.recap_md: - Previous sections focused on informal limit discovery. - This section aims to define limits precisely. - A precise definition allows for certain establishment of limits and proof of theorems.

idea_1_4_motivation_two_sided_limit.title: Motivation for the Definition of a Two-Sided Limit
idea_1_4_motivation_two_sided_limit.one_liner: This section provides the motivation for defining a two-sided limit rigorously by making the informal phrases "as close as we like to $L$" and "sufficiently close to $a$" mathematically precise using $\epsilon$ and $\delta$.
idea_1_4_motivation_two_sided_limit.content: The statement $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ can be interpreted informally to mean that we can make the value of $f(x)$ as close as we like to the real number $L$ by making the value of $x$ sufficiently close to $a$. Our goal is to make the informal phrases 'as close as we like to $L$' and 'sufficiently close to $a$' mathematically precise. To do this, consider the function $f$ graphed in Figure 1.4.1a, for which $f(x) \rightarrow L$ as $x \rightarrow a$. For visual simplicity, the graph of $f$ is drawn to be increasing on an open interval containing $a$, and a hole is intentionally placed at $x=a$ to emphasize that $f$ need not be defined at $x=a$ to have a limit there. (see figure: This figure contains three graphs illustrating the definition of a limit. Each graph shows a curve $y=f(x)$ in the first quadrant of a Cartesian coordinate system. Graph (a) shows an intuitive...) Next, let us choose any positive number $\epsilon$ and ask how close $x$ must be to $a$ in order for the values of $f(x)$ to be within $\epsilon$ units of $L$. We can answer this geometrically by drawing horizontal lines from the points $L+\epsilon$ and $L-\epsilon$ on the $y$-axis until they meet the curve $y=f(x)$, and then drawing vertical lines from those points on the curve to the $x$-axis (Figure 1.4.1b). As indicated in the figure, let $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ be the points where those vertical lines intersect the $x$-axis. [FIGURE:52ef983b97adacfd | The figure illustrates the epsilon-delta definition of a limit with two diagrams. The top diagram shows a graph of a function $y=f(x)$ on an $xy$-plane, where for a given $\epsilon$-interval...] Now imagine that $x$ gets closer and closer to $a$ (from either side). Eventually, $x$ will lie inside the interval $\left(x_{0}, x_{1}\right)$, which is marked in green in Figure 1.4.1c; and when this happens, the value of $f(x)$ will fall between $L-\epsilon$ and $L+\epsilon$, marked in red in the figure. Thus, we conclude: If $f(x) \rightarrow L$ as $x \rightarrow a$, then for any positive number $\epsilon$, we can find an open interval $\left(x_{0}, x_{1}\right)$ on the $x$-axis that contains $a$ and has the property that for each $x$ in that interval (except possibly for $x=a$), the value of $f(x)$ is between $L-\epsilon$ and $L+\epsilon$. What is important about this result is that it holds no matter how small we make $\epsilon$. However, making $\epsilon$ smaller and smaller forces $f(x)$ closer and closer to $L$-which is precisely the concept we were trying to capture mathematically. Observe that in Figure 1.4.1 the interval $\left(x_{0}, x_{1}\right)$ extends farther on the right side of $a$ than on the left side. However, for many purposes it is preferable to have an interval that extends the same distance on both sides of $a$. For this purpose, let us choose any positive number $\delta$ that is smaller than both $x_{1}-a$ and $a-x_{0}$, and consider the interval $$(a-\delta, a+\delta)$$ This interval extends the same distance $\delta$ on both sides of $a$ and lies inside of the interval $\left(x_{0}, x_{1}\right)$ (Figure 1.4.2). Moreover, the condition $$L-\epsilon<f(x)<L+\epsilon$$ holds for every $x$ in this interval (except possibly $x=a$), since this condition holds on the larger interval $\left(x_{0}, x_{1}\right)$. Since this can be expressed as $$|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$$ and the condition that $x$ lies in the interval $(a-\delta, a+\delta)$, but $x \neq a$, can be expressed as $$0<|x-a|<\delta$$ we are led to the following precise definition of a two-sided limit.
idea_1_4_motivation_two_sided_limit.motivation_md: To move beyond an intuitive understanding of limits, it's essential to formalize the concepts of "arbitrarily close" and "sufficiently close." This motivation introduces the $\epsilon-\delta$ framework, visually demonstrating how to quantify closeness, which is fundamental for proving limit properties and establishing calculus theorems rigorously.
idea_1_4_motivation_two_sided_limit.recap_md: - The goal is to precisely define "as close as we like to $L$" and "sufficiently close to $a$". - For any $\epsilon > 0$, we need to find a $\delta > 0$ such that if $x$ is within $\delta$ of $a$ (but not equal to $a$), then $f(x)$ is within $\epsilon$ of $L$. - This geometric interpretation leads to the formal $\epsilon-\delta$ definition of a two-sided limit.

def_1_4_1_two_sided_limit.title: Two-Sided Limit Definition (Epsilon-Delta)
def_1_4_1_two_sided_limit.one_liner: The two-sided limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ means that for any $\epsilon>0$, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that if $0<|x-a|<\delta$, then $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$.
def_1_4_1_two_sided_limit.content: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing the number $a$, with the possible exception that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We will write $$\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$ we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $$|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-a|<\delta$$
def_1_4_1_two_sided_limit.motivation_md: This formal definition provides the bedrock for all limit-related proofs and theorems in calculus. It precisely quantifies the intuitive idea of "closeness," allowing mathematicians to rigorously verify limit values and establish properties of continuity, derivatives, and integrals.
def_1_4_1_two_sided_limit.recap_md: - The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ is defined using $\epsilon$ and $\delta$. - For every $\epsilon > 0$ (how close $f(x)$ is to $L$), there must be a $\delta > 0$ (how close $x$ is to $a$). - The condition is: if $0<|x-a|<\delta$, then $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$.

idea_1_4_general_limit_proof.title: General Form of a Limit Proof
idea_1_4_general_limit_proof.one_liner: A general limit proof involves assuming a positive $\epsilon$, then finding and proving a positive $\delta$ (expressed as a function of $\epsilon$) such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ when $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
idea_1_4_general_limit_proof.content: This example illustrates the general form of a limit proof: We assume that we are given a positive number $\epsilon$, and we try to prove that we can find a positive number $\delta$ such that $$|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \text { if } 0<|x-a|<\delta$$ This is done by first discovering $\delta$, and then proving that the discovered $\delta$ works. Since the argument has to be general enough to work for all positive values of $\epsilon$, the quantity $\delta$ has to be expressed as a function of $\epsilon$. In Example 1, we found the function $\delta=\epsilon / 3$ by some simple algebra; however, most limit proofs require a little more algebraic and logical ingenuity. Thus, if you find our ensuing discussion of '$\epsilon-\delta$' proofs challenging, do not become discouraged; the concepts and techniques are intrinsically difficult. In fact, a precise understanding of limits evaded the finest mathematical minds for more than 150 years after the basic concepts of calculus were discovered.
idea_1_4_general_limit_proof.motivation_md: Understanding the structure of an $\epsilon-\delta$ proof is crucial for mastering the rigorous definition of limits. This concept outlines the two-step process of discovering $\delta$ and then formally proving its validity, preparing students for the logical ingenuity required in more complex limit proofs.
idea_1_4_general_limit_proof.recap_md: - A limit proof starts by assuming an arbitrary $\epsilon > 0$. - The goal is to find a $\delta > 0$ (often a function of $\epsilon$) such that if $0<|x-a|<\delta$, then $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$. - The process involves discovering $\delta$ through algebraic manipulation and then formally proving that this $\delta$ satisfies the definition.

idea_1_4_delta_not_unique.title: The Value of Delta is Not Unique
idea_1_4_delta_not_unique.one_liner: The value of $\delta$ in the epsilon-delta limit definition is not unique; any positive number smaller than a valid $\delta$ will also satisfy the definition.
idea_1_4_delta_not_unique.content: In preparation for our next example, we note that the value of $\delta$ in Definition 1.4.1 is not unique. Once we have found a value of $\delta$ that fulfills the requirements of the definition, then any smaller positive number $\delta_{1}$ will also fulfill those requirements. That is, if it is true that $$|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-a|<\delta$$ then it will also be true that $$|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-a|<\delta_{1}$$ This is because $\left\{x: 0<|x-a|<\delta_{1}\right\}$ is a subset of $\{x: 0<|x-a|<\delta\}$ (Figure 1.4.3). Hence, if $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ is satisfied for all $x$ in the larger set, then it will automatically be satisfied for all $x$ in the subset. Thus, in Example 1, where we used $\delta=\epsilon / 3$, we could have used any smaller value of $\delta$ such as $\delta=\epsilon / 4, \delta=\epsilon / 5$, or $\delta=\epsilon / 6$.
idea_1_4_delta_not_unique.motivation_md: Understanding that $\delta$ is not unique simplifies the process of finding a suitable $\delta$ in limit proofs. It means that once a valid $\delta$ is found, there's no need to search for the "largest" possible $\delta$; any smaller positive value will also work, making proofs more flexible.
idea_1_4_delta_not_unique.recap_md: - If a $\delta$ satisfies the limit definition for a given $\epsilon$, any $\delta_1$ such that $0 < \delta_1 < \delta$ will also satisfy it. - This is because the interval defined by $\delta_1$ is a subset of the interval defined by $\delta$. - Therefore, when proving limits, one does not need to find the largest possible $\delta$.

idea_chain_rule_notation_flexibility.title: Chain Rule Notation Flexibility
idea_chain_rule_notation_flexibility.one_liner: The chain rule notation allows for flexibility in variable names, where a "canceling" device helps deduce the correct form, such as $dw/dt = (dw/dx) \cdot (dx/dt)$.
idea_chain_rule_notation_flexibility.content: The chain rule formula is easy to remember because its left side is exactly what results if the $du$ terms on the right side are "canceled." This "canceling" device provides a good way to deduce the correct form of the chain rule when different variables are used. For example, if $w$ is a function of $x$ and $x$ is a function of $t$, then the chain rule takes the form:$$ \frac{d w}{d t}=\frac{d w}{d x} \cdot \frac{d x}{d t} $$
idea_chain_rule_notation_flexibility.motivation_md: Understanding the flexibility in chain rule notation helps apply it correctly across various contexts where different variable names are used. This allows for a more intuitive derivation of the rule's form.
idea_chain_rule_notation_flexibility.recap_md: - The chain rule can be remembered by imagining "canceling" intermediate differential terms.

technique_chain_rule_alternative_version.title: Alternative Version of the Chain Rule
technique_chain_rule_alternative_version.one_liner: An alternative version of the chain rule expresses the derivative of a composite function $f(g(x))$ as $f'(g(x))g'(x)$, often remembered as the derivative of the "outside function" evaluated at the "inside function" times the derivative of the "inside function."
technique_chain_rule_alternative_version.content: The standard formula for the chain rule can be unwieldy in some problems due to involving many variables. As you become more comfortable with the chain rule, you may prefer to express it without explicitly writing out the dependent variables, using the form:$$ \frac{d}{d x}[f(g(x))]=(f \circ g)^{\prime}(x)=f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x) \tag{2} $$A convenient way to remember this formula is to call $f$ the "outside function" and $g$ the "inside function" in the composition $f(g(x))$. In words, the derivative of $f(g(x))$ is the derivative of the outside function evaluated at the inside function, multiplied by the derivative of the inside function.
technique_chain_rule_alternative_version.motivation_md: This alternative notation simplifies the application of the chain rule by focusing on the structure of composite functions, making it easier to apply in problems where the standard multi-variable notation might feel cumbersome.
technique_chain_rule_alternative_version.recap_md: - The derivative of $f(g(x))$ is $(f \circ g)^{\prime}(x)=f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x)$.

technique_generalized_derivative_formula.title: Generalized Derivative Formulas
technique_generalized_derivative_formula.one_liner: A useful variation of the chain rule, striking a middle ground, is given by the formula $d/dx[f(u)] = f'(u) du/dx$, where $u=g(x)$.
technique_generalized_derivative_formula.content: There is a useful third variation of the chain rule that strikes a middle ground between the two previously discussed formulas. If we let $u=g(x)$ in the alternative chain rule formula, we can rewrite that formula as:$$ \frac{d}{d x}[f(u)]=f^{\prime}(u) \frac{d u}{d x} \tag{3} $$
technique_generalized_derivative_formula.motivation_md: This generalized formula provides a flexible way to apply the chain rule, especially when dealing with functions where a substitution $u=g(x)$ simplifies the differentiation process, bridging the gap between explicit function notation and multi-variable notation.
technique_generalized_derivative_formula.recap_md: - The generalized chain rule formula is $\frac{d}{d x}[f(u)]=f^{\prime}(u) \frac{d u}{d x}$ where $u$ is a function of $x$.

idea_differentiating_with_cas.title: Differentiating Using Computer Algebra Systems
idea_differentiating_with_cas.one_liner: Computer Algebra Systems (CAS) like Mathematica, Maple, or Sage are often used by engineers and scientists to compute complicated derivatives efficiently and with fewer errors.
idea_differentiating_with_cas.content: Even with the chain rule and other differentiation rules, some derivative computations can be tedious to perform by hand. For complicated derivatives, engineers and scientists often use computer algebra systems such as Mathematica, Maple, or Sage. For example, although all the mathematical tools exist to compute the following derivative by hand, the computation is sufficiently involved that it may be more efficient (and less error-prone) to use a computer algebra system:$$ \frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{10} \sin ^{3}(\sqrt{x})}{\sqrt{1+\csc x}}\right] \tag{4} $$
idea_differentiating_with_cas.motivation_md: Computer Algebra Systems (CAS) are valuable tools for handling complex differentiation tasks that would otherwise be tedious, time-consuming, and prone to human error, allowing professionals to focus on analysis rather than computation.
idea_differentiating_with_cas.recap_md: - Some derivative computations are too tedious or complex for manual calculation.

idea_extending_differentiation_applicati.title: Extending Differentiation and its Applications
idea_extending_differentiation_applicati.one_liner: This chapter extends differentiation to functions difficult to differentiate directly, including logarithmic, exponential, and inverse trigonometric functions, and explores new applications like related rates, linear approximations, and L'Hôpital's rule.
idea_extending_differentiation_applicati.content: The growth and decline of animal populations and natural resources can be effectively modeled using basic functions studied in calculus. This chapter begins by extending the process of differentiation to functions that are either difficult or impossible to differentiate directly. We will discuss a combination of direct and indirect methods of differentiation, which will allow us to develop new derivative formulas for logarithmic, exponential, and inverse trigonometric functions. Later in the chapter, we will consider some applications of the derivative. These applications will include ways in which different rates of change can be related, as well as the use of linear functions to approximate nonlinear functions. Finally, we will discuss L'Hôpital's rule, a powerful tool for evaluating limits.
idea_extending_differentiation_applicati.motivation_md: Extending differentiation techniques allows us to analyze a broader range of functions, including those that model real-world phenomena like population changes. This expansion also unlocks new applications of derivatives, enhancing our ability to solve complex problems in various fields.
idea_extending_differentiation_applicati.recap_md: - Differentiation methods are extended to handle logarithmic, exponential, and inverse trigonometric functions.

idea_explicit_implicit_functions.title: Functions Defined Explicitly and Implicitly
idea_explicit_implicit_functions.one_liner: An equation defines $y$ explicitly as a function of $x$ if $y$ is isolated on one side, whereas it defines $y$ implicitly if $y$ is not isolated but can still be expressed as a function of $x$.
idea_explicit_implicit_functions.content: An equation of the form $y=f(x)$ is said to define $y$ explicitly as a function of $x$ because the variable $y$ appears alone on one side of the equation and does not appear at all on the other side. However, sometimes functions are defined by equations in which $y$ is not alone on one side; for example, the equation:$$ y x+y+1=x \tag{1} $$is not of the form $y=f(x)$, but it still defines $y$ as a function of $x$ since it can be rewritten as:$$ y=\frac{x-1}{x+1} $$Thus, we say that (1) defines $y$ implicitly as a function of $x$, with the function being:$$ f(x)=\frac{x-1}{x+1} $$
idea_explicit_implicit_functions.motivation_md: Distinguishing between explicit and implicit functions is crucial because not all relationships between variables can be easily expressed in the $y=f(x)$ form. Implicit functions allow us to work with these relationships directly, even when solving for $y$ is difficult or impossible.
idea_explicit_implicit_functions.recap_md: - An explicit function is of the form $y=f(x)$, where $y$ is isolated.

def_implicitly_defined_function.title: Implicitly Defined Function
def_implicitly_defined_function.one_liner: An equation in $x$ and $y$ defines a function $f$ implicitly if the graph of $y=f(x)$ coincides with a portion of the graph of the equation.
def_implicitly_defined_function.content: We will say that a given equation in $x$ and $y$ defines the function $f$ implicitly if the graph of $y=f(x)$ coincides with a portion of the graph of the equation.
def_implicitly_defined_function.motivation_md: This definition formalizes how an equation can represent a function even when it's not explicitly solved for $y$. It's essential for understanding relationships where $y$ is not directly isolated as a function of $x$.
def_implicitly_defined_function.recap_md: - An equation implicitly defines a function $f$ if $y=f(x)$ matches part of the equation's graph.

tech_implicit_differentiation.title: Implicit Differentiation
tech_implicit_differentiation.one_liner: Implicit differentiation is a method to find $dy/dx$ by differentiating both sides of an equation with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a differentiable function of $x$, without first solving for $y$ explicitly.
tech_implicit_differentiation.content: In general, it is not necessary to solve an equation for $y$ in terms of $x$ in order to differentiate the functions defined implicitly by the equation. To illustrate this, consider the simple equation:$$ x y=1 \tag{5} $$One way to find $d y / d x$ is to rewrite this equation as:$$ y=\frac{1}{x} \tag{6} $$from which it follows that:$$ \frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{1}{x^{2}} \tag{7} $$Another way to obtain this derivative is to differentiate both sides of (5) before solving for $y$ in terms of $x$, treating $y$ as a (temporarily unspecified) differentiable function of $x$. With this approach, we obtain:$$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{d}{d x}[x y]=\frac{d}{d x}[1] \\ & x \frac{d}{d x}[y]+y \frac{d}{d x}[x]=0 \\ & x \frac{d y}{d x}+y=0 \\ & \frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{y}{x} \end{aligned} $$If we now substitute (6) into the last expression, we obtain:$$ \frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{1}{x^{2}} $$which agrees with Equation (7). This method of obtaining derivatives is called implicit differentiation.
tech_implicit_differentiation.motivation_md: Implicit differentiation is a powerful technique for finding derivatives of functions that are difficult or impossible to express explicitly in the form $y=f(x)$. It allows us to work directly with the given equation, simplifying the process.
tech_implicit_differentiation.recap_md: - Implicit differentiation involves differentiating both sides of an equation with respect to $x$.

idea_increasing_decreasing_functions.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

idea_increasing_decreasing_functions.one_liner: The terms increasing, decreasing, and constant describe a function's behavior as its graph is traversed from left to right.
idea_increasing_decreasing_functions.content: The terms increasing, decreasing, and constant are used to describe the behavior of a function as we travel left to right along its graph. For example, a function can be described as increasing to the left of $x=0$, decreasing from $x=0$ to $x=2$, increasing from $x=2$ to $x=4$, and constant to the right of $x=4$. The definitions of "increasing," "decreasing," and "constant" describe the behavior of a function on an interval, not at a single point. Therefore, it is consistent to say that a function is decreasing on the interval $[0,2]$ and increasing on the interval $[2,4]$.
idea_increasing_decreasing_functions.motivation_md: Understanding whether a function is increasing or decreasing helps us describe its overall shape and behavior. This concept provides the foundational language to analyze how a function's output changes relative to its input.
idea_increasing_decreasing_functions.recap_md: - Functions can exhibit increasing, decreasing, or constant behavior. - This behavior is defined over intervals, not at individual points.

def_4_1_1_increasing_decreasing_constant.title: Increasing, Decreasing, and Constant Functions

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

def_4_1_1_increasing_decreasing_constant.one_liner: A function is increasing if $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ whenever $x_1 < x_2$, decreasing if $f(x_1) > f(x_2)$, and constant if $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ for all $x_1, x_2$ in an interval.
def_4_1_1_increasing_decreasing_constant.content: Let $f$ be defined on an interval, and let $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ denote points in that interval. (a) $f$ is increasing on the interval if $f\left(x_{1}\right)<f\left(x_{2}\right)$ whenever $x_{1}<x_{2}$. (b) $f$ is decreasing on the interval if $f\left(x_{1}\right)>f\left(x_{2}\right)$ whenever $x_{1}<x_{2}$. (c) $f$ is constant on the interval if $f\left(x_{1}\right)=f\left(x_{2}\right)$ for all points $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$. This segment is visually defined by two vertical dashed lines extending from the...] Each tangent line has zero slope.
def_4_1_1_increasing_decreasing_constant.motivation_md: This definition provides the precise mathematical criteria for formally classifying a function's behavior as increasing, decreasing, or constant over an interval. It moves beyond informal descriptions to a rigorous foundation for calculus.
def_4_1_1_increasing_decreasing_constant.recap_md: - Increasing: $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ when $x_1 < x_2$. - Decreasing: $f(x_1) > f(x_2)$ when $x_1 < x_2$. - Constant: $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ for all $x_1, x_2$.

idea_derivative_and_function_behavior.title: Derivative and Function Behavior

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

idea_derivative_and_function_behavior.one_liner: The sign of a differentiable function's tangent line slope suggests whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or constant on an interval.
idea_derivative_and_function_behavior.content: Figure 4.1.3 suggests that a differentiable function $f$ is increasing on any interval where each tangent line to its graph has a positive slope. Conversely, it is decreasing on any interval where each tangent line to its graph has a negative slope, and it is constant on any interval where each tangent line to its graph has a zero slope. This intuitive observation leads to an important theorem that will be proved in Section 4.8.
idea_derivative_and_function_behavior.motivation_md: This concept bridges the visual understanding of a function's behavior with the analytical power of calculus. By connecting the derivative (slope of the tangent line) to increasing or decreasing trends, we gain a powerful tool for analyzing functions without relying solely on their graphs.
idea_derivative_and_function_behavior.recap_md: - A positive tangent slope (derivative) suggests an increasing function. - A negative tangent slope (derivative) suggests a decreasing function. - A zero tangent slope (derivative) suggests a constant function.

thm_4_1_2_test_for_increasing_decreasing.title: Test for Increasing and Decreasing Functions

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

thm_4_1_2_test_for_increasing_decreasing.one_liner: Theorem 4.1.2 states that a continuous and differentiable function is increasing if $f'(x)>0$, decreasing if $f'(x)<0$, and constant if $f'(x)=0$ on an interval.
thm_4_1_2_test_for_increasing_decreasing.content: Let $f$ be a function that is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$. (a) If $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is increasing on $[a, b]$. (b) If $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is decreasing on $[a, b]$. (c) If $f^{\prime}(x)=0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$.
thm_4_1_2_test_for_increasing_decreasing.motivation_md: This theorem provides a rigorous analytical method to determine the intervals where a function is increasing, decreasing, or constant. By examining the sign of the first derivative, we can precisely characterize a function's behavior without needing to graph it.
thm_4_1_2_test_for_increasing_decreasing.recap_md: - If $f'(x)>0$ on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is increasing on $[a,b]$. - If $f'(x)<0$ on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is decreasing on $[a,b]$. - If $f'(x)=0$ on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is constant on $[a,b]$.

idea_concavity_introduction.title: Concavity

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

idea_concavity_introduction.one_liner: Concavity describes the direction of a function's curvature, distinguishing between 'concave up' (upward curvature) and 'concave down' (downward curvature).
idea_concavity_introduction.content: Although the sign of the derivative of $f$ reveals where the graph of $f$ is increasing or decreasing, it does not reveal the direction of curvature. For example, the graph is increasing on both sides of the point in Figure 4.1.7, but on the left side it has an upward curvature ("holds water") and on the right side it has a downward curvature ("spills water"). On intervals where the graph of $f$ has upward curvature, we say that $f$ is concave up, and on intervals where the graph has downward curvature, we say that $f$ is concave down. Figure 4.1.8 suggests two ways to characterize the concavity of a differentiable function $f$ on an open interval: - $f$ is concave up on an open interval if its tangent lines have increasing slopes on that interval and is concave down if they have decreasing slopes. - $f$ is concave up on an open interval if its graph lies above its tangent lines on that interval and is concave down if it lies below its tangent lines. Our formal definition for "concave up" and "concave down" corresponds to the first of these characterizations.
idea_concavity_introduction.motivation_md: Concavity provides crucial information about the shape of a function's graph beyond just whether it's rising or falling. It helps identify points of inflection and better understand the behavior of the function, which is essential for optimization and curve sketching.
idea_concavity_introduction.recap_md: - Concavity describes the direction of a graph's curvature. - Concave up means upward curvature (tangent slopes are increasing). - Concave down means downward curvature (tangent slopes are decreasing).

def_4_1_3_concave_up_down.title: Concave Up and Concave Down

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

def_4_1_3_concave_up_down.one_liner: A function $f$ is concave up on an open interval if its derivative $f'$ is increasing, and concave down if $f'$ is decreasing on that interval.
def_4_1_3_concave_up_down.content: If $f$ is differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is said to be concave up on the open interval if $f^{\prime}$ is increasing on that interval, and $f$ is said to be concave down on the open interval if $f^{\prime}$ is decreasing on that interval.
def_4_1_3_concave_up_down.motivation_md: This definition provides a precise mathematical way to characterize concavity. By linking concavity directly to the increasing or decreasing behavior of the first derivative, it establishes a rigorous foundation for using calculus to analyze the curvature of functions.
def_4_1_3_concave_up_down.recap_md: - A function $f$ is concave up if its derivative $f'$ is increasing. - A function $f$ is concave down if its derivative $f'$ is decreasing.

idea_second_derivative_and_concavity.title: Second Derivative and Concavity

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

idea_second_derivative_and_concavity.one_liner: The sign of the second derivative $f''$ determines the increasing or decreasing behavior of the first derivative $f'$, which in turn indicates the concavity of $f$.
idea_second_derivative_and_concavity.content: Since the slopes of the tangent lines to the graph of a differentiable function $f$ are the values of its derivative $f^{\prime}$, it follows from Theorem 4.1.2 (applied to $f^{\prime}$ rather than $f$) that $f^{\prime}$ will be increasing on intervals where $f^{\prime \prime}$ is positive and that $f^{\prime}$ will be decreasing on intervals where $f^{\prime \prime}$ is negative. Thus, we have the following theorem.
idea_second_derivative_and_concavity.motivation_md: This concept establishes the crucial link between the second derivative and concavity. It provides a powerful analytical tool, allowing us to determine the curvature of a function's graph by simply examining the sign of its second derivative.
idea_second_derivative_and_concavity.recap_md: - $f'' > 0$ implies $f'$ is increasing. - $f'' < 0$ implies $f'$ is decreasing. - This directly links the second derivative to the concavity of $f$.

thm_4_1_4_test_for_concavity.title: Test for Concavity

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

thm_4_1_4_test_for_concavity.one_liner: Theorem 4.1.4 states that a twice-differentiable function is concave up if $f''(x)>0$ and concave down if $f''(x)<0$ on an open interval.
thm_4_1_4_test_for_concavity.content: Let $f$ be twice differentiable on an open interval. (a) If $f^{\prime \prime}(x)>0$ for every value of $x$ in the open interval, then $f$ is concave up on that interval. (b) If $f^{\prime \prime}(x)<0$ for every value of $x$ in the open interval, then $f$ is concave down on that interval.
thm_4_1_4_test_for_concavity.motivation_md: This theorem provides a direct and efficient method for determining the concavity of a function's graph. By simply analyzing the sign of the second derivative, we can quickly identify intervals where the function is concave up or concave down, which is vital for sketching graphs and understanding function behavior.
thm_4_1_4_test_for_concavity.recap_md: - If $f''(x)>0$ on an open interval, then $f$ is concave up. - If $f''(x)<0$ on an open interval, then $f$ is concave down.

technique_3_6_evaluating_0_infinity.title: Evaluating Indeterminate Forms of Type 0 * infinity
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_infinity.one_liner: Indeterminate forms of type $0 \cdot \infty$ can sometimes be evaluated by rewriting the product as a ratio, then applying L'Hôpital's rule for $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$ forms.
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_infinity.content: Indeterminate forms of type $0 \cdot \infty$ can sometimes be evaluated by rewriting the product as a ratio. Once in ratio form, L'Hôpital's rule can then be applied, as the expression will typically become an indeterminate form of type $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$.
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_infinity.motivation_md: This technique is necessary because $0 \cdot \infty$ is an indeterminate form, meaning its limit cannot be determined by simply multiplying zero by infinity. Rewriting it allows us to use L'Hôpital's rule, a powerful tool for evaluating such limits.
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_infinity.recap_md: - Rewrite the product $f(x) \cdot g(x)$ as a ratio, such as $f(x) / (1/g(x))$ or $g(x) / (1/f(x))$.- Apply L'Hôpital's rule to the resulting $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$ indeterminate form.

idea_3_6_warning_0_infinity_not_zero.title: Warning: 0 * infinity is not necessarily zero
idea_3_6_warning_0_infinity_not_zero.one_liner: It is a fallacy to assume that an indeterminate form of type $0 \cdot \infty$ has a value of 0, as it represents a statement about limits, not a product of numbers.
idea_3_6_warning_0_infinity_not_zero.content: It is tempting to argue that an indeterminate form of type $0 \cdot \infty$ has a value of 0, based on the idea that "zero times anything is zero." However, this reasoning is fallacious because $0 \cdot \infty$ is not a product of numbers; instead, it is a statement about limits. For instance, consider these two indeterminate forms of type $0 \cdot \infty$ whose limits are not zero:$$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(x \cdot \frac{1}{x}ight) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} 1=1 \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}\left(\sqrt{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x}ight) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}ight) \\ & =+\infty \end{aligned} $$
idea_3_6_warning_0_infinity_not_zero.motivation_md: This warning is crucial to prevent a common misconception in calculus. Understanding why $0 \cdot \infty$ is indeterminate, rather than simply zero, is fundamental for correctly evaluating limits and applying techniques like L'Hôpital's Rule.
idea_3_6_warning_0_infinity_not_zero.recap_md: - Do not assume $0 \cdot \infty$ equals 0; it is an indeterminate form, not a numerical product.- The value of $0 \cdot \infty$ depends on the specific functions involved in the limit.- Examples show that limits of type $0 \cdot \infty$ can be 1, $\infty$, or other values.

def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_minu.title: Indeterminate Form of Type infinity - infinity
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_minu.one_liner: An indeterminate form of type $\infty-\infty$ arises when a limit problem leads to expressions like $(+\infty)-(+\infty)$ or $(+\infty)+(-\infty)$, where terms exert conflicting influences.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_minu.content: A limit problem that results in one of the expressions $(+\infty)-(+\infty)$, $(-\infty)-(-\infty)$, $(+\infty)+(-\infty)$, or $(-\infty)+(+\infty)$ is classified as an indeterminate form of type $\infty-\infty$. Such limits are indeterminate because the two terms involved exert conflicting influences on the overall expression: one term tends to push the expression in the positive direction, while the other pushes it in the negative direction.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_minu.motivation_md: This form is called indeterminate because the competing infinities make the limit's value unclear without further analysis. It's not simply zero or infinity, as the exact balance between the growing terms determines the actual limit.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_minu.recap_md: - An indeterminate form of type $\infty-\infty$ occurs when a limit results in expressions like $(+\infty)-(+\infty)$ or $(+\infty)+(-\infty)$.- These forms are indeterminate because the terms have conflicting influences, pushing the expression in opposite directions.

technique_3_6_evaluating_infinity_minus_.title: Evaluating Indeterminate Forms of Type infinity - infinity
technique_3_6_evaluating_infinity_minus_.one_liner: Indeterminate forms of type $\infty-\infty$ can be evaluated by combining terms and manipulating the result to produce a $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$ form.
technique_3_6_evaluating_infinity_minus_.content: Indeterminate forms of type $\infty-\infty$ can sometimes be evaluated by first combining the terms in the expression. The result of this combination can then be manipulated to produce an indeterminate form of type $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$, which can then be evaluated using L'Hôpital's rule.
technique_3_6_evaluating_infinity_minus_.motivation_md: This technique is essential for resolving the ambiguity of $\infty-\infty$ limits. By transforming the expression into a ratio, we can apply L'Hôpital's Rule, which is designed to handle the indeterminate forms $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$, thereby finding the true limit.
technique_3_6_evaluating_infinity_minus_.recap_md: - Combine the terms in the expression to simplify it.- Manipulate the combined expression to convert it into an indeterminate form of type $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$.- Apply L'Hôpital's rule to evaluate the transformed limit.

def_3_6_indeterminate_forms_0_0_infinity.title: Indeterminate Forms of Type 0^0, infinity^0, 1^infinity
def_3_6_indeterminate_forms_0_0_infinity.one_liner: Limits of the form $\lim f(x)^{g(x)}$ can result in indeterminate forms of types $\mathbf{0}^{\boldsymbol{0}}$, $\boldsymbol{\infty}^{\boldsymbol{0}}$, and $\mathbf{1}^{\boldsymbol{\infty}}$.
def_3_6_indeterminate_forms_0_0_infinity.content: Limits of the form $\lim f(x)^{g(x)}$ can give rise to indeterminate forms of the types $\mathbf{0}^{\boldsymbol{0}}$, $\boldsymbol{\infty}^{\boldsymbol{0}}$, and $\mathbf{1}^{\boldsymbol{\infty}}$. The interpretations of these symbols should be clear. For example, the limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}(1+x)^{1 / x}$, whose value is known to be $e$, is an indeterminate form of type $1^{\infty}$. It is indeterminate because the expressions $1+x$ and $1/x$ exert two conflicting influences: the base $1+x$ approaches 1, which drives the overall expression toward 1, while the exponent $1/x$ approaches $+\infty$, which drives the expression toward $+\infty$.
def_3_6_indeterminate_forms_0_0_infinity.motivation_md: These forms are indeterminate because the base and exponent each push the limit towards different, conflicting values. For instance, in $1^\infty$, the base approaching 1 suggests a limit of 1, while the exponent approaching infinity suggests a limit of infinity, making the outcome uncertain without further analysis.
def_3_6_indeterminate_forms_0_0_infinity.recap_md: - Indeterminate forms $\mathbf{0}^{\boldsymbol{0}}$, $\boldsymbol{\infty}^{\boldsymbol{0}}$, and $\mathbf{1}^{\boldsymbol{\infty}}$ arise from limits of the form $\lim f(x)^{g(x)}$.- These forms are indeterminate due to conflicting influences from the base and exponent.- An example is $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}(1+x)^{1 / x}$, which is of type $1^{\infty}$ and evaluates to $e$.

technique_3_6_evaluating_0_0_infinity_0_.title: Evaluating Indeterminate Forms of Type 0^0, infinity^0, 1^infinity
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_0_infinity_0_.one_liner: Indeterminate forms of types $0^{0}, \infty^{0}$, and $1^{\infty}$ can be evaluated by introducing a dependent variable $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$ and computing the limit of $\ln y$.
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_0_infinity_0_.content: Indeterminate forms of types $0^{0}, \infty^{0}$, and $1^{\infty}$ can sometimes be evaluated by first introducing a dependent variable $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$. Then, one computes the limit of $\ln y$. Since $\ln y=\ln \left[f(x)^{g(x)}\right]=g(x) \cdot \ln [f(x)]$, the limit of $\ln y$ will transform into an indeterminate form of type $0 \cdot \infty$. This $0 \cdot \infty$ form can then be evaluated using methods previously studied (e.g., rewriting as a ratio for L'Hôpital's rule). Once the limit of $\ln y$ is known, it is straightforward to determine the limit of the original expression $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$ by exponentiating the result.
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_0_infinity_0_.motivation_md: This technique uses logarithms to transform complex exponential indeterminate forms into simpler $0 \cdot \infty$ forms. This transformation allows us to apply L'Hôpital's Rule, which is effective for products or ratios, thereby providing a systematic way to evaluate these otherwise intractable limits.
technique_3_6_evaluating_0_0_infinity_0_.recap_md: - Introduce $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$ and take the natural logarithm: $\ln y = g(x) \cdot \ln[f(x)]$.- Evaluate the limit of $\ln y$, which will be an indeterminate form of type $0 \cdot \infty$.- Use known methods (e.g., L'Hôpital's rule) to find the limit of $\ln y$.- Exponentiate the result to find the limit of the original expression $y=f(x)^{g(x)}$.

ch4_intro_derivative_applications.title: The Derivative in Graphing and Applications

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

ch4_intro_derivative_applications.one_liner: This chapter explores various applications of the derivative, including analyzing functions and their graphs, solving optimization problems, studying motion, and approximating equation solutions.
ch4_intro_derivative_applications.content: This chapter focuses on various applications of the derivative. For example, methods of calculus will be used to analyze functions and their graphs, demonstrating how calculus and graphing utilities can together provide important information about function behavior. Another key application of the derivative is in solving optimization problems. Here, if time is a primary concern, one might seek the quickest way to perform a task, or if cost is the main consideration, the least expensive way. Mathematically, optimization problems involve finding the largest or smallest value of a function over a given interval and determining where these extreme values occur. The derivative provides the mathematical tools necessary for solving such problems. Additionally, the derivative will be used to study the motion of a particle along a line and to approximate solutions of equations.
ch4_intro_derivative_applications.motivation_md: Understanding derivative applications is crucial because it bridges theoretical calculus with practical problem-solving. Derivatives provide powerful tools for analyzing function behavior, solving real-world optimization challenges (like minimizing cost or maximizing efficiency), modeling physical phenomena, and approximating solutions to complex equations.
ch4_intro_derivative_applications.recap_md: - Derivatives are used to analyze functions and their graphs, often in conjunction with graphing utilities.- They are essential for solving optimization problems, which involve finding maximum or minimum values.- Derivatives help study the motion of particles along a line and approximate solutions to equations.

sec4_1_intro_analysis_functions.title: Analysis of Functions I: Increase, Decrease, and Concavity

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

sec4_1_intro_analysis_functions.one_liner: This section develops mathematical tools to precisely determine the exact shape and key features of a graph, going beyond the general shapes provided by graphing utilities.
sec4_1_intro_analysis_functions.content: Although graphing utilities are useful for determining the general shape of a graph, many problems require more precision than these tools can provide. The purpose of this section is to develop mathematical tools that can be used to determine the exact shape of a graph and the precise locations of its key features, such as points of increase, decrease, and concavity.
sec4_1_intro_analysis_functions.motivation_md: While graphing utilities offer a visual overview, precise analysis of function behavior—like exact turning points, intervals of increase/decrease, and concavity—requires mathematical tools. This section introduces calculus-based methods to achieve that precision, enabling a deeper understanding of a function's graph.
sec4_1_intro_analysis_functions.recap_md: - Graphing utilities provide a general shape, but lack precision for many problems.- Mathematical tools are needed to determine the exact shape of a graph.- These tools help pinpoint the precise locations of key features like increase, decrease, and concavity.

idea_derivative_of_product_initial.title: Derivative of a product (initial exploration)
idea_derivative_of_product_initial.one_liner: A common misconception is that the derivative of a product of functions is the product of their derivatives, but a simple example demonstrates this is false.
idea_derivative_of_product_initial.content: You might be tempted to conjecture that the derivative of a product of two functions is the product of their derivatives. However, a simple example will show this to be false. Consider the functions $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^{2}$. The product of their derivatives is $f^{\prime}(x) g^{\prime}(x)=(1)(2 x)=2 x$. But their product is $h(x)=f(x) g(x)=x^{3}$, so the derivative of the product is $h^{\prime}(x)=3 x^{2}$. Thus, the derivative of the product is not equal to the product of the derivatives. The correct relationship, which is credited to Leibniz, is given by the following theorem. Formula (1) can also be expressed as $(f \cdot g)^{\prime}=f \cdot g^{\prime}+g \cdot f^{\prime}$.
idea_derivative_of_product_initial.motivation_md: Students often assume derivatives distribute over products. This concept highlights that this assumption is incorrect, setting the stage for the actual product rule by demonstrating the error with a concrete example.
idea_derivative_of_product_initial.recap_md: - The derivative of a product of functions is generally not the product of their individual derivatives.- For $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2$, $(fg)'(x) = 3x^2$, while $f'(x)g'(x) = 2x$.

thm_2_4_1_product_rule.title: The Product Rule
thm_2_4_1_product_rule.one_liner: The Product Rule states that if $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions, the derivative of their product $f \cdot g$ is $f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x)$.
thm_2_4_1_product_rule.content: 2.4.1 THEOREM (The Product Rule) If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$, then so is the product $f \cdot g$, and $$\frac{d}{d x}[f(x) g(x)]=f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]+g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)] \tag{1}$$
thm_2_4_1_product_rule.motivation_md: This rule provides the correct method for finding the derivative of a product of two functions, correcting the common misconception that it's simply the product of their individual derivatives.
thm_2_4_1_product_rule.recap_md: - If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable, their product $f \cdot g$ is also differentiable.- The derivative of the product is given by $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x) g(x)]=f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]+g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$.

idea_derivative_of_quotient_initial.title: Derivative of a quotient (initial exploration)
idea_derivative_of_quotient_initial.one_liner: Similar to products, the derivative of a quotient of functions is generally not the quotient of their derivatives.
idea_derivative_of_quotient_initial.content: Just as the derivative of a product is not generally the product of the derivatives, so the derivative of a quotient is not generally the quotient of the derivatives. The correct relationship is given by the following theorem.
idea_derivative_of_quotient_initial.motivation_md: This concept addresses another common misconception, clarifying that derivatives do not distribute over quotients. It sets the stage for introducing the specific rule needed for differentiating quotients.
idea_derivative_of_quotient_initial.recap_md: - The derivative of a quotient is not simply the quotient of the derivatives.- A specific rule is required to correctly differentiate functions that are quotients.

thm_2_4_2_quotient_rule.title: The Quotient Rule
thm_2_4_2_quotient_rule.one_liner: The Quotient Rule provides the formula for differentiating a quotient of two functions, stating that if $g(x) \neq 0$, then $(f/g)'(x) = (g(x)f'(x) - f(x)g'(x)) / [g(x)]^2$.
thm_2_4_2_quotient_rule.content: 2.4.2 THEOREM (The Quotient Rule) If $f$ and $g$ are both differentiable at $x$ and if $g(x) \neq 0$, then $f / g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $$\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]-f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]}{[g(x)]^{2}} \tag{2}$$
thm_2_4_2_quotient_rule.motivation_md: This theorem provides the essential formula for correctly calculating the derivative of a function expressed as a ratio of two other differentiable functions, which is crucial for many calculus problems.
thm_2_4_2_quotient_rule.recap_md: - If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable and $g(x) \neq 0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable.- The derivative of a quotient is $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{g(x) f^{\prime}(x)-f(x) g^{\prime}(x)}{[g(x)]^{2}}$.

technique_simplify_before_quotient_rule.title: Simplifying before differentiating quotients
technique_simplify_before_quotient_rule.one_liner: Simplifying a function algebraically before applying the quotient rule can often make differentiation significantly easier.
technique_simplify_before_quotient_rule.content: Sometimes it is better to simplify a function first than to apply the quotient rule immediately. For example, it is easier to differentiate $$f(x)=\frac{x^{3 / 2}+x}{\sqrt{x}}$$ by rewriting it as $$f(x)=x+\sqrt{x}$$ as opposed to using the quotient rule.
technique_simplify_before_quotient_rule.motivation_md: While the Quotient Rule is powerful, algebraic simplification can transform complex quotients into simpler sums or differences of power functions, making differentiation much faster and less prone to error.
technique_simplify_before_quotient_rule.recap_md: - Always look for opportunities to simplify a function algebraically before differentiating.- Rewriting a quotient as a sum or difference of terms can avoid the Quotient Rule.- For example, $\frac{x^{3 / 2}+x}{\sqrt{x}}$ simplifies to $x+\sqrt{x}$.

idea_deriv_trig_functions_intro.title: Introduction to Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
idea_deriv_trig_functions_intro.one_liner: This section aims to derive formulas for the derivatives of the six basic trigonometric functions, assuming all angles are measured in radians.
idea_deriv_trig_functions_intro.content: This section focuses on obtaining formulas for the derivatives of the six basic trigonometric functions. It is crucial to note that these formulas (including Formulas (1) and (2), and the derivations for (3) and (4)) are only valid if $h$ and $x$ are in radians. For how these formulas change when $x$ is measured in degrees, refer to Exercise 49. We will assume throughout this section that the variable $x$ in functions like $\sin x, \cos x$, $\tan x, \cot x, \sec x$, and $\csc x$ is measured in radians. A review of trigonometric functions can be found in Appendix B if needed. Additionally, we will utilize the limits from Theorem 1.6.5, restated with $h$ as the variable instead of $x$.
idea_deriv_trig_functions_intro.motivation_md: Understanding the derivatives of trigonometric functions is fundamental for analyzing periodic phenomena in physics, engineering, and other sciences. This section establishes these essential differentiation rules.
idea_deriv_trig_functions_intro.recap_md: - The goal is to find derivatives for $\sin x, \cos x, \tan x, \cot x, \sec x$, and $\csc x$.- All variables ($x$ and $h$) must be measured in radians for these formulas to be valid.- Prior knowledge of trigonometric functions and certain limits (Theorem 1.6.5) is assumed.

technique_derive_sin_x.title: Deriving the Derivative of Sine Function
technique_derive_sin_x.one_liner: The derivative of $f(x)=\sin x$ can be derived using the limit definition of the derivative, trigonometric identities, and special limits, ultimately showing it equals $\cos x$.
technique_derive_sin_x.content: Let us start with the problem of differentiating $f(x)=\sin x$. Using the definition of the derivative we obtain $$\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(x) & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \\& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin (x+h)-\sin x}{h} \\& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x \cos h+\cos x \sin h-\sin x}{h} \\& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left[\sin x\left(\frac{\cos h-1}{h}\right)+\cos x\left(\frac{\sin h}{h}\right)\right] \\& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left[\cos x\left(\frac{\sin h}{h}\right)-\sin x\left(\frac{1-\cos h}{h}\right)\right] \\& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \cos x \cdot \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin h}{h}-\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \sin x \cdot \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos h}{h} \\& =\left(\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \cos x\right)(1)-\left(\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \sin x\right)(0) \quad \text { Algebraic reorganization } \\& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \cos x=\cos x \quad \begin{array}{l}\cos x \text { does not involve the variable } h \text { and hence } \\ \text { is treated as a constant in the limit computation. }\end{array}\end{aligned}$$
technique_derive_sin_x.motivation_md: This derivation demonstrates how the fundamental definition of the derivative, combined with trigonometric identities and special limits, leads to a crucial differentiation rule. It builds a foundational understanding for other trigonometric derivatives.
technique_derive_sin_x.recap_md: - Start with the limit definition of the derivative for $f(x)=\sin x$.- Use the angle addition formula $\sin(x+h) = \sin x \cos h + \cos x \sin h$.- Apply the special limits $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{h} = 1$ and $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1-\cos h}{h} = 0$.- The result is $\frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] = \cos x$.

theorem_derivative_of_sin_x.title: Derivative of Sine Function
theorem_derivative_of_sin_x.one_liner: The derivative of the sine function with respect to $x$ is the cosine function of $x$, provided $x$ is in radians.
theorem_derivative_of_sin_x.motivation_md: This fundamental theorem provides a direct rule for differentiating the sine function, which is essential for solving problems involving periodic motion and oscillations in calculus and its applications.
theorem_derivative_of_sin_x.recap_md: - The derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$.- This rule is valid when $x$ is measured in radians.

logarithmic_differentiation_technique.title: Logarithmic Differentiation
logarithmic_differentiation_technique.one_liner: Logarithmic differentiation is a technique useful for differentiating functions composed of products, quotients, and powers.
logarithmic_differentiation_technique.content: Logarithmic differentiation is a technique useful for differentiating functions that are composed of products, quotients, and powers.
logarithmic_differentiation_technique.motivation_md: This technique simplifies the differentiation of complex functions involving products, quotients, and powers by transforming them into sums and differences using logarithms, making the derivative calculation more straightforward.
logarithmic_differentiation_technique.recap_md: - Logarithmic differentiation simplifies derivatives of complex products, quotients, and powers.- It involves taking the natural logarithm of both sides before differentiating implicitly.

logarithmic_differentiation_validity_rem.title: Remark on Logarithmic Differentiation Validity
