(a) If $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ on an open interval extending left from $x_0$ and $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ on an open interval extending right from $x_0$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_0$. (b) If $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ on an open interval extending left from $x_0$ and $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ on an open interval extending right from $x_0$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_0$. (c) If $f^{\prime}(x)$ has the same sign on an open interval extending left from $x_0$ as it does on an open interval extending right from $x_0$, then $f$ does not have a relative extremum at $x_0$. Proof for part (a): We assume $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ on $(a, x_0)$ and $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ on $(x_0, b)$. We want to show that $$ f\left(x_{0}\right) \geq f(x) $$ for all $x$ in the interval $(a, b)$. These hypotheses, along with Theorem 4.1.2, imply that $f$ is increasing on the interval $(a, x_0]$ and decreasing on the interval $[x_0, b)$. Therefore, $f(x_0) \geq f(x)$ for all $x$ in $(a, b)$, with equality only at $x_0$.
theorem_4_2_3_first_derivative_test.motivation_md: This theorem provides a definitive method for classifying critical points as relative maxima, minima, or neither. By analyzing the sign changes of the first derivative, it allows for a systematic approach to finding and characterizing local extrema of continuous functions.
theorem_4_2_3_first_derivative_test.recap_md: - If $f'$ changes from positive to negative at $x_0$, $f$ has a relative maximum. - If $f'$ changes from negative to positive at $x_0$, $f$ has a relative minimum. - If $f'$ does not change sign at $x_0$, $f$ has no relative extremum there.

idea_second_derivative_test_intuition.title: Intuition for Second Derivative Test

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

idea_second_derivative_test_intuition.one_liner: A function has a relative maximum at a stationary point if its graph is concave down, and a relative minimum if it is concave up.
idea_second_derivative_test_intuition.content: Another test for relative extrema is based on a geometric observation: A function $f$ has a relative maximum at a stationary point if its graph is concave down on an open interval containing that point. Conversely, it has a relative minimum if its graph is concave up (Figure 4.2.7).
idea_second_derivative_test_intuition.motivation_md: This intuition connects the concavity of a function's graph to the presence of relative extrema. It provides a visual and conceptual basis for the Second Derivative Test, offering an alternative way to classify stationary points without analyzing derivative sign changes.
idea_second_derivative_test_intuition.recap_md: - Relative maxima occur at stationary points where the graph is concave down. - Relative minima occur at stationary points where the graph is concave up.

theorem_4_2_4_second_derivative_test.title: Theorem 4.2.4: Second Derivative Test

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

theorem_4_2_4_second_derivative_test.one_liner: The Second Derivative Test uses the sign of $f''(x_0)$ at a stationary point $x_0$ to determine if it's a relative minimum ($f''>0$), maximum ($f''<0$), or if the test is inconclusive ($f''=0$).
theorem_4_2_4_second_derivative_test.content: Suppose that $f$ is twice differentiable at the point $x_0$. (a) If $f^{\prime}(x_0)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_0)>0$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_0$. (b) If $f^{\prime}(x_0)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_0)<0$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_0$. (c) If $f^{\prime}(x_0)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_0)=0$, then the test is inconclusive; $f$ may have a relative maximum, a relative minimum, or neither at $x_0$. [FIGURE:95b13d49a12faabf | The graph displays the function $y = 3x^5 - 5x^3$ on a Cartesian coordinate system with x and y axes labeled. The curve has a local maximum at approximately $x = -1$ with a y-value of $2$, and a...] Proof for part (a): Given $f^{\prime}(x_0)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_0)>0$. We express $f^{\prime \prime}(x_0)$ as a limit: $$ f^{\prime \prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f^{\prime}(x)-f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{x-x_{0}}>0 $$ This implies that for $x$ sufficiently close to, but different from, $x_0$, we have $\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{x-x_{0}}>0$. Thus, there is an open interval extending left from $x_0$ and an open interval extending right from $x_0$ where this inequality holds. On the interval to the left, the denominator is negative, so $f^{\prime}(x)<0$. On the interval to the right, the denominator is positive, so $f^{\prime}(x)>0$. By part (b) of the First Derivative Test (Theorem 4.2.3), $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_0$. Proof for part (c): To prove this, we need examples of functions where $f^{\prime}(x_0)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_0)=0$ at some $x_0$, but which exhibit different behaviors. Examples are $f(x)=x^4$ (relative minimum at $x=0$), $f(x)=-x^4$ (relative maximum at $x=0$), and $f(x)=x^3$ (neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum at $x_0=0$).
theorem_4_2_4_second_derivative_test.motivation_md: This test offers an alternative, often simpler, way to classify relative extrema at stationary points by using the second derivative. It leverages the concept of concavity to quickly determine if a critical point corresponds to a maximum or minimum, streamlining the analysis of function behavior.
theorem_4_2_4_second_derivative_test.recap_md: - If $f'(x_0)=0$ and $f''(x_0)>0$, $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_0$. - If $f'(x_0)=0$ and $f''(x_0)<0$, $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_0$. - If $f'(x_0)=0$ and $f''(x_0)=0$, the test is inconclusive.

idea_second_derivative_test_applicabilit.one_liner: The Second Derivative Test is often easier but applies only to stationary points where the second derivative exists, unlike the First Derivative Test which works for any critical point of a continuous function.
idea_second_derivative_test_applicabilit.content: The Second Derivative Test is often easier to apply than the First Derivative Test. However, the First Derivative Test can be used at any critical point of a continuous function, whereas the Second Derivative Test applies only at stationary points where the second derivative exists.
idea_second_derivative_test_applicabilit.motivation_md: Understanding the applicability of each test helps in choosing the most efficient method for finding extrema. This clarifies when the Second Derivative Test is a convenient shortcut and when the First Derivative Test is necessary due to broader applicability.
idea_second_derivative_test_applicabilit.recap_md: - Second Derivative Test is often easier to apply. - First Derivative Test applies to any critical point of a continuous function. - Second Derivative Test applies only to stationary points where $f''$ exists.

definition_multiplicity_of_root.title: Multiplicity of a Root

definition_multiplicity_of_root.one_liner: A root $x=r$ of a polynomial $p(x)$ has multiplicity $m$ if $(x-r)^m$ divides $p(x)$ but $(x-r)^{m+1}$ does not.
definition_multiplicity_of_root.content: To analyze and graph polynomials, it is helpful to understand how the graph behaves near its roots. For instance, one might wonder what property of a polynomial causes an inflection point and horizontal tangent at a root. A root $x=r$ of a polynomial $p(x)$ has multiplicity $m$ if $(x-r)^m$ divides $p(x)$ but $(x-r)^{m+1}$ does not. A root with multiplicity 1 is called a simple root. The behavior of a polynomial near a real root is determined by its multiplicity (Figure 4.2.9).
definition_multiplicity_of_root.motivation_md: Understanding the multiplicity of a root is crucial for predicting the behavior of a polynomial's graph near its x-intercepts. It helps explain phenomena like horizontal tangents or inflection points at roots, which is essential for accurate curve sketching and analysis.
definition_multiplicity_of_root.recap_md: - A root $x=r$ has multiplicity $m$ if $(x-r)^m$ divides $p(x)$ but $(x-r)^{m+1}$ does not. - A root of multiplicity 1 is called a simple root. - Multiplicity determines the polynomial's behavior near the root.

idea_3_6_warning_lhopitals_rule_differen.title: Warning: L'Hôpital's Rule Differentiates Separately
idea_3_6_warning_lhopitals_rule_differen.one_liner: L'Hôpital's rule requires differentiating the numerator and denominator individually, which is distinct from differentiating the quotient $f(x)/g(x)$.
idea_3_6_warning_lhopitals_rule_differen.content: When applying L'Hôpital's rule, it is important to note that the numerator and denominator are differentiated individually. This process is not equivalent to differentiating the entire quotient $f(x) / g(x)$ using the quotient rule.
idea_3_6_warning_lhopitals_rule_differen.motivation_md: This warning highlights a common mistake when applying L'Hôpital's Rule. Understanding this distinction is crucial to correctly evaluate limits of indeterminate forms and avoid misapplying differentiation rules.
idea_3_6_warning_lhopitals_rule_differen.recap_md: - L'Hôpital's rule differentiates $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ separately. - This is not the same as applying the quotient rule to $f(x)/g(x)$.

thm_3_6_1_lhopitals_rule_0_0.title: L'Hôpital's Rule for Form 0/0
thm_3_6_1_lhopitals_rule_0_0.one_liner: L'Hôpital's Rule for the indeterminate form $0/0$ states that if $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = 0$, then $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$, provided the latter limit exists.
thm_3_6_1_lhopitals_rule_0_0.content: Theorem 3.6.1, known as L'Hôpital's Rule for the indeterminate form $0/0$, applies when $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions on an open interval containing $x=a$ (except possibly at $x=a$), and both $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=0$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=0$. If the limit of the ratio of their derivatives, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}\left[f^{\prime}(x) / g^{\prime}(x)\right]$, exists (or is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$), then the limit of the original ratio is equal to it: $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)} $$ This rule also holds for one-sided limits ($x \rightarrow a^{-}$ or $x \rightarrow a^{+}$) and limits at infinity ($x \rightarrow-\infty$ or $x \rightarrow+\infty$).
thm_3_6_1_lhopitals_rule_0_0.motivation_md: L'Hôpital's Rule provides a powerful method for evaluating limits of rational functions or quotients that result in the indeterminate form $0/0$. Without it, many such limits would be difficult or impossible to solve using algebraic manipulation alone, making it a fundamental tool in calculus.
thm_3_6_1_lhopitals_rule_0_0.recap_md: - If $\lim f(x)=0$ and $\lim g(x)=0$, then $\lim \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ is an indeterminate form $0/0$. - L'Hôpital's Rule states that $\lim \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$ if the latter limit exists. - This rule applies to limits as $x \rightarrow a$, $x \rightarrow a^{\pm}$, and $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$.

technique_3_6_applying_lhopitals_rule.title: Applying L'Hôpital's Rule (Three-Step Process)
technique_3_6_applying_lhopitals_rule.one_liner: Applying L'Hôpital's Rule involves a three-step process: checking for an indeterminate form, differentiating the numerator and denominator separately, and then finding the limit of the new ratio.
technique_3_6_applying_lhopitals_rule.content: To apply L'Hôpital's rule, follow this three-step process: Step 1. First, verify that the limit of the ratio $f(x) / g(x)$ is an indeterminate form, specifically of type $0 / 0$ or $\infty / \infty$. Step 2. Next, differentiate the numerator function $f(x)$ and the denominator function $g(x)$ separately to obtain $f'(x)$ and $g'(x)$. Step 3. Finally, find the limit of the new ratio $f^{\prime}(x) / g^{\prime}(x)$. If this limit is finite, $+\infty$, or $-\infty$, then this value is equal to the original limit of $f(x) / g(x)$.
technique_3_6_applying_lhopitals_rule.motivation_md: This structured approach ensures L'Hôpital's Rule is applied correctly and efficiently. Following these steps helps prevent common errors, such as applying the rule to non-indeterminate forms or incorrectly differentiating the quotient.
technique_3_6_applying_lhopitals_rule.recap_md: - Step 1: Confirm the limit is an indeterminate form ($0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$). - Step 2: Differentiate the numerator and denominator individually. - Step 3: Evaluate the limit of the ratio of the derivatives; this is the original limit.

idea_3_6_warning_non_indeterminate_forms.title: Warning: L'Hôpital's Rule on Non-Indeterminate Forms
idea_3_6_warning_non_indeterminate_forms.one_liner: Applying L'Hôpital's rule to limits that are not indeterminate forms can lead to incorrect results, as demonstrated by an example where direct substitution yields the correct answer.
idea_3_6_warning_non_indeterminate_forms.content: It is crucial to understand that applying L'Hôpital's rule to limits that are not indeterminate forms will produce incorrect results. For instance, consider the limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{x+6}{x+2}$. If one were to incorrectly apply L'Hôpital's rule, the computation would be: $$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{x+6}{x+2} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{d}{d x}[x+6]}{\frac{d}{d x}[x+2]} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{1}=1 \end{aligned} $$ This result is invalid because the original limit is not an indeterminate form; direct substitution yields $\frac{0+6}{0+2}=3$, which is the correct result.
idea_3_6_warning_non_indeterminate_forms.motivation_md: This warning emphasizes the critical prerequisite for L'Hôpital's Rule: the limit must be an indeterminate form. Failing to check this condition can lead to significant errors, reinforcing the importance of understanding when and when not to apply the rule.
idea_3_6_warning_non_indeterminate_forms.recap_md: - L'Hôpital's Rule is only valid for indeterminate forms ($0/0$, $\infty/\infty$, etc.). - Applying the rule to non-indeterminate forms yields incorrect results. - Always check the form of the limit before applying L'Hôpital's Rule.

def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_infi.title: Indeterminate Form of Type infinity/infinity
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_infi.one_liner: An indeterminate form of type $\infty/\infty$ occurs when the limit of a ratio $f(x)/g(x)$ has both its numerator and denominator approaching $\infty$ (either $+\infty$ or $-\infty$).
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_infi.content: When discussing limits, if a function's limit (or a one-sided limit) approaches either $+\infty$ or $-\infty$, we can generally denote this as the limit being $\infty$ without specifying the sign. For example: $$ \begin{array}{ccccc} \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=\infty & \text { means } & \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty & \text { or } & \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=\infty & \text { means } & \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty & \text { or } & \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=-\infty \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=\infty & \text { means } & \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)= \pm \infty & \text { and } & \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)= \pm \infty \end{array} $$ An indeterminate form of type $\infty / \infty$ arises when the limit of a ratio $f(x) / g(x)$ involves both the numerator and the denominator approaching $\infty$. A version of L'Hôpital's rule exists to evaluate limits of this type.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_infi.motivation_md: Just as $0/0$ presents an ambiguous situation, $\infty/\infty$ also represents an indeterminate form where the relative 'speed' of growth of the numerator and denominator determines the limit. Defining this form is essential for extending L'Hôpital's Rule to a broader range of complex limit problems.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_infinity_infi.recap_md: - The symbol $\infty$ can represent either $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ in the context of limits. - An indeterminate form of type $\infty/\infty$ occurs when $\lim f(x)=\infty$ and $\lim g(x)=\infty$ for a ratio $f(x)/g(x)$. - L'Hôpital's Rule can be applied to evaluate limits of this type.

thm_3_6_2_lhopitals_rule_infinity_infini.title: L'Hôpital's Rule for Form infinity/infinity
thm_3_6_2_lhopitals_rule_infinity_infini.one_liner: L'Hôpital's Rule for the indeterminate form $\infty/\infty$ states that if $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \infty$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \infty$, then $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$, provided the latter limit exists.
thm_3_6_2_lhopitals_rule_infinity_infini.content: Theorem 3.6.2, L'Hôpital's Rule for the indeterminate form $\infty / \infty$, applies when $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions on an open interval containing $x=a$ (except possibly at $x=a$), and both $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=\infty$. If the limit of the ratio of their derivatives, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}\left[f^{\prime}(x) / g^{\prime}(x)\right]$, exists (or is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$), then the limit of the original ratio is equal to it: $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)} $$ This rule also holds for one-sided limits ($x \rightarrow a^{-}$ or $x \rightarrow a^{+}$) and limits at infinity ($x \rightarrow-\infty$ or $x \rightarrow+\infty$).
thm_3_6_2_lhopitals_rule_infinity_infini.motivation_md: This extension of L'Hôpital's Rule is crucial for evaluating limits where both the numerator and denominator grow without bound. It allows us to compare the 'strength' of growth of different functions, which is fundamental in analyzing function behavior at extremes.
thm_3_6_2_lhopitals_rule_infinity_infini.recap_md: - If $\lim f(x)=\infty$ and $\lim g(x)=\infty$, then $\lim \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ is an indeterminate form $\infty/\infty$. - L'Hôpital's Rule states that $\lim \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$ if the latter limit exists. - This rule applies to limits as $x \rightarrow a$, $x \rightarrow a^{\pm}$, and $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$.

idea_3_6_growth_exponential_functions.title: Analyzing the Growth of Exponential Functions using L'Hôpital's Rule
idea_3_6_growth_exponential_functions.one_liner: L'Hôpital's Rule can be used to demonstrate that exponential functions like $e^x$ eventually grow more rapidly than any positive integer power of $x$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$.
idea_3_6_growth_exponential_functions.content: Integer powers of $x$, such as $x^n$, approach $+\infty$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and serve as 'measuring sticks' for comparing function growth rates. While $e^x$ also grows rapidly as $x \rightarrow+\infty$, L'Hôpital's Rule can be used to compare its growth to that of $x^n$. By examining the ratio $x^{n} / e^{x}$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$, we can determine which function grows faster. For example, graphs suggest that $x^{5} / e^{x} \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$, implying $e^x$ grows more rapidly than $x^5$. Conversely, $e^{x} / x^{5} \rightarrow+\infty$ confirms this. More generally, L'Hôpital's rule proves that $e^x$ grows more rapidly than any positive integer power of $x$, leading to the limits: $$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{e^{x}}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{e^{x}}{x^{n}}=+\infty \tag{5-6} \end{equation*} $$ Both are indeterminate forms of type $\infty / \infty$. To establish the first limit, L'Hôpital's rule must be applied $n$ times. Each differentiation of $x^n$ reduces its exponent by one, eventually yielding $n!$ as the $n$th derivative. Since the derivative of $e^x$ is always $e^x$, applying the rule $n$ times results in: $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{e^{x}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{n!}{e^{x}}=0 $$ The second limit can be established similarly.
idea_3_6_growth_exponential_functions.motivation_md: Understanding the relative growth rates of functions, especially exponential versus polynomial, is crucial for analyzing asymptotic behavior and computational complexity. L'Hôpital's Rule provides a rigorous method to compare these growth rates, offering insights into how functions behave for very large inputs.
idea_3_6_growth_exponential_functions.recap_md: - L'Hôpital's Rule helps compare the growth rates of functions like $x^n$ and $e^x$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$. - The limits $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{e^{x}}=0$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{e^{x}}{x^{n}}=+\infty$ show $e^x$ grows faster than any $x^n$. - These limits are evaluated by applying L'Hôpital's Rule repeatedly ($n$ times).

def_3_6_indeterminate_form_0_infinity.title: Indeterminate Form of Type 0 * infinity
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_0_infinity.one_liner: An indeterminate form of type $0 \cdot \infty$ occurs when the limit of a product $f(x) \cdot g(x)$ has one factor approaching 0 and the other approaching $\infty$, creating conflicting influences.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_0_infinity.content: Beyond $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$, other indeterminate forms exist. Generally, an expression's limit is an indeterminate form if the individual limits of its components, such as $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, exert conflicting influences on the overall expression's limit. These forms can include: $$ \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}, \quad f(x) \cdot g(x), \quad f(x)^{g(x)}, \quad f(x)-g(x), \quad f(x)+g(x) $$ For example, the limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} x \ln x$ is an indeterminate form of type $\mathbf{0} \cdot \infty$. This is because the first factor, $x$, approaches 0, while the second factor, $\ln x$, approaches $-\infty$. These conflicting tendencies make the product's limit indeterminate.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_0_infinity.motivation_md: Recognizing various indeterminate forms is essential because L'Hôpital's Rule, in its direct form, only applies to $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$. Understanding other forms like $0 \cdot \infty$ allows us to algebraically manipulate them into a suitable ratio for L'Hôpital's Rule, expanding its applicability.
def_3_6_indeterminate_form_0_infinity.recap_md: - Indeterminate forms arise when individual limits of components conflict, like $0 \cdot \infty$. - $0 \cdot \infty$ occurs when one factor approaches 0 and the other approaches $\infty$. - Other indeterminate forms include $f(x)^{g(x)}$, $f(x)-g(x)$, and $f(x)+g(x)$.

idea_4_3_graphing_other_functions.one_liner: The calculus tools used for graphing polynomials and rational functions can also analyze and graph trigonometric, logarithmic, exponential, and other functions.
idea_4_3_graphing_other_functions.content: The methods discussed for graphing polynomials, rational functions, and functions with cusps and vertical tangent lines can be extended. The same calculus tools used to analyze these functions are applicable to analyze and graph trigonometric functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, and an endless variety of other kinds of functions.
idea_4_3_graphing_other_functions.motivation_md: This concept highlights the versatility of calculus tools. It shows that the techniques learned for graphing basic function types like polynomials and rational functions are not limited to them, but can be universally applied to understand and visualize a much broader range of mathematical functions.
idea_4_3_graphing_other_functions.recap_md: - Calculus tools are useful for graphing various function types.- These tools apply to polynomials, rational functions, trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions.

idea_conclusions_and_graph.one_liner: Analyzing the signs of $y$, $dy/dx$, and $d^2y/dx^2$ for $f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$ reveals the graph is always above the x-axis, has a relative maximum at $x=0$, and inflection points at $x=\pm 1$.
idea_conclusions_and_graph.content: The sign analysis of $y$ (as shown in Figure 4.3.8a) is based on the fact that $e^{-x^{2} / 2}>0$ for all $x$, indicating the graph is always above the $x$-axis. The sign analysis of $d y / d x$ (also in Figure 4.3.8a) is based on $d y / d x=-x e^{-x^{2} / 2}$ having the same sign as $-x$. This analysis, combined with the first derivative test, shows a stationary point at $x=0$ which is a relative maximum, where $y=e^{0}=1$. Furthermore, the sign analysis of $d^{2} y / d x^{2}$ (in Figure 4.3.8a) relies on $d^{2} y / d x^{2}= \left(x^{2}-1\right) e^{-x^{2} / 2}$ having the same sign as $x^{2}-1$. This reveals inflection points at $x=-1$ and $x=1$, where the graph changes concavity from up to down at $x=-1$ and from down to up at $x=1$. The coordinates of these inflection points are $\left(-1, e^{-1 / 2}\right) \approx(-1,0.61)$ and $\left(1, e^{-1 / 2}\right) \approx(1,0.61)$. The complete graph is presented in Figure 4.3.8b.
idea_conclusions_and_graph.motivation_md: This concept demonstrates how to systematically interpret the results of first and second derivative tests to understand the complete behavior of a function's graph. By analyzing the signs of the function and its derivatives, one can precisely locate extrema, inflection points, and determine concavity, leading to an accurate sketch.
idea_conclusions_and_graph.recap_md: - The sign of $y$ determines if the graph is above or below the x-axis.- The sign of $dy/dx$ identifies relative extrema and intervals of increase/decrease.- The sign of $d^2y/dx^2$ indicates concavity and inflection points.

idea_graphing_calculus_technology.title: Graphing using calculus and technology together

idea_graphing_calculus_technology.one_liner: This concept explores using calculus to precisely analyze features like extrema and inflection points on a graph initially produced by technology, and to identify any potentially missed features.
idea_graphing_calculus_technology.content: Up to this point, calculus has been used to produce graphs of functions, with the graph being the final outcome. This section reverses that process: starting with a graph generated by a graphing utility, the goal is to apply calculus tools to determine the exact locations of relative extrema, inflection points, and other features suggested by the technological graph. Additionally, calculus helps ascertain whether the graph might be missing important features that should be visible.
idea_graphing_calculus_technology.motivation_md: While graphing utilities are powerful, they can sometimes obscure or inaccurately represent critical features of a function. This approach combines the speed of technology with the precision of calculus, allowing for a thorough verification and enhancement of computer-generated graphs, ensuring all significant characteristics are identified and accurately located.
idea_graphing_calculus_technology.recap_md: - Calculus can refine graphs generated by technology.- Use calculus to find exact extrema and inflection points from a technological graph.- Calculus helps identify features a graphing utility might miss.

idea_absolute_maxima_minima_intro.title: Introduction to Absolute Maxima and Minima

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_absolute_maxima_minima_intro.one_liner: This section introduces the concept of absolute maxima and minima, which are the highest and lowest points of a function over an entire interval, in contrast to relative extrema which are local.
idea_absolute_maxima_minima_intro.content: As observed earlier in Section 4.2, if a function's graph is visualized as a two-dimensional mountain range (Figure 4.2.1), relative maxima and minima represent the tops of hills and bottoms of valleys, respectively, signifying high and low points within their immediate vicinity. This section, however, addresses the broader challenge of identifying the highest and lowest points across the entire mountain range. Mathematically, this means finding the largest and smallest values a function attains over a given interval.
idea_absolute_maxima_minima_intro.motivation_md: While relative extrema identify local peaks and valleys, many real-world problems require finding the absolute best or worst outcome over a given domain. This concept provides the framework for identifying the global maximum or minimum value of a function, which is crucial for optimization problems in various fields.
idea_absolute_maxima_minima_intro.recap_md: - Relative extrema are local high or low points.- Absolute extrema are the highest or lowest points over an entire interval.- Finding absolute extrema means identifying the function's largest and smallest values.

def_absolute_extrema.title: Absolute maximum, minimum, and extremum

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

def_absolute_extrema.one_liner: A function $f$ has an absolute maximum at $x_0$ if $f(x) \leq f(x_0)$ for all $x$ in the interval, and an absolute minimum if $f(x_0) \leq f(x)$ for all $x$ in the interval.
def_absolute_extrema.content: DEFINITION 4.4.1: Consider an interval within the domain of a function $f$ and a point $x_{0}$ located in that interval. The function $f$ is said to have an absolute maximum at $x_{0}$ if $f(x) \leq f\left(x_{0}\right)$ for all $x$ in the given interval. Conversely, $f$ has an absolute minimum at $x_{0}$ if $f\left(x_{0}\right) \leq f(x)$ for all $x$ in the interval. If $f$ possesses either an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum at $x_{0}$, it is said to have an absolute extremum at that point.
def_absolute_extrema.motivation_md: This definition formalizes the concept of global highest and lowest points for a function over a specified domain. It provides the precise mathematical language needed to identify and discuss the overall maximum or minimum values a function can attain, which is fundamental for solving optimization problems in calculus and applied sciences.
def_absolute_extrema.recap_md: - An absolute maximum occurs at $x_0$ if $f(x_0)$ is the largest value in the interval.- An absolute minimum occurs at $x_0$ if $f(x_0)$ is the smallest value in the interval.- An absolute extremum refers to either an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum.

thm_4_4_2_extreme_value_theorem.title: Extreme-Value Theorem

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_4_4_2_extreme_value_theorem.one_liner: The Extreme-Value Theorem states that a function continuous on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$ is guaranteed to have both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on that interval.
thm_4_4_2_extreme_value_theorem.content: THEOREM 4.4.2 (Extreme-Value Theorem): If a function $f$ is continuous on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then it is guaranteed that $f$ has both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on that interval $[a, b]$.
thm_4_4_2_extreme_value_theorem.motivation_md: This theorem is fundamental because it guarantees the existence of absolute extrema under specific, common conditions. Without this guarantee, searching for maximum or minimum values might be futile. It provides the theoretical basis for optimization problems, ensuring that a solution (an absolute extremum) actually exists before one attempts to find it.
thm_4_4_2_extreme_value_theorem.recap_md: - The theorem applies to continuous functions.- The interval must be finite and closed, denoted as $[a, b]$.- Under these conditions, an absolute maximum and minimum are guaranteed to exist.

technique_finding_absolute_extrema_close.title: Procedure for Finding Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

technique_finding_absolute_extrema_close.one_liner: To find absolute extrema of a continuous function on a finite closed interval, find critical points, evaluate the function at these points and the endpoints, then identify the largest and smallest values.
technique_finding_absolute_extrema_close.content: A Procedure for Finding the Absolute Extrema of a Continuous Function $f$ on a Finite Closed Interval $[a, b]$: Step 1: Identify all critical points of the function $f$ that lie within the open interval $(a, b)$. Step 2: Evaluate the function $f$ at each of these critical points, as well as at the endpoints $a$ and $b$ of the interval. Step 3: From the collection of values obtained in Step 2, the largest value represents the absolute maximum value of $f$ on $[a, b]$, and the smallest value represents the absolute minimum.
technique_finding_absolute_extrema_close.motivation_md: This procedure provides a systematic and reliable method for finding the absolute maximum and minimum values of a continuous function on a closed interval. It leverages the Extreme-Value Theorem's guarantee of existence and the fact that extrema can only occur at critical points or endpoints, simplifying the search process for optimization problems.
technique_finding_absolute_extrema_close.recap_md: - Find critical points within the open interval $(a, b)$.- Evaluate the function at all critical points and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$.- The largest value is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.

idea_absolute_extrema_infinite_intervals.title: Absolute Extrema on Infinite Intervals

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_absolute_extrema_infinite_intervals.one_liner: A continuous function may or may not have absolute extrema on an infinite interval, but their existence can be inferred from the function's behavior as $x$ approaches $\pm\infty$.
idea_absolute_extrema_infinite_intervals.content: As previously observed (see Figure 4.4.1), a continuous function might or might not possess absolute extrema when considered over an infinite interval. Nevertheless, specific conclusions regarding the existence of absolute extrema for a continuous function $f$ on the interval $(-\infty,+\infty)$ can be derived by analyzing the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $-\infty$ and as $x$ approaches $+\infty$ (refer to Table 4.4.2).
idea_absolute_extrema_infinite_intervals.motivation_md: Unlike closed intervals where the Extreme-Value Theorem guarantees extrema, infinite intervals present a more complex scenario. This concept addresses how to determine the existence of absolute extrema in such cases by examining the function's end behavior, which is crucial for understanding global properties of functions over their entire natural domain.
idea_absolute_extrema_infinite_intervals.recap_md: - Absolute extrema are not guaranteed for continuous functions on infinite intervals.- The existence of extrema depends on the function's behavior as $x \rightarrow \pm\infty$.- Analyzing limits at infinity helps determine if absolute extrema exist.

idea_velocity_interpretation_mvt.title: Velocity Interpretation of the Mean-Value Theorem

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_velocity_interpretation_mvt.one_liner: The Mean-Value Theorem implies that for a car's journey, its instantaneous velocity must equal its average velocity at least once during the trip.
idea_velocity_interpretation_mvt.content: The Mean-Value Theorem has a useful interpretation when $x=f(t)$ represents the position of a car moving along a straight road over time. In this scenario, the right side of the theorem's equation (1) signifies the car's average velocity over the time interval from $a \leq t \leq b$, while the left side represents the instantaneous velocity at some time $t=c$. Consequently, the Mean-Value Theorem states that at least once during the time interval, the car's instantaneous velocity must be equal to its average velocity. This aligns with real-world experience: if a trip's average velocity is $40 \mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$, the speedometer must read $40 \mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$ at some point during the journey.
idea_velocity_interpretation_mvt.motivation_md: This interpretation helps ground the abstract Mean-Value Theorem in a tangible, real-world scenario. By relating it to the familiar concept of a car's velocity, it provides an intuitive understanding of what the theorem implies about instantaneous versus average rates of change, making its implications more accessible and easier to grasp.
idea_velocity_interpretation_mvt.recap_md: - The Mean-Value Theorem can be applied to a car's position-time curve. - It states that instantaneous velocity must equal average velocity at least once during a trip. - This aligns with everyday experience, like a speedometer reading the average speed.

thm_4_1_2_revisited_increasing_decreasin.title: Increasing/Decreasing/Constant Function Theorem (Revisited)

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_4_1_2_revisited_increasing_decreasin.one_liner: This theorem states that the sign of the first derivative determines whether a continuous and differentiable function is increasing, decreasing, or constant on an interval.
thm_4_1_2_revisited_increasing_decreasin.content: 4.1.2 THEOREM (Revisited) Let $f$ be a function that is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$. (a) If $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is increasing on $[a, b]$. (b) If $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is decreasing on $[a, b]$. (c) If $f^{\prime}(x)=0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$.
thm_4_1_2_revisited_increasing_decreasin.motivation_md: This theorem is fundamental because it establishes a direct connection between the sign of a function's derivative and its behavior. It provides a powerful tool for analyzing the shape of a graph, allowing us to determine where a function is rising, falling, or staying flat without needing to plot many points.
thm_4_1_2_revisited_increasing_decreasin.recap_md: - If $f'(x)>0$ on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is increasing on $[a,b]$. - If $f'(x)<0$ on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is decreasing on $[a,b]$. - If $f'(x)=0$ on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is constant on $[a,b]$.

thm_4_8_3_constant_difference_theorem.title: Constant Difference Theorem

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_4_8_3_constant_difference_theorem.one_liner: The Constant Difference Theorem states that if two functions have identical derivatives over an interval, then their difference must be a constant on that interval.
thm_4_8_3_constant_difference_theorem.content: 4.8.3 THEOREM (Constant Difference Theorem) If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable on an interval, and if $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x)$ for all $x$ in that interval, then $f-g$ is constant on the interval; that is, there is a constant $k$ such that $f(x)-g(x)=k$ or, equivalently, $$f(x)=g(x)+k$$ for all $x$ in the interval.
thm_4_8_3_constant_difference_theorem.motivation_md: This theorem is crucial for understanding the relationship between functions and their antiderivatives. It explains why indefinite integrals always include an arbitrary constant ' $+C$', by showing that any two functions with the same derivative must differ by a constant value.
thm_4_8_3_constant_difference_theorem.recap_md: - If $f'(x)=g'(x)$ on an interval, then $f(x)-g(x)$ is constant on that interval. - This means $f(x)=g(x)+k$ for some constant $k$. - It highlights that functions with the same derivative differ only by a constant.

def_n_factorial.title: n-factorial

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

def_n_factorial.one_liner: The expression $n!$, read as n-factorial, denotes the product of the first $n$ positive integers for $n \geq 1$.
def_n_factorial.content: For $n \geq 1$, the expression $n!$, read as $\boldsymbol{n}$-factorial, denotes the product of the first $n$ positive integers.
def_n_factorial.motivation_md: The factorial function is essential in mathematics, particularly in combinatorics for counting permutations, in probability theory, and in calculus for defining Taylor series and power series. It provides a concise notation for products of consecutive integers.
def_n_factorial.recap_md: - $n!$ is read as "n-factorial". - It represents the product of the first $n$ positive integers. - This definition applies for $n \geq 1$.

thm_4_4_3_absolute_extremum_open_interva.title: Theorem 4.4.3: Absolute Extremum on an Open Interval

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_4_4_3_absolute_extremum_open_interva.one_liner: If a function has an absolute extremum on an open interval, this extremum must occur at a critical point of the function.
thm_4_4_3_absolute_extremum_open_interva.content: 4.4.3 THEOREM If $f$ has an absolute extremum on an open interval $(a, b)$, then it must occur at a critical point of $f$.
thm_4_4_3_absolute_extremum_open_interva.motivation_md: This theorem is vital for finding absolute extrema on open intervals. It simplifies the search by directing us to examine only the critical points, rather than the entire interval, thus providing a systematic approach to optimization problems.
thm_4_4_3_absolute_extremum_open_interva.recap_md: - This theorem applies to functions with absolute extrema on open intervals. - Any such extremum must be located at a critical point of the function. - It helps narrow down the search for absolute maximums or minimums.

least_squares_principle.title: Least Squares Principle

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

least_squares_principle.one_liner: The least squares principle states that an estimate $\bar{x}$ of an unknown quantity $x$, based on multiple measurements, should be chosen to minimize a certain quantity.
least_squares_principle.content: When an unknown physical quantity $x$ is measured $n$ times, the measurements $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ often vary due to uncontrollable factors like temperature or atmospheric pressure. Scientists frequently need to use these $n$ different observed measurements to obtain an estimate $\bar{x}$ of the unknown quantity $x$. One method for making such an estimate is based on the least squares principle, which states that the estimate $\bar{x}$ should be chosen to minimize
least_squares_principle.motivation_md: Measurements of physical quantities are rarely exact due to various factors. The least squares principle provides a systematic method for finding the "best" estimate of an unknown quantity from multiple, potentially varying, observations, aiming to minimize the discrepancies between the estimate and the observed data.
least_squares_principle.recap_md: - The least squares principle is a method for estimating an unknown quantity $x$ from multiple measurements $x_1, \ldots, x_n$.- It states that the estimate $\bar{x}$ should be chosen to minimize a specific quantity (implied by the truncated text).

rectilinear_motion_definition.title: Rectilinear Motion

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

rectilinear_motion_definition.one_liner: Rectilinear motion describes a particle moving in either direction along a single coordinate line, with its position $s(t)$ being a function of time.
rectilinear_motion_definition.content: A particle that can move in either direction along a coordinate line is said to be in rectilinear motion. This line could be an $x$-axis, a $y$-axis, or a coordinate line inclined at some angle; in general discussions, it will be designated as the $s$-axis. We assume that units are chosen for measuring distance and time, and that observations begin at time $t=0$. As the particle moves along the $s$-axis, its coordinate $s$ is a function of time, denoted $s=s(t)$. This $s(t)$ is called the position function of the particle, and its graph versus $t$ is the position versus time curve. If a particle's coordinate at time $t_{1}$ is $s(t_{1})$ and at a later time $t_{2}$ is $s(t_{2})$, then $s(t_{2})-s(t_{1})$ is defined as the displacement of the particle over the time interval $[t_{1}, t_{2}]$. Displacement describes the change in the particle's position.
rectilinear_motion_definition.motivation_md: Understanding motion along a straight line is fundamental in physics and calculus. Rectilinear motion provides a simplified model to introduce concepts like position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration before moving to more complex multi-dimensional motion. It lays the groundwork for analyzing rates of change.
rectilinear_motion_definition.recap_md: - Rectilinear motion refers to a particle moving along a single coordinate line (e.g., the $s$-axis).- The particle's coordinate $s$ is a function of time, $s(t)$, called the position function.- Displacement over $[t_1, t_2]$ is the change in position, $s(t_2) - s(t_1)$.

position_function.title: Position Function

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

position_function.one_liner: The position function, $s(t)$, describes a particle's coordinate $s$ along a coordinate line as a function of time $t$ in rectilinear motion.
position_function.content: In rectilinear motion, where a particle moves along a coordinate line, its coordinate $s$ is a function of time, denoted $s=s(t)$. This $s(t)$ is called the position function of the particle. The graph of $s$ versus $t$ is known as the position versus time curve. If the particle's coordinate at time $t_{1}$ is $s(t_{1})$ and at a later time $t_{2}$ is $s(t_{2})$, then $s(t_{2})-s(t_{1})$ is defined as the displacement of the particle over the time interval $[t_{1}, t_{2}]$, which describes the change in position.
position_function.motivation_md: The position function is crucial for mathematically describing and analyzing motion. By expressing position as a function of time, we can use calculus to determine other important kinematic quantities like velocity and acceleration, and predict future positions.
position_function.recap_md: - The position function $s(t)$ gives the coordinate $s$ of a particle at time $t$.- It is used to describe rectilinear motion along a coordinate line.- The difference $s(t_2) - s(t_1)$ represents the displacement over the interval $[t_1, t_2]$.

position_versus_time_curve.title: Position versus Time Curve

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

position_versus_time_curve.one_liner: The position versus time curve is the graph of a particle's position function $s(t)$ against time $t$, illustrating its motion along a coordinate line.
position_versus_time_curve.content: In rectilinear motion, where a particle moves along a coordinate line, its coordinate $s$ is a function of time, denoted $s=s(t)$. This $s(t)$ is called the position function of the particle, and the graph of $s$ versus $t$ is specifically called the position versus time curve. If the particle's coordinate at time $t_{1}$ is $s(t_{1})$ and at a later time $t_{2}$ is $s(t_{2})$, then $s(t_{2})-s(t_{1})$ is defined as the displacement of the particle over the time interval $[t_{1}, t_{2}]$, which describes the change in position.
position_versus_time_curve.motivation_md: Visualizing motion is often easier than just looking at equations. The position versus time curve provides a graphical representation of a particle's movement, allowing for quick interpretation of its position, direction, and changes in motion over time.
position_versus_time_curve.recap_md: - The position versus time curve is a graph of the position function $s(t)$ against time $t$.- It visually represents a particle's rectilinear motion.- The curve helps to understand changes in position and displacement over time.

velocity_function_definition.title: Velocity Function

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

velocity_function_definition.one_liner: The velocity function $v(t)$ for a particle in rectilinear motion is defined as the instantaneous rate of change of its position function $s(t)$, given by its derivative $s'(t)$.
velocity_function_definition.content: The instantaneous velocity of a particle in rectilinear motion is the derivative of its position function. Therefore, if a particle in rectilinear motion has a position function $s(t)$, its velocity function $v(t)$ is defined as:$$ \begin{equation*} v(t)=s^{\prime}(t)=\frac{d s}{d t} \tag{1} \end{equation*} $$
velocity_function_definition.motivation_md: Velocity quantifies both the speed and direction of motion, providing more information than just position. Defining it as the derivative of the position function connects the geometric idea of a tangent line to the physical concept of instantaneous rate of change, which is central to calculus.
velocity_function_definition.recap_md: - The velocity function $v(t)$ describes the instantaneous velocity of a particle in rectilinear motion.- It is defined as the derivative of the position function $s(t)$.- Mathematically, $v(t) = s'(t) = \frac{ds}{dt}$.

speed_definition.title: Speed

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

speed_definition.one_liner: Speed is defined as the absolute value of velocity, distinguishing how fast a particle is moving from its direction of motion.
speed_definition.content: For a particle in rectilinear motion, it is important to differentiate between its velocity and its speed. Velocity describes both how fast and in what direction the particle is moving, whereas speed describes only how fast it is moving. This distinction is made by defining speed as the absolute value of velocity. For example, a particle with a velocity of $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ has a speed of $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and moves in the positive direction. Conversely, a particle with a velocity of $-2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ also has a speed of $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ but moves in the negative direction. Since instantaneous speed is the absolute value of instantaneous velocity, the speed function is defined as:$$ \begin{equation*} |v(t)|=\left|s^{\prime}(t)\right|=\left|\frac{d s}{d t}\right| \tag{2} \end{equation*} $$
speed_definition.motivation_md: In many real-world scenarios, knowing "how fast" something is moving is more relevant than its precise direction. Speed provides a scalar measure of motion, simplifying analysis when direction is secondary, and is crucial for understanding energy and collision dynamics.
speed_definition.recap_md: - Speed is a scalar quantity that describes only how fast a particle is moving.- Velocity is a vector quantity that describes both speed and direction.- Speed is defined as the absolute value of velocity, i.e., $|v(t)|$.

acceleration_function_definition.title: Acceleration Function

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

acceleration_function_definition.one_liner: The acceleration function $a(t)$ is defined as the instantaneous rate of change of a particle's velocity function $v(t)$, or the second derivative of its position function $s(t)$.
acceleration_function_definition.content: In rectilinear motion, the instantaneous acceleration of a particle is defined as the rate at which its instantaneous velocity changes with time. Therefore, if a particle has a velocity function $v(t)$, its acceleration function is defined as:$$ \begin{equation*} a(t)=v^{\prime}(t)=\frac{d v}{d t} \tag{3} \end{equation*} $$Alternatively, since $v(t)=s^{\prime}(t)$, the acceleration function can also be expressed in terms of the position function as:$$ \begin{equation*} a(t)=s^{\prime \prime}(t)=\frac{d^{2} s}{d t^{2}} \tag{4} \end{equation*} $$
acceleration_function_definition.motivation_md: Acceleration describes how velocity changes over time, which is crucial for understanding forces and predicting future motion. As the second derivative of position, it demonstrates the power of calculus to model complex physical phenomena and provides a link to Newton's laws of motion.
acceleration_function_definition.recap_md: - Instantaneous acceleration is the rate of change of instantaneous velocity.- The acceleration function $a(t)$ is the derivative of the velocity function $v(t)$, so $a(t) = v'(t)$.- It is also the second derivative of the position function $s(t)$, so $a(t) = s''(t)$.

speeding_up_slowing_down_definition.title: Speeding Up and Slowing Down

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

speeding_up_slowing_down_definition.one_liner: A particle in rectilinear motion is speeding up when its speed is increasing and slowing down when its speed is decreasing.
speeding_up_slowing_down_definition.content: A particle in rectilinear motion is defined as speeding up when its speed is increasing and slowing down when its speed is decreasing. In everyday language, an object that is speeding up is often called "accelerating," and one that is slowing down is called "decelerating." Consequently, one might intuitively expect a particle to speed up when its acceleration is positive and slow down when its acceleration is negative. However, while this holds true for a particle moving in the positive direction, it is not universally true for a particle moving in the...
speeding_up_slowing_down_definition.motivation_md: Understanding when an object is speeding up or slowing down is crucial for analyzing its motion accurately. This concept clarifies the distinction between acceleration's sign and the change in speed, highlighting that positive acceleration doesn't always mean speeding up, especially when direction is considered.
speeding_up_slowing_down_definition.recap_md: - A particle is speeding up if its speed is increasing.- A particle is slowing down if its speed is decreasing.- The relationship between acceleration's sign and speeding up/slowing down is not always straightforward, especially for negative velocities.

def_cost_revenue_profit_functions.title: Cost, Revenue, and Profit Functions

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

def_cost_revenue_profit_functions.one_liner: The cost function $C(x)$, revenue function $R(x)$, and profit function $P(x)$ are important for economists and manufacturers, representing total cost, revenue, and profit for $x$ units.
def_cost_revenue_profit_functions.content: For an economist or manufacturer, three key functions are defined: $C(x)$ represents the total cost of producing $x$ units of a product during a specific time period; $R(x)$ represents the total revenue generated from selling $x$ units of the product during that period; and $P(x)$ represents the total profit obtained from selling $x$ units of the product during that period. These are known as the cost function, revenue function, and profit function, respectively. If all units produced are sold, these functions are related.
def_cost_revenue_profit_functions.motivation_md: Understanding cost, revenue, and profit functions is fundamental for businesses and economists to analyze financial performance. These functions allow for the calculation of profitability, optimization of production, and informed decision-making regarding pricing and output levels, providing a clear financial model for operations.
def_cost_revenue_profit_functions.recap_md: - $C(x)$ is the total cost of producing $x$ units. - $R(x)$ is the total revenue from selling $x$ units. - $P(x)$ is the total profit from selling $x$ units. - If all units are sold, these functions are related.

def_total_cost_components.title: Total Cost, Overhead, and Manufacturing Cost

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

def_total_cost_components.one_liner: The total cost $C(x)$ of producing $x$ units is the sum of a constant overhead $a$ and a manufacturing cost function $M(x)$.
def_total_cost_components.content: The total cost $C(x)$ of producing $x$ units can be expressed as a sum: $$C(x)=a+M(x)$$ where $a$ is a constant, referred to as overhead, and $M(x)$ is a function representing the manufacturing cost. Overhead includes fixed costs like rent and insurance, and it does not depend on $x$; it must be paid even if no units are produced. In contrast, the manufacturing cost $M(x)$, which covers items such as materials and labor, depends on the number of items manufactured. In economics, with suitable simplifying assumptions, $M(x)$ can often be expressed in a specific form.
def_total_cost_components.motivation_md: Breaking down total cost into its components (fixed overhead and variable manufacturing costs) is crucial for accurate financial analysis. This distinction helps businesses understand how costs behave with varying production levels, enabling better budgeting, pricing strategies, and decisions about scaling operations.
def_total_cost_components.recap_md: - Total cost $C(x)$ is the sum of overhead $a$ and manufacturing cost $M(x)$. - Overhead $a$ is a constant fixed cost, independent of production volume. - Manufacturing cost $M(x)$ varies with the number of units produced.

idea_marginal_analysis.title: Marginal Analysis

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_marginal_analysis.one_liner: Marginal analysis is an economic concept that examines the additional benefits or costs of one more unit of an activity.
idea_marginal_analysis.motivation_md: Marginal analysis is a fundamental tool in economics and business for making optimal decisions. It helps determine whether to produce one more unit, hire one more employee, or invest in one more project by comparing the incremental benefits against the incremental costs.
idea_marginal_analysis.recap_md: - Marginal analysis focuses on the change in an outcome from one additional unit of input. - It is used to make decisions at the 'margin' of production or consumption.

def_marginal_profit_revenue_cost.title: Marginal Profit, Revenue, and Cost

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

def_marginal_profit_revenue_cost.one_liner: Economists define marginal profit, marginal revenue, and marginal cost as the derivatives $P^{\prime}(x)$, $R^{\prime}(x)$, and $C^{\prime}(x)$, interpreting them as the additional profit, revenue, or cost from producing and selling one more unit.
def_marginal_profit_revenue_cost.content: Economists refer to $P^{\prime}(x)$, $R^{\prime}(x)$, and $C^{\prime}(x)$ as the marginal profit, marginal revenue, and marginal cost, respectively. These quantities are interpreted as the additional profit, revenue, and cost that result from producing and selling one additional unit of a product when the current production and sales levels are at $x$ units. This interpretation stems from the local linear approximations of the profit, revenue, and cost functions. For instance, based on Formula (2) of Section 3.5, the local linear approximation of the profit function when production and sales are at $x$ units is given by: $$P(x+\Delta x) \approx P(x)+P^{\prime}(x) \Delta x$$ If $\Delta x=1$ (representing one additional unit produced and sold), this formula implies: $$P(x+1) \approx P(x)+P^{\prime}(x)$$ Consequently, the additional profit from producing and selling one additional unit can be approximated as: $$P(x+1)-P(x) \approx P^{\prime}(x)$$ Similarly, the additional revenue and cost can be approximated as $R(x+1)-R(x) \approx R^{\prime}(x)$ and $C(x+1)-C(x) \approx C^{\prime}(x)$.
def_marginal_profit_revenue_cost.motivation_md: Marginal concepts are essential for businesses to make incremental decisions. By understanding the marginal profit, revenue, and cost, companies can determine the optimal production level, price points, and resource allocation to maximize profitability and efficiency, focusing on the impact of each additional unit.
def_marginal_profit_revenue_cost.recap_md: - Marginal profit, revenue, and cost are the derivatives $P^{\prime}(x)$, $R^{\prime}(x)$, and $C^{\prime}(x)$. - They approximate the change in profit, revenue, or cost from producing one additional unit. - This interpretation is based on local linear approximation: $P(x+1)-P(x) \approx P^{\prime}(x)$.

idea_basic_principle_economics.title: A Basic Principle of Economics

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_basic_principle_economics.one_liner: A basic principle of economics often relates to optimizing outcomes by balancing marginal costs and benefits.
idea_basic_principle_economics.content: This section introduces a basic principle of economics.
idea_basic_principle_economics.motivation_md: Economic principles provide foundational insights into how markets, individuals, and businesses behave. Understanding these principles is crucial for analyzing economic phenomena, predicting outcomes, and formulating policies that promote efficiency and welfare.
idea_basic_principle_economics.recap_md: - Economics relies on fundamental principles to explain behavior and outcomes. - These principles often involve concepts like scarcity, incentives, and trade-offs.

thm_maximum_profit_principle.title: Maximum Profit Principle

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_maximum_profit_principle.one_liner: The Maximum Profit Principle states that maximum profit occurs when marginal revenue equals marginal cost, meaning the cost of an additional unit approximately equals its generated revenue.
thm_maximum_profit_principle.content: It follows from (23) that the equation $P^{\prime}(x)=0$ has the same solution as $C^{\prime}(x)=R^{\prime}(x)$. This implies that the maximum profit must occur at a point where the marginal revenue is equal to the marginal cost. Therefore, if profit is maximized, the cost of manufacturing and selling an additional unit of a product is approximately equal to the revenue generated by that additional unit.
thm_maximum_profit_principle.motivation_md: This principle is a cornerstone for businesses aiming to maximize their profits. By equating marginal revenue and marginal cost, companies can identify the optimal production level where producing more units would decrease overall profit, providing a clear target for operational efficiency.
thm_maximum_profit_principle.recap_md: - Maximum profit occurs when marginal revenue equals marginal cost ($R^{\prime}(x) = C^{\prime}(x)$). - This condition is derived from setting the marginal profit $P^{\prime}(x)$ to zero. - At maximum profit, the cost of one more unit approximately equals its revenue.

fermat_principle.title: Fermat's Principle

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

fermat_principle.one_liner: Fermat's principle in optics states that light travels along the path of minimum total travel time, which in a uniform medium means the shortest distance.
fermat_principle.content: Fermat's principle (biography on p.275) in optics states that light traveling from one point to another follows the path for which the total travel time is minimum. In a uniform medium, the paths of "minimum time" and "shortest distance" are the same, so that light, if unobstructed, travels along a straight line. Assume that we have a light source, a flat mirror, and an observer in a uniform medium. If a light ray leaves the source, bounces off the mirror, and travels on to the observer, then its path will consist of two line segments, as shown in Figure Ex-62. According to Fermat's principle, the path will be such that the total travel time $t$ is minimum or, since the medium is uniform, the path will be such that the total distance traveled from $A$ to $P$ to $B$ is as small as possible. Assuming the minimum occurs when $d t / d x=0$, show that the light ray will strike the mirror at the point $P$ where the "angle of incidence" $\theta_{1}$ equals the "angle of reflection" $\theta_{2}$.
fermat_principle.motivation_md: Fermat's principle provides a fundamental variational approach to understanding light's behavior, explaining phenomena like reflection and refraction from a single unifying concept. It demonstrates how calculus can be applied to derive physical laws, showing that nature often follows paths of least action or time.
fermat_principle.recap_md: - Fermat's principle states light follows the path of minimum travel time. - In a uniform medium, this means the path of shortest distance. - Applying this principle to reflection shows that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

snells_law_of_refraction.title: Snell's Law of Refraction

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

snells_law_of_refraction.one_liner: Snell's law of refraction, derived from Fermat's principle, describes how light bends when traveling between two media, relating the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction to the speeds of light in each medium.
snells_law_of_refraction.content: Fermat's principle (Exercise 62) also explains why light rays traveling between air and water undergo bending (refraction). Imagine that we have two uniform media (such as air and water) and a light ray traveling from a source $A$ in one medium to an observer $B$ in the other medium (Figure Ex-63). It is known that light travels at a constant speed in a uniform medium, but more slowly in a dense medium (such as water) than in a thin medium (such as air). Consequently, the path of shortest time from $A$ to $B$ is not necessarily a straight line, but rather some broken line path $A$ to $P$ to $B$ allowing the light to take greatest advantage of its higher speed through the thin medium. Snell's law of refraction (biography on p. 288) states that the path of the light ray will be such that $$\frac{\sin \theta_{1}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sin \theta_{2}}{v_{2}}$$ where $v_{1}$ is the speed of light in the first medium, $v_{2}$ is the speed of light in the second medium, and $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ are the angles shown in Figure Ex-63. Show that this follows from the assumption that the path of minimum time occurs when $d t / d x=0$.
snells_law_of_refraction.motivation_md: Snell's Law is crucial for understanding how lenses, prisms, and optical fibers work, forming the basis of many optical technologies. It explains why objects appear distorted underwater and is fundamental to fields like ophthalmology, photography, and telecommunications, where light manipulation is key.
snells_law_of_refraction.recap_md: - Snell's law describes light refraction (bending) when passing between two media. - It relates the ratio of the sine of the angle to the speed of light in each medium: $\frac{\sin \theta_{1}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sin \theta_{2}}{v_{2}}$. - This law can be derived from Fermat's principle of minimum travel time.

theorem_4_2_5_geometric_implications_mul.title: Theorem 4.2.5: Geometric Implications of Multiplicity

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

theorem_4_2_5_geometric_implications_mul.one_liner: This theorem describes the geometric behavior of a polynomial's graph at a root $x=r$ based on the multiplicity $m$ of that root.
theorem_4_2_5_geometric_implications_mul.content: Suppose that $p(x)$ is a polynomial with a root of multiplicity $m$ at $x=r$. (a) If $m$ is even, then the graph of $y=p(x)$ is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$, does not cross the $x$-axis there, and does not have an inflection point there. (b) If $m$ is odd and greater than 1, then the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$, crosses the $x$-axis there, and also has an inflection point there. (c) If $m=1$ (so that the root is simple), then the graph is not tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$, crosses the $x$-axis there, and may or may not have an inflection point there.
theorem_4_2_5_geometric_implications_mul.motivation_md: Understanding root multiplicity helps predict the shape of a polynomial's graph at its x-intercepts without extensive calculations, providing insight into tangency, crossing behavior, and inflection points.
theorem_4_2_5_geometric_implications_mul.recap_md: - If multiplicity $m$ is even, the graph is tangent to the x-axis at $x=r$ but does not cross it, and has no inflection point there. - If $m$ is odd and greater than 1, the graph is tangent to the x-axis at $x=r$, crosses it, and has an inflection point there. - If $m=1$ (a simple root), the graph crosses the x-axis at $x=r$ but is not tangent, and an inflection point may or may not exist.

idea_analysis_of_polynomials.title: Analysis of Polynomials and Curve Sketching

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

idea_analysis_of_polynomials.one_liner: Curve sketching now focuses on identifying important features of a function's graph, often starting with a computer-generated plot, rather than drawing it by hand.
idea_analysis_of_polynomials.content: Historically, the term "curve sketching" meant using calculus to help draw the graph of a function by hand; the graph was the goal. Since graphs can now be produced with great precision using calculators and computers, the purpose of curve sketching has changed. Today, we typically start with a graph produced by a calculator or computer, then use curve sketching to identify important features of the graph that the calculator or computer might have missed. Thus, the goal of curve sketching is no longer the graph itself, but rather the information it reveals about the function. Polynomials are among the simplest functions to graph and analyze. Their significant features are symmetry, intercepts, relative extrema, inflection points, and the behavior as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. Figure 4.2.11 shows the graphs of four polynomials in $x$. The graphs in Figure 4.2.11 have properties that are common to all polynomials: - The natural domain of a polynomial is $(-\infty,+\infty)$. - Polynomials are continuous everywhere. - Polynomials are differentiable everywhere, so their graphs have no corners or vertical tangent lines. - The graph of a nonconstant polynomial eventually increases or decreases without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. This is because the limit of a nonconstant polynomial as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ is $\pm \infty$, depending on the sign of the term of highest degree and whether the polynomial has even or odd degree [see Formulas (17) and (18) of Section 1.3 and the related discussion]. - The graph of a polynomial of degree $n(>2)$ has at most $n$ $x$-intercepts, at most $n-1$ relative extrema, and at most $n-2$ inflection points. This is because the $x$-intercepts, relative extrema, and inflection points of a polynomial $p(x)$ are among the real solutions of the equations $p(x)=0$, $p^{\prime}(x)=0$, and $p^{\prime \prime}(x)=0$, and the polynomials in these equations have degree $n$, $n-1$, and $n-2$, respectively. Thus, for example, the graph of a quadratic polynomial has at most two $x$-intercepts, one relative extremum, and no inflection points; and the graph of a cubic polynomial has at most three $x$-intercepts, two relative extrema, and one inflection point.
idea_analysis_of_polynomials.motivation_md: Understanding polynomial properties is crucial for analyzing their behavior and accurately interpreting their graphs, especially when using computational tools that might obscure subtle features. Curve sketching helps reveal these important characteristics.
idea_analysis_of_polynomials.recap_md: - Curve sketching now focuses on identifying key graph features like extrema and inflection points, complementing computer-generated graphs. - Polynomials are continuous and differentiable everywhere, with domains $(-\infty, +\infty)$. - A polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ x-intercepts, $n-1$ relative extrema, and $n-2$ inflection points.

idea_4_3_properties_of_graphs.title: Properties of Graphs

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

idea_4_3_properties_of_graphs.one_liner: Analyzing a function's graph involves identifying key properties like symmetries, intercepts, extrema, asymptotes, and concavity, with relevance varying by function type and analysis objective.
idea_4_3_properties_of_graphs.content: In many problems, the properties of interest in the graph of a function are: symmetries, $x$-intercepts, relative extrema, intervals of increase and decrease, asymptotes, periodicity, $y$-intercepts, concavity, inflection points, and behavior as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. Some of these properties may not be relevant in certain cases; for example, asymptotes are characteristic of rational functions but not of polynomials, and periodicity is characteristic of trigonometric functions but not of polynomial or rational functions. Thus, when analyzing the graph of a function $f$, it helps to know something about the general properties of the family to which it belongs. In a given problem you will usually have a definite objective for your analysis of a graph. For example, you may be interested in showing all of the important characteristics of the function, you may only be interested in the behavior of the graph as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, or you may be interested in some specific feature such as a particular inflection point. Thus, your objectives in the problem will dictate those characteristics on which you want to focus.
idea_4_3_properties_of_graphs.motivation_md: Identifying specific graphical properties helps in understanding a function's behavior and solving problems, as different function types exhibit different relevant features, and the analysis can be tailored to specific objectives.
idea_4_3_properties_of_graphs.recap_md: - Key graph properties include symmetries, intercepts, extrema, asymptotes, concavity, and end behavior. - The relevance of properties varies by function type (e.g., asymptotes for rational, periodicity for trigonometric). - Analysis objectives determine which specific graph characteristics to focus on.

technique_4_3_graphing_rational_function.title: Graphing a Rational Function (No Common Factors)

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

technique_4_3_graphing_rational_function.one_liner: This technique outlines a seven-step process for graphing rational functions $f(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$ where $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have no common factors, covering symmetries, intercepts, asymptotes, sign analysis, and derivatives.
technique_4_3_graphing_rational_function.content: To graph a rational function $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$ if $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have no Common Factors, follow these steps: Step 1. (Symmetries). Determine whether there is symmetry about the $y$-axis or the origin. Step 2. ($x$- and $y$-intercepts). Find the $x$- and $y$-intercepts. Step 3. (Vertical asymptotes). Find the values of $x$ for which $Q(x)=0$. The graph has a vertical asymptote at each such value. Step 4. (Sign of $f(x)$). The only places where $f(x)$ can change sign are at the $x$-intercepts or vertical asymptotes. Mark the points on the $x$-axis at which these occur and calculate a sample value of $f(x)$ in each of the open intervals determined by these points. This will tell you whether $f(x)$ is positive or negative over that interval. Step 5. (End behavior). Determine the end behavior of the graph by computing the limits of $f(x)$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. If either limit has a finite value $L$, then the line $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote. Step 6. (Derivatives). Find $f^{\prime}(x)$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x)$. Step 7. (Conclusions and graph). Analyze the sign changes of $f^{\prime}(x)$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x)$ to determine the intervals where $f(x)$ is increasing, decreasing, concave up, and concave down. Determine the locations of all stationary points, relative extrema, and inflection points. Use the sign analysis of $f(x)$ to determine the behavior of the graph in the vicinity of the vertical asymptotes. Sketch a graph of $f$ that exhibits these conclusions.
technique_4_3_graphing_rational_function.motivation_md: This systematic approach ensures all critical features of a rational function's graph are identified, allowing for an accurate sketch and comprehensive understanding of its behavior, especially when $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ share no common factors.
technique_4_3_graphing_rational_function.recap_md: - Start by finding symmetries, $x$- and $y$-intercepts, and vertical asymptotes. - Analyze the sign of $f(x)$ in intervals and determine end behavior to find horizontal asymptotes. - Use first and second derivatives to find intervals of increase/decrease, concavity, extrema, and inflection points, then sketch the graph.

idea_4_3_rational_functions_oblique_curv.title: Rational Functions with Oblique or Curvilinear Asymptotes

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

idea_4_3_rational_functions_oblique_curv.one_liner: Rational functions where the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's can have oblique (slant) or curvilinear asymptotes, which are determined by the quotient polynomial from polynomial division.
idea_4_3_rational_functions_oblique_curv.content: When the degree of the numerator of a rational function is greater than the degree of the denominator, other kinds of "asymptotes" are possible. For example, consider the rational functions $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}+1}{x}$ and $g(x)=\frac{x^{3}-x^{2}-8}{x-1}$. By division we can rewrite these as $f(x)=x+\frac{1}{x}$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-\frac{8}{x-1}$. Since the second terms both approach 0 as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, it follows that $(f(x)-x) \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ and $(g(x)-x^{2}) \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. Geometrically, this means that the graph of $y=f(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the line $y=x$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The line $y=x$ is called an oblique or slant asymptote of $f$. Similarly, the graph of $y=g(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The parabola is called a curvilinear asymptote of $g$. The graphs of the functions in (1) are shown in Figures 4.3.3 and 4.3.4. In general, if $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$ is a rational function, then we can find quotient and remainder polynomials $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ such that $f(x)=q(x)+\frac{r(x)}{Q(x)}$ and the degree of $r(x)$ is less than the degree of $Q(x)$. Then $r(x) / Q(x) \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, so $y=q(x)$ is an asymptote of $f$. This asymptote will be an oblique line if the degree of $P(x)$ is one greater than the degree of $Q(x)$, and it will be curvilinear if the degree of $P(x)$ exceeds that of $Q(x)$ by two or more. Problems involving these kinds of asymptotes are given in the exercises (Exercises 17 and 18).
idea_4_3_rational_functions_oblique_curv.motivation_md: Understanding oblique and curvilinear asymptotes allows for a complete analysis of rational functions where the numerator's degree is greater than the denominator's, revealing their long-term behavior beyond simple horizontal asymptotes.
idea_4_3_rational_functions_oblique_curv.recap_md: - If $\text{deg}(P(x)) > \text{deg}(Q(x))$, rational functions can have oblique or curvilinear asymptotes. - These asymptotes are found by performing polynomial division, where $f(x) = q(x) + r(x)/Q(x)$. - The asymptote is $y=q(x)$, which is oblique if $\text{deg}(P(x)) = \text{deg}(Q(x)) + 1$ and curvilinear if $\text{deg}(P(x)) \ge \text{deg}(Q(x)) + 2$.

definition_4_3_oblique_curvilinear_asymp.title: Oblique and Curvilinear Asymptotes
