position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

definition_4_3_oblique_curvilinear_asymp.one_liner: An oblique or curvilinear asymptote $y=q(x)$ describes the long-term behavior of a rational function $f(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$ when the degree of $P(x)$ is greater than or equal to the degree of $Q(x)$.
definition_4_3_oblique_curvilinear_asymp.content: If the graph of $y=f(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to a line $y=mx+b$ (where $m \ne 0$) as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, that line is called an oblique or slant asymptote of $f$. If it approaches a curve $y=q(x)$ (where $q(x)$ is a polynomial of degree 2 or higher), that curve is called a curvilinear asymptote of $f$. In general, for a rational function $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$, we can use polynomial division to find quotient and remainder polynomials $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ such that $f(x)=q(x)+\frac{r(x)}{Q(x)}$, where the degree of $r(x)$ is less than the degree of $Q(x)$. As $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, the term $r(x) / Q(x) \rightarrow 0$, so $y=q(x)$ is an asymptote of $f$. This asymptote will be an oblique line if the degree of $P(x)$ is one greater than the degree of $Q(x)$. It will be curvilinear if the degree of $P(x)$ exceeds that of $Q(x)$ by two or more.
definition_4_3_oblique_curvilinear_asymp.motivation_md: These definitions provide precise language to describe the asymptotic behavior of rational functions whose numerators have a higher degree than their denominators, extending the concept of asymptotes beyond horizontal lines.
definition_4_3_oblique_curvilinear_asymp.recap_md: - An oblique (slant) asymptote is a line $y=mx+b$ ($m \ne 0$) that a function approaches as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. - A curvilinear asymptote is a curve $y=q(x)$ (degree $\ge 2$) that a function approaches as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. - For $f(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$, the asymptote is $y=q(x)$ from polynomial division $P(x)/Q(x) = q(x) + r(x)/Q(x)$.

idea_4_3_graphs_vertical_tangents_cusps.title: Graphs with Vertical Tangents and Cusps

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

idea_4_3_graphs_vertical_tangents_cusps.one_liner: Graphs can exhibit vertical tangent lines or cusps at points where the function is not differentiable, often seen in functions involving radicals or fractional exponents.
idea_4_3_graphs_vertical_tangents_cusps.content: Figure 4.3.5 shows four curve elements that are commonly found in graphs of functions that involve radicals or fractional exponents. In all four cases, the function is not differentiable at $x_{0}$ because the secant line through $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$ and $(x, f(x))$ approaches a vertical position as $x$ approaches $x_{0}$ from either side. Thus, in each case, the curve has a vertical tangent line at $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$. In parts (a) and (b) of the figure, there is an inflection point at $x_{0}$ because there is a change in concavity at that point. In parts (c) and (d), where $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_{0}$ and $-\infty$ from the other side, we say that the graph has a cusp at $x_{0}$.
idea_4_3_graphs_vertical_tangents_cusps.motivation_md: Recognizing vertical tangents and cusps is essential for accurately sketching graphs and understanding function behavior at points where differentiability fails, particularly for functions with radicals or fractional exponents.
idea_4_3_graphs_vertical_tangents_cusps.recap_md: - Vertical tangent lines occur where a function is not differentiable, and secant lines approach a vertical position. - An inflection point can occur at a vertical tangent if there's a change in concavity. - A cusp occurs at $x_0$ if $f'(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_0$ and $-\infty$ from the other side (or vice versa).

definition_4_3_vertical_tangent_line_cus.title: Vertical Tangent Line and Cusp

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS
position.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

definition_4_3_vertical_tangent_line_cus.one_liner: A vertical tangent line occurs at $x_0$ if the function is not differentiable there and secant lines approach a vertical position; a cusp is a specific case where $f'(x)$ approaches opposite infinities from either side of $x_0$.
definition_4_3_vertical_tangent_line_cus.content: A function has a vertical tangent line at $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$ if it is not differentiable at $x_{0}$ because the secant line through $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$ and $(x, f(x))$ approaches a vertical position as $x$ approaches $x_{0}$ from either side. In such cases, there may or may not be an inflection point at $x_{0}$ depending on whether there is a change in concavity. A graph has a cusp at $x_{0}$ if $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_{0}$ and $-\infty$ from the other side (or vice versa).
definition_4_3_vertical_tangent_line_cus.motivation_md: These definitions provide precise terms for describing specific non-differentiable points on a graph, which are crucial for accurately characterizing the local behavior of functions, especially those with sharp turns or vertical slopes.
definition_4_3_vertical_tangent_line_cus.recap_md: - A vertical tangent line exists at $x_0$ if the function is not differentiable there and secant lines become vertical. - A cusp occurs at $x_0$ when $f'(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side and $-\infty$ from the other (or vice versa). - Inflection points can coincide with vertical tangents if concavity changes.

idea_absolute_extrema_open_intervals.title: Absolute Extrema on Open Intervals

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_absolute_extrema_open_intervals.one_liner: While continuous functions on open intervals may lack absolute extrema, their existence can be inferred from the function's behavior at the interval's endpoints.
idea_absolute_extrema_open_intervals.content: A continuous function may or may not have absolute extrema on an open interval. However, for a continuous function $f$ on a finite open interval $(a, b)$, conclusions about the existence of absolute extrema can be drawn by examining the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$ and as $x \rightarrow b^{-}$ (Table 4.4.3). Similar conclusions apply to infinite open intervals like $(-\infty, b)$ or $(a,+\infty)$.
idea_absolute_extrema_open_intervals.motivation_md: The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees extrema on closed intervals, but open intervals are more complex. This concept helps determine if absolute extrema exist on open intervals by analyzing function behavior at boundaries, extending our ability to find maximums and minimums in more general cases.
idea_absolute_extrema_open_intervals.recap_md: - A continuous function on an open interval may not have absolute extrema.- The existence of extrema can be inferred from the function's behavior as $x$ approaches the interval's endpoints.- This applies to both finite open intervals $(a,b)$ and infinite intervals like $(-\infty, b)$ or $(a, +\infty)$.

idea_single_relative_extremum_implies_ab.title: Absolute Extrema of Functions with One Relative Extremum

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_single_relative_extremum_implies_ab.one_liner: For a continuous function with only one relative extremum on an interval, that extremum is also an absolute extremum.
idea_single_relative_extremum_implies_ab.content: If a continuous function possesses only one relative extremum on a given finite or infinite interval, then this relative extremum must also be an absolute extremum. To illustrate why this is true, consider a function $f$ with a relative maximum at $x_0$ within an interval, and assume there are no other relative extrema of $f$ on that interval. If $f(x_0)$ were not the absolute maximum of $f$ on the interval, the graph of $f$ would need to make an upward turn somewhere to exceed $f(x_0)$. However, this scenario is impossible because making an upward turn would inherently create a second relative extremum (Figure 4.4.6). Therefore, $f(x_0)$ must serve as both the absolute maximum and a relative maximum. This principle is formally stated in a theorem, presented without proof. [FIGURE:e36b6b31685e497d | A graph displays a continuous curve with two relative extrema. The curve first rises to a relative maximum, whose x-coordinate is marked as $x_0$, then falls to a relative minimum, and subsequently...] △ Figure 4.4.6 [FIGURE:4383cc2898da9911 | A 2D graph plots the function $f(x) = e^{(x^3 - 3x^2)}$ on the interval $(0, +\infty)$. The blue curve starts at $(0, 1)$, decreases to a local minimum near $(2, e^{-4})$, and then increases sharply...] △ Figure 4.4.7 Does the function in Example 6 have an absolute minimum on the interval $(-\infty,+\infty)$ ?
idea_single_relative_extremum_implies_ab.motivation_md: This concept provides a powerful shortcut for finding absolute extrema. When a function has only one "peak" or "valley" on an interval, we don't need to check endpoints or other critical points, simplifying optimization problems significantly. It's especially useful for functions on open or infinite intervals where the Extreme Value Theorem doesn't directly apply.
idea_single_relative_extremum_implies_ab.recap_md: - If a continuous function has only one relative extremum on an interval, it is also an absolute extremum.- This applies to both relative minima and relative maxima.- The absence of other extrema prevents the function from surpassing this single extremum.

thm_4_4_4_single_relative_extremum_impli.title: Theorem 4.4.4: Single Relative Extremum Implies Absolute Extremum

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_4_4_4_single_relative_extremum_impli.one_liner: Theorem 4.4.4 states that if a continuous function has exactly one relative extremum on an interval, that extremum is also the absolute extremum.
thm_4_4_4_single_relative_extremum_impli.content: Theorem 4.4.4: Suppose that $f$ is continuous and has exactly one relative extremum on an interval, say at $x_{0}$. (a) If $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_{0}$, then $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the absolute minimum of $f$ on the interval. (b) If $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_{0}$, then $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the absolute maximum of $f$ on the interval.
thm_4_4_4_single_relative_extremum_impli.motivation_md: This theorem provides a rigorous mathematical basis for identifying absolute extrema in specific scenarios. It's particularly useful in optimization problems where a function might only have one critical point within a given domain, simplifying the process of finding global maximums or minimums without needing to check boundary conditions extensively.
thm_4_4_4_single_relative_extremum_impli.recap_md: - If a continuous function $f$ has only one relative extremum at $x_0$ on an interval:- A relative minimum at $x_0$ implies $f(x_0)$ is the absolute minimum.- A relative maximum at $x_0$ implies $f(x_0)$ is the absolute maximum.

idea_4_5_classification_optimization_pro.title: Classification of Optimization Problems

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_4_5_classification_optimization_pro.one_liner: Optimization problems are classified into two types: those on finite closed intervals, where solutions are guaranteed, and those on open or infinite intervals, which may or may not have solutions.
idea_4_5_classification_optimization_pro.content: Applied optimization problems are categorized into two main types: 1. Problems that involve maximizing or minimizing a continuous function over a finite closed interval. 2. Problems that involve maximizing or minimizing a continuous function over an infinite interval or a finite interval that is not closed. For the first type of problem, the Extreme-Value Theorem (4.4.2) ensures that a solution exists. This solution can be found by evaluating the function at its critical points and at the endpoints of the interval. In contrast, problems of the second type may or may not have a solution. If the function is continuous and has exactly one relative extremum of the correct type on the interval, Theorem 4.4.4 guarantees a solution and outlines a method for finding it. When Theorem 4.4.4 is not applicable, solving the problem may require additional ingenuity.
idea_4_5_classification_optimization_pro.motivation_md: Classifying optimization problems helps students choose the correct strategy for finding solutions. Knowing whether a problem falls into a "guaranteed solution" category (closed interval) or a "may or may not have a solution" category (open/infinite interval) directs the application of theorems like the Extreme Value Theorem or Theorem 4.4.4, streamlining problem-solving.
idea_4_5_classification_optimization_pro.recap_md: - Optimization problems are categorized by the type of interval: finite closed or open/infinite.- Finite closed interval problems guarantee a solution via the Extreme-Value Theorem.- Open or infinite interval problems may or may not have a solution, sometimes solvable by Theorem 4.4.4.

idea_pierre_de_fermat_biography.title: Pierre de Fermat (1601-1665) and his contributions to calculus and number theory

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_pierre_de_fermat_biography.one_liner: Pierre de Fermat (1601-1665) was a French lawyer and amateur mathematician who made significant contributions to calculus, analytic geometry, number theory, and probability, famously posing 'Fermat's Last Theorem'.
idea_pierre_de_fermat_biography.content: Pierre de Fermat (1601-1665), the son of a successful French leather merchant, was a lawyer who pursued mathematics as a hobby. He earned a Bachelor of Civil Laws degree from the University of Orleans in 1631 and subsequently held various government positions, including a post as councillor to the Toulouse parliament. Although he was financially successful, historical documents suggest his performance in office and as a lawyer was poor, possibly due to his extensive devotion to mathematics. Throughout his life, Fermat resisted all attempts to publish his mathematical findings. He often scribbled his work in book margins and sent results to friends without keeping copies, leading to him not receiving credit for many major achievements until the mid-nineteenth century. It is now recognized that Fermat, independently of Descartes, developed analytic geometry, though they famously argued over various problems, preventing cooperation. Fermat solved many fundamental calculus problems, including the first procedure for differentiating polynomials and important maximization, minimization, area, and tangent problems, inspiring Isaac Newton. He is most renowned for his work in number theory, studying properties and relationships of whole numbers, becoming the first mathematician to make substantial contributions after Diophantus. Unfortunately, his contemporaries did not appreciate his number theory work, leading to his isolation later in life. Besides calculus and number theory, Fermat co-founded probability theory and made major contributions to optics. Outside mathematics, he was a notable classical scholar, fluent in French, Italian, Spanish, Latin, and Greek, and composed Latin poetry. A great mystery in mathematics stems from Fermat's work in number theory. In a book margin by Diophantus, he wrote that for integer values of $n > 2$, the equation $x^n + y^n = z^n$ has no nonzero integer solutions for $x, y,$ and $z$. He famously added, "I have discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which however the margin is not large enough to contain." This result, known as "Fermat's Last Theorem," remained unproven for 300 years until Professor Andrew Wiles of Princeton University presented a proof in June 1993, which drew international media attention. The initial proof had a serious gap, which Wiles and Richard Taylor fixed and published in 1995. A 100,000 German marks prize offered in 1908 for the solution is now worthless due to inflation.
idea_pierre_de_fermat_biography.motivation_md: Understanding the historical context and the contributions of mathematicians like Pierre de Fermat enriches the study of calculus. It shows that mathematical concepts often have deep roots, evolve over centuries, and are the result of passionate individuals, even those who pursued it as a hobby, inspiring students with the human story behind the formulas.
idea_pierre_de_fermat_biography.recap_md: - Pierre de Fermat (1601-1665) was a French lawyer and amateur mathematician.- He made significant contributions to calculus (differentiation, max/min problems), analytic geometry, number theory, and probability.- Fermat famously proposed "Fermat's Last Theorem," which remained unproven for 300 years until Andrew Wiles's proof in 1995.

technique_procedure_applied_max_min_prob.title: Procedure for Solving Applied Maximum and Minimum Problems

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

technique_procedure_applied_max_min_prob.one_liner: This procedure outlines five steps for solving applied maximum and minimum problems, from drawing a figure to using calculus techniques.
technique_procedure_applied_max_min_prob.content: A Procedure for Solving Applied Maximum and Minimum Problems: Step 1. Draw an appropriate figure and label all quantities relevant to the problem. Step 2. Develop a formula for the quantity that needs to be maximized or minimized. Step 3. Use the conditions provided in the problem to eliminate variables, expressing the quantity to be maximized or minimized as a function of a single variable. Step 4. Determine the interval of possible values for this variable, based on the physical restrictions inherent in the problem. Step 5. If applicable, apply the techniques discussed in the preceding section to find the maximum or minimum value.
technique_procedure_applied_max_min_prob.motivation_md: Applied maximum and minimum problems are common in various fields, from engineering to economics. This structured procedure provides a systematic approach to tackle these problems, breaking down complex scenarios into manageable steps. It ensures that all necessary information is considered and that the appropriate calculus techniques are applied to find optimal solutions.
technique_procedure_applied_max_min_prob.recap_md: - Start by drawing and labeling a figure for the problem.- Formulate the quantity to be optimized as a function of one variable.- Determine the domain (interval) for this variable based on physical constraints.- Apply calculus techniques (from previous sections) to find the maximum or minimum.

idea_ill_posed_optimization_problems.title: Ill-posed optimization problems

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_ill_posed_optimization_problems.one_liner: Optimization problems that have no solution, such as finding an absolute maximum when the function increases without bound, are referred to as ill-posed problems.
idea_ill_posed_optimization_problems.content: As seen in Example 5, the surface area $S$ may not have an absolute maximum if $S$ increases without bound as the radius $r$ approaches 0 (Figure 4.5.8). Consequently, if the problem had sought the dimensions of a can requiring the maximum amount of material, no solution would exist. Optimization problems that lack a solution are sometimes termed ill-posed.
idea_ill_posed_optimization_problems.motivation_md: It's crucial to understand that not all optimization problems have solutions. Recognizing "ill-posed" problems prevents wasted effort in searching for non-existent extrema. This concept highlights the importance of analyzing function behavior and domain constraints, ensuring that the problem is well-defined before attempting a solution.
idea_ill_posed_optimization_problems.recap_md: - Not all optimization problems have a solution.- If a quantity to be optimized increases or decreases without bound, an absolute extremum may not exist.- Optimization problems with no solution are called ill-posed problems.

idea_application_to_economics.title: An Application to Economics

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_application_to_economics.one_liner: This section explores how calculus concepts, specifically optimization, can be applied to solve problems in economics.
idea_application_to_economics.content: This section focuses on an application of calculus to the field of economics.
idea_application_to_economics.motivation_md: Calculus provides powerful tools for modeling and solving real-world problems. This concept introduces how optimization techniques, such as finding maximum profit or minimum cost, are directly relevant and widely used in economic analysis, demonstrating the practical utility of the mathematical concepts learned.
idea_application_to_economics.recap_md: - Calculus principles have direct applications in economics.- Optimization techniques are particularly useful for economic problems.- This section will demonstrate these applications.

interpreting_sign_of_acceleration.title: Interpreting the Sign of Acceleration

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

interpreting_sign_of_acceleration.one_liner: A particle in rectilinear motion speeds up when its velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and slows down when they have opposite signs.
interpreting_sign_of_acceleration.content: A particle undergoing rectilinear motion speeds up when its velocity and acceleration share the same sign. Conversely, the particle slows down when its velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.
interpreting_sign_of_acceleration.motivation_md: Understanding the relationship between the signs of velocity and acceleration is crucial for describing the motion of an object. This concept provides a straightforward rule to determine whether an object is speeding up or slowing down, which is fundamental in kinematics.
interpreting_sign_of_acceleration.recap_md: - Speeding up occurs when velocity and acceleration have the same sign. - Slowing down occurs when velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.

analyzing_position_time_curve.title: Analyzing the Position versus Time Curve

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

analyzing_position_time_curve.one_liner: The position versus time curve provides comprehensive information about a particle's position, velocity (from slope), and acceleration (from concavity) in rectilinear motion.
analyzing_position_time_curve.content: The position versus time curve contains all significant information regarding a particle's position and velocity in rectilinear motion. Specifically: If $s(t)>0$, the particle is located on the positive side of the $s$-axis. If $s(t)<0$, the particle is on the negative side of the $s$-axis. The slope of the curve at any given time is equal to the instantaneous velocity at that time. Where the curve has a positive slope, the velocity is positive, indicating the particle is moving in the positive direction. Conversely, where the curve has a negative slope, the velocity is negative, meaning the particle is moving in the negative direction. If the slope of the curve is zero, the velocity is zero, and the particle is momentarily stopped. Information about a particle's acceleration in rectilinear motion can also be deduced from the position versus time curve by examining its concavity. For instance, the position versus time curve will be concave up on intervals where $s^{\prime \prime}(t)>0$ and concave down on intervals where $s^{\prime \prime}(t)<0$. Since $s^{\prime \prime}(t)$ represents the acceleration, a concave up curve indicates positive acceleration, while a concave down curve indicates negative acceleration.
analyzing_position_time_curve.motivation_md: Analyzing the position versus time curve is a powerful graphical method to understand the motion of a particle. It allows for a visual interpretation of position, direction of movement, speed changes, and acceleration without needing to perform complex calculations, making it a fundamental tool in kinematics.
analyzing_position_time_curve.recap_md: - The sign of $s(t)$ indicates the particle's position relative to the origin. - The slope of the curve represents instantaneous velocity. - The concavity of the curve indicates the sign of the acceleration.

newtons_method_intro.title: Newton's Method Introduction

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

newtons_method_intro.one_liner: Newton's Method is an efficient technique for approximating the roots of an equation $f(x)=0$, especially when exact solutions are difficult or impossible to find.
newtons_method_intro.content: Newton's Method is a technique for approximating the roots of an equation $f(x)=0$, which is usually more efficient than methods like the Intermediate-Value Theorem. It is widely used by many commercial and scientific computer programs for finding roots. While formulas exist for solving first- and second-degree equations, and even for third- and fourth-degree equations (though complicated), it was proven in 1826 by Niels Henrik Abel that a similar general formula is impossible for fifth-degree equations or higher. This means that for specific higher-degree polynomial equations, such as $x^{5}-9 x^{4}+2 x^{3}-5 x^{2}+17 x-8=0$, finding exact values for all solutions can be difficult or impossible. Similar challenges arise for nonpolynomial equations like $x-\cos x=0$. For such equations, solutions are generally approximated, often using Newton's Method.
newtons_method_intro.motivation_md: Many equations, especially those of degree five or higher, or non-polynomial equations, do not have simple algebraic formulas for their exact roots. Newton's Method provides a powerful and generally efficient numerical technique to approximate these roots, making it possible to solve a wide range of practical problems.
newtons_method_intro.recap_md: - Newton's Method approximates roots of $f(x)=0$. - It is more efficient than some other approximation methods. - It is particularly useful for equations without exact algebraic solutions.

newtons_method_formula.title: Newton's Method Formula

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

newtons_method_formula.one_liner: Newton's Method uses an iterative formula, $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f(x_{n})}{f^{\prime}(x_{n})}$, to refine approximations of a function's root by finding the x-intercept of the tangent line.
newtons_method_formula.content: To implement Newton's Method analytically, a formula is derived to calculate each improved approximation from the preceding one. This derivation begins by considering the point-slope form of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at an initial approximation $x_{1}$: $y-f\left(x_{1}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(x_{1}\right)\left(x-x_{1}\right)$. If $f^{\prime}\left(x_{1}\right) \neq 0$, this tangent line is not parallel to the $x$-axis and thus crosses it at some point $\left(x_{2}, 0\right)$. Substituting these coordinates into the tangent line equation yields $-f\left(x_{1}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(x_{1}\right)\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)$. Solving for $x_{2}$ gives the second approximation: $x_{2}=x_{1}-\frac{f\left(x_{1}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{1}\right)}$. The next approximation, $x_{3}$, can be found by applying the same logic with $x_{2}$ as the starting point: $x_{3}=x_{2}-\frac{f\left(x_{2}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{2}\right)}$, provided $f^{\prime}\left(x_{2}\right) \neq 0$. Following this pattern, if $x_{n}$ is the $n$th approximation, the improved approximation $x_{n+1}$ is given by Newton's Method formula: $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f\left(x_{n}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)}, \quad n=1,2,3, \ldots$. [FIGURE:5debe03b5e9dfcc7 | A graph of the cubic function $y = x^3 - x - 1$ is displayed on a coordinate plane. The viewing window is set from $x=-2$ to $x=4$ and $y=-3$ to $y=3$, with both x and y scales set to 1. The curve...] Many calculators and computer programs calculate internally with more digits than they display. Where possible, you should use stored calculated values rather than values displayed from earlier calculations. For example, the value of $x_{2}$ used in the iterative formula should be the stored value, not a rounded displayed value. [FIGURE:3a476cbadd7ea3af | A black and white portrait depicts Niels Henrik Abel, a Norwegian mathematician, whose work on the insolvability of quintic equations is discussed in the text.] Niels Henrik Abel (1802-1829) was a Norwegian mathematician who, despite a brief life of 26 years marked by poverty and adversity, proved major results that transformed mathematics. At thirteen, he was recognized for his extraordinary mathematical ability by his teacher, Bernt Michael Holmboe, and studied the works of Euler, Newton, and French mathematicians. After his father's death in 1820, Abel entered the University of Christiania with financial support from professors. In 1824, he self-published the proof that it is impossible to solve the general fifth-degree polynomial equation algebraically. His landmark paper on transcendental functions, submitted to the French Academy of Sciences in 1826, was initially ignored or misplaced but later recognized as a monumental discovery. Abel continued to produce significant work despite illness and debt, and his fame grew. He died in April 1829 from a violent hemorrhage, just two days before receiving news of a secured mathematical appointment in Berlin.
newtons_method_formula.motivation_md: The iterative formula for Newton's Method provides a concrete, step-by-step procedure to numerically approximate roots. It translates the geometric idea of using tangent lines into an algebraic expression that can be applied repeatedly to achieve increasingly accurate solutions.
newtons_method_formula.recap_md: - The formula $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f(x_{n})}{f^{\prime}(x_{n})}$ calculates the next approximation. - Each approximation $x_{n+1}$ is the x-intercept of the tangent line to $f(x)$ at $x_n$. - The method requires the function to be differentiable and its derivative to be non-zero at the approximation points.

newtons_method_difficulties.title: Some Difficulties with Newton's Method

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

newtons_method_difficulties.one_liner: Newton's Method can fail if the derivative is zero, if it converges to an unintended root, or if it diverges entirely, as seen with $x^{1/3}=0$.
newtons_method_difficulties.content: While Newton's Method often converges rapidly, there are situations where it can fail. One such difficulty arises if $f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)=0$ for some approximation $x_n$. In this case, the formula involves division by zero, making it impossible to generate $x_{n+1}$. Geometrically, this occurs when the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x_n$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, meaning it will not cross the $x$-axis to provide the next approximation (Figure 4.7.4). Newton's Method can also fail for other reasons. Sometimes it may overlook the desired root and converge to a different one, or it may fail to converge at all. For example, consider the equation $x^{1 / 3}=0$, which has $x=0$ as its only solution. If we attempt to approximate this solution using Newton's Method with a starting value of $x_{0}=1$, letting $f(x)=x^{1 / 3}$, the formula becomes $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{\left(x_{n}\right)^{1 / 3}}{\frac{1}{3}\left(x_{n}\right)^{-2 / 3}}=x_{n}-3 x_{n}=-2 x_{n}$. Beginning with $x_{1}=1$, the successive values generated are $x_{1}=1, \quad x_{2}=-2, \quad x_{3}=4, \quad x_{4}=-8, \ldots$, which clearly do not converge to $x=0$. [FIGURE:638bfe4a801f37f1 | A graph of the function $y = x^{1/3}$ is shown, illustrating the divergence of Newton's Method when approximating the root $x=0$. The sequence of approximations starts at $x_1=1$. A vertical dashed...] Figure 4.7.5 illustrates this geometric divergence. For more detailed information on the conditions for convergence and error analysis, consult a book on numerical analysis. For a deeper discussion of Newton's Method's connection to chaos and fractals, refer to Philip Straffin's article, "Newton's Method and Fractal Patterns," in Applications of Calculus, MAA Notes, Vol. 3, No. 29, 1993.
newtons_method_difficulties.motivation_md: Understanding the potential difficulties and failure modes of Newton's Method is crucial for its effective application. Knowing when and why it might fail helps users choose appropriate starting values, interpret results, and select alternative methods when necessary, ensuring reliable root approximation.
newtons_method_difficulties.recap_md: - Newton's Method fails if $f^{\prime}(x_n)=0$, as it leads to division by zero. - The method may converge to an unintended root or diverge completely. - An example of divergence is approximating the root of $x^{1/3}=0$ starting at $x_1=1$.

thm_4_8_1_rolles_theorem.title: Rolle's Theorem

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_4_8_1_rolles_theorem.one_liner: Rolle's Theorem states that if a function is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)=0$, then there is at least one point $c$ in $(a, b)$ where $f'(c)=0$.
thm_4_8_1_rolles_theorem.content: 4.8.1 THEOREM (Rolle's Theorem) Let $f$ be continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$. If $f(a)=0 \quad \text { and } \quad f(b)=0$, then there is at least one point $c$ in the interval $(a, b)$ such that $f^{\prime}(c)=0$.
thm_4_8_1_rolles_theorem.motivation_md: Rolle's Theorem is a foundational result in calculus that provides a specific condition under which the derivative of a function must be zero. It serves as a crucial stepping stone for proving the more general Mean-Value Theorem and helps establish properties of differentiable functions.
thm_4_8_1_rolles_theorem.recap_md: - The function $f$ must be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$. - The function values at the endpoints must be equal to zero: $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=0$. - Under these conditions, there exists at least one $c \in (a, b)$ where $f'(c)=0$.

thm_4_8_2_mean_value_theorem.title: Mean-Value Theorem

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

thm_4_8_2_mean_value_theorem.one_liner: The Mean-Value Theorem states that for a continuous function on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, there is a point $c$ in $(a, b)$ where the instantaneous rate of change $f'(c)$ equals the average rate of change $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
thm_4_8_2_mean_value_theorem.content: 4.8.2 THEOREM (Mean-Value Theorem) Let $f$ be continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$. Then there is at least one point $c$ in $(a, b)$ such that $f^{\prime}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
thm_4_8_2_mean_value_theorem.motivation_md: The Mean-Value Theorem is a cornerstone of differential calculus, generalizing Rolle's Theorem. It establishes a fundamental connection between the average rate of change of a function over an interval and its instantaneous rate of change at some point within that interval. This theorem has wide-ranging applications in proving other theorems and understanding function behavior.
thm_4_8_2_mean_value_theorem.recap_md: - The function $f$ must be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$. - There exists at least one point $c \in (a, b)$ where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line. - This means $f'(c)$ equals the average rate of change of $f$ over $[a, b]$.

idea_motivation_mvt_proof.title: Motivation for the Proof of Mean-Value Theorem

position.chapter_title: THE DERIVATIVE IN GRAPHING AND APPLICATIONS

idea_motivation_mvt_proof.one_liner: The proof of the Mean-Value Theorem is motivated by finding a point where the vertical distance between the curve $y=f(x)$ and the secant line joining $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$ is maximal.
idea_motivation_mvt_proof.content: Figure 4.8.6 suggests that the Mean-Value Theorem's conclusion, $f^{\prime}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, will hold (i.e., the tangent line will be parallel to the secant line) at a point $c$ where the vertical distance between the curve and the secant line is maximum. Therefore, to prove the Mean-Value Theorem, it is natural to begin by deriving a formula for the vertical distance $v(x)$ between the curve $y=f(x)$ and the secant line connecting $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$.
idea_motivation_mvt_proof.motivation_md: Understanding the geometric motivation behind a theorem's proof can make the proof itself more intuitive and memorable. For the Mean-Value Theorem, visualizing the relationship between the curve, its secant line, and the point of maximum vertical distance provides a clear path to constructing the formal proof.
idea_motivation_mvt_proof.recap_md: - The Mean-Value Theorem's proof is motivated by a geometric insight. - It involves finding a point where the vertical distance between the curve and its secant line is maximal. - This point corresponds to where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line.

theorem_1_1_3_one_two_sided_limits.title: Relationship between One-Sided and Two-Sided Limits
theorem_1_1_3_one_two_sided_limits.prompt_md: In order for the two-sided limit of a function $f(x)$ to exist at a point $a$, the values of $f(x)$ must approach some real number $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$, and this number must be the same regardless of whether $x$ approaches $a$ from the left or the right. This suggests the following result, which we state without formal proof.1.1.3 THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ONE-SIDED AND TWO-SIDED LIMITS The twosided limit of a function $f(x)$ exists at $a$ if and only if both of the one-sided limits exist at $a$ and have the same value; that is, $$\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L \quad \text { if and only if } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$$

example_4_abs_x_over_x_no_limit.solution_md: As $x$ approaches 0 , the values of $f(x)=|x| / x$ approach -1 from the left and approach 1 from the right [see(13)]. Thus, the one-sided limits at 0 are not the same.

example_1_1_7.title: Example 7: Describing limits at x=a
example_1_1_7.prompt_md: For the functions in Figure 1.1.16, describe the limits at $x=a$ in appropriate limit notation.
example_1_1_7.solution_md:
Solution (a). In Figure 1.1.16a, the function increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right and decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left. Thus,

$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{1}{x-a}=+\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{1}{x-a}=-\infty $$

Solution (b). In Figure 1.1.16b, the function increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both the left and right. Thus,

$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=+\infty $$

Solution (c). In Figure 1.1.16c, the function decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right and increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left. Thus,

$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{-1}{x-a}=-\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{-1}{x-a}=+\infty $$

Solution (d). In Figure 1.1.16d, the function decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both the left and right. Thus,

$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=-\infty $$

example_2_numerical_limit_conjecture.title: Example 2: Numerical conjecture for limit of (x-1)/(sqrt(x)-1)

example_2_numerical_limit_conjecture.solution_md: Although the function $f(x)=\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$ is undefined at $x=1$, this has no bearing on the limit. Table 1.1.1 shows sample $x$-values approaching 1 from the left side and from the right side. In both cases the corresponding values of $f(x)$, calculated to six decimal places, appear to get closer and closer to 2 , and hence we conjecture that $$\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}=2$$ This is consistent with the graph of $f$ shown in Figure 1.1.9. In the next section we will show how to obtain this result algebraically.

example_5_one_sided_limits_figure_1_1_13.title: Example 5: One-sided and two-sided limits for Figure 1.1.13
example_5_one_sided_limits_figure_1_1_13.prompt_md: For the functions in Figure 1.1.13, find the one-sided and two-sided limits at $x=a$ if they exist.
example_5_one_sided_limits_figure_1_1_13.solution_md: The functions in all three figures have the same one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a$, since the functions are identical, except at $x=a$. These limits are $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=3 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=1 $$ In all three cases the two-sided limit does not exist as $x \rightarrow a$ because the one-sided limits are not equal.
example_5_one_sided_limits_figure_1_1_13.answer: $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=3$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=1$, two-sided limit does not exist.

example_6_one_sided_limits_figure_1_1_14.title: Example 6: One-sided and two-sided limits for Figure 1.1.14
example_6_one_sided_limits_figure_1_1_14.prompt_md: For the functions in Figure 1.1.14, find the one-sided and two-sided limits at $x=a$ if they exist.
example_6_one_sided_limits_figure_1_1_14.solution_md: As in the preceding example, the value of $f$ at $x=a$ has no bearing on the limits as $x \rightarrow a$, so in all three cases we have $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=2 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=2 $$ Since the one-sided limits are equal, the two-sided limit exists and $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=2 $$

example_1_tangent_line_parabola.title: Example 1: Tangent line to y=x^2 at P(1,1)
example_1_tangent_line_parabola.prompt_md: Find an equation for the tangent line to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ at the point $P(1,1)$.
example_1_tangent_line_parabola.solution_md: If we can find the slope $m_{	an }$ of the tangent line at $P$, then we can use the point $P$ and the point-slope formula for a line (Web Appendix G) to write the equation of the tangent line as $$ y-1=m_{	an }(x-1) \tag{1} $$ To find the slope $m_{	ext {tan }}$, consider the secant line through $P$ and a point $Q\left(x, x^{2}\right)$ on the parabola that is distinct from $P$. The slope $m_{	ext {sec }}$ of this secant line is $$ m_{\mathrm{sec}}=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1} \tag{2} $$ Figure 1.1.4a suggests that if we now let $Q$ move along the parabola, getting closer and closer to $P$, then the limiting position of the secant line through $P$ and $Q$ will coincide with that of the tangent line at $P$. This in turn suggests that the value of $m_{\mathrm{sec}}$ will get closer and closer to the value of $m_{\tan }$ as $P$ moves toward $Q$ along the curve. However, to say that $Q\left(x, x^{2}\right)$ gets closer and closer to $P(1,1)$ is algebraically equivalent to saying that $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 . Thus, the problem of finding $m_{\tan }$ reduces to finding the "limiting value" of $m_{\text {sec }}$ in Formula (2) as $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 (but with $x \neq 1$ to ensure that $P$ and $Q$ remain distinct). [FIGURE:134839e73258cc63 | A graph in a Cartesian coordinate system shows the parabola $y=x^2$ in blue and the line $y=2x-1$ in purple. The line is tangent to the parabola at the point $P(1,1)$, which is marked with a blue...] - Figure 1.1.5 [FIGURE:63559c4dfcf0643c | The image displays two diagrams illustrating area decomposition. The left diagram shows an L-shaped region composed of two rectangles, labeled $A_1$ and $A_2$. The right diagram shows a pentagon...] Δ Figure 1.1.6 We can rewrite (2) as $$ m_{\mathrm{sec}}=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1}=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)}=x+1 $$ where the cancellation of the factor $(x-1)$ is allowed because $x \neq 1$. It is now evident that $m_{\text {sec }}$ gets closer and closer to 2 as $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 . Thus, $m_{\tan }=2$ and (1) implies that the equation of the tangent line is $$ y-1=2(x-1) \quad \text { or equivalently } \quad y=2 x-1 $$ Figure 1.1.5 shows the graph of $y=x^{2}$ and this tangent line. $\square$

thm_1_2_2.title: Theorem 1.2.2 Properties of Limits (Limit Laws)
thm_1_2_2.prompt_md: 1.2.2 THEOREM Let a be a real number, and suppose that$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{2} $$That is, the limits exist and have values $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$, respectively. Then:(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)+g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}+L_{2}$(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}-L_{2}$(c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)=L_{1} L_{2}$(d) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)}=\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}, \quad$ provided $L_{2} \neq 0$(e) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L_{1}}$, provided $L_{1}>0$ if $n$ is even.Moreover, these statements are also true for the one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a^{-}$or as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$.This theorem can be stated informally as follows:(a) The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits.(b) The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits.(c) The limit of a product is the product of the limits.(d) The limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, provided the limit of the denominator is not zero.(e) The limit of an $n$th root is the $n$th root of the limit.For the special case of part (c) in which $f(x)=k$ is a constant function, we have$$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow a}(k g(x))=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} k \cdot \lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=k \lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x) \tag{1} \end{equation*} $$

ex_1_2_4.title: Example 4: Applying Limit Laws to Combinations of Functions
ex_1_2_4.prompt_md: $$\begin{array}{lc}\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)+2 h(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)+2 \lim _{x \rightarrow a} h(x) \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x) h(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} h(x)\right) \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)]^{3}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{3} & \text { Take } g(x)=h(x)=f(x) \text { in the last equation. } \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)]^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{n} & \begin{array}{l} \text { The extension of Theorem 1.2.2(c) in which } \\ \text { there are } n \text { factors, each of which is } f(x) \end{array} \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x\right)^{n}=a^{n} & \text { Apply the previous result with } f(x)=x . \end{array}$$

thm_1_2_3.title: Theorem 1.2.3 Limit of a Polynomial
thm_1_2_3.prompt_md: For any polynomial$$ p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n} $$and any real number $a$,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a) $$
thm_1_2_3.proof_md: $$\begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow a}\left(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{0}+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{1} x+\cdots+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{n} x^{n} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{0}+c_{1} \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x+\cdots+c_{n} \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x^{n} \\ & =c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a) \end{aligned}$$

ex_1_2_8.title: Example 8: Limits of Rational Functions with Zero Denominator
ex_1_2_8.solution_md: Solution. In all three parts the limit of the numerator is -2 , and the limit of the denominator is 0 , so the limit of the ratio does not exist. To be more specific than this, we need to analyze the sign of the ratio. The sign of the ratio, which is given in Figure 1.2.3, is determined by the signs of $2-x, x-4$, and $x+2$. (The method of test points, discussed in Web Appendix E, provides a way of finding the sign of the ratio here.) It follows from this figure that as $x$ approaches 4 from the right, the ratio is always negative; and as $x$ approaches 4 from the left, the ratio is eventually positive. Thus, $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 4^{+}} \frac{2-x}{(x-4)(x+2)}=-\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 4^{-}} \frac{2-x}{(x-4)(x+2)}=+\infty $$ Because the one-sided limits have opposite signs, all we can say about the two-sided limit is that it does not exist.

ex_1_3_11.title: Example 11

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

ex_1_3_11.solution_md: Solution. Graphs of the functions $f(x)=\sqrt{x^{6}+5}-x^{3}$, and $g(x)=\sqrt{x^{6}+5 x^{3}}-x^{3}$ for $x \geq 0$, are shown in Figure 1.3.6. From the graphs we might conjecture that the requested limits are 0 and $\frac{5}{2}$, respectively. To confirm this, we treat each function as a fraction with a denominator of 1 and rationalize the numerator. $$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(\sqrt{x^{6}+5}-x^{3}\right) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(\sqrt{x^{6}+5}-x^{3}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{x^{6}+5}+x^{3}}{\sqrt{x^{6}+5}+x^{3}}\right) \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{\left(x^{6}+5\right)-x^{6}}{\sqrt{x^{6}+5}+x^{3}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5}{\sqrt{x^{6}+5}+x^{3}} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{\frac{5}{x^{3}}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{5}{x^{6}}}+1} \\ & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{1+0}+1}=0 \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(\sqrt{x^{6}+5 x^{3}}-x^{3}\right) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(\sqrt{x^{6}+5 x^{3}}-x^{3}\right) \\ & \left.=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{\left(x^{6}+5 x^{3}\right)-x^{6}}{\sqrt{x^{6}+5 x^{3}}+x^{3}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}}{\sqrt{x^{6}+5 x^{3}}+x^{3}}\right) \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5}{\sqrt{1+\frac{5}{x^{3}}}+1} \quad \sqrt{\sqrt{x^{6}}=x^{3} \text { for } x>0} \\ & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{1+0}+1}=\frac{5}{2} \end{aligned} $$

item_thm_1_3_limit_laws_for_infinity.title: Limit Laws for Limits at Infinity

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

item_thm_1_3_limit_laws_for_infinity.prompt_md: It can be shown that the limit laws in Theorem 1.2.2 carry over without change to limits at $+\infty$ and $-\infty$. Moreover, it follows by the same argument used in Section 1.2 that if $n$ is a positive integer, then $$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}(f(x))^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)\right)^{n} \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}(f(x))^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)\right)^{n} \tag{9-10} \end{equation*} $$ provided the indicated limit of $f(x)$ exists. It also follows that constants can be moved through the limit symbols for limits at infinity: $$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} k f(x)=k \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x) \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} k f(x)=k \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x) \tag{11-12} \end{equation*} $$ provided the indicated limit of $f(x)$ exists. Finally, if $f(x)=k$ is a constant function, then the values of $f$ do not change as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, so $$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} k=k \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} k=k \tag{13-14} \end{equation*}

ex_1_3_7.title: Example 7

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

ex_1_3_7.solution_md: Solution. Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{1}=x$. We obtain$$ \begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{3 x+5}{6 x-8}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{3+\frac{5}{x}}{6-\frac{8}{x}} \\ &=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(3+\frac{5}{x}\right)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(6-\frac{8}{x}\right)} \quad \text { Divide each term by } x . \\ &=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 3+\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5}{x}}{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 6-\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{8}{x}} \quad \text { quotient of the limits. } \\ &=\frac{\begin{array}{l} \text { Limit of a sum is the } \\ \text { sum of the limits. } \end{array}}{3+5 \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}}=\frac{3+0}{6-8 \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}}=\frac{1}{2} \quad \text { A constant can be moved through a } \\ \text { limit symbol; Formulas (2) and (13). } \end{aligned} $$

ex_1_3_8.title: Example 8

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

ex_1_3_8.prompt_md: Find (a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}-x}{2 x^{3}-5}$ (b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}$
ex_1_3_8.solution_md: Solution (a). Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{3}$. We obtain$$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}-x}{2 x^{3}-5} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}}{2-\frac{5}{x^{3}}} \\ & =\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(2-\frac{5}{x^{3}}\right)} \quad \text { Divide each term by } x^{3} . \\ & =\frac{}{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4}{x}-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}} \quad \begin{array}{l} \text { Limit of a quotient is the } \\ \text { quotient of the limits. } \end{array} \\ & \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} 2-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{5}{x^{3}} \\ & =\frac{4 \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x}-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{2-5 \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{3}}}=\frac{0-0}{2-0}=0 \quad \begin{array}{l} \text { A constant a difference is the be moved through } \\ \text { a limit symbol; Formula (14) and } \\ \text { Example 4. } \end{array} \end{aligned} $$Solution (b). Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{1}=x$. We obtain$$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{2}-2 x+\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{x}-3} \tag{19} \end{equation*} $$In this case we cannot argue that the limit of the quotient is the quotient of the limits because the limit of the numerator does not exist. However, we have$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 5 x^{2}-2 x=+\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}=0, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(\frac{1}{x}-3\right)=-3 $$Thus, the numerator on the right side of (19) approaches $+\infty$ and the denominator has a finite negative limit. We conclude from this that the quotient approaches $-\infty$; that is,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{2}-2 x+\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{x}-3}=-\infty $$

ex_1_3_9.title: Example 9

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

ex_1_3_9.prompt_md: Use the preceding observation to compute the limits in Examples 7 and 8.
ex_1_3_9.solution_md: Solution.$$ \begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{3 x+5}{6 x-8}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{3 x}{6 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ & \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}-x}{2 x^{3}-5}=\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}}{2 x^{3}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{2}{x}=0 \\ & \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}}{(-3 x)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(-\frac{5}{3} x^{2}\right)=-\infty \end{aligned} $$

ex_1_3_10.title: Example 10

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

ex_1_3_10.solution_md: In both parts it would be helpful to manipulate the function so that the powers of $x$ are transformed to powers of $1 / x$. This can be achieved in both cases by dividing the numerator and denominator by $|x|$ and using the fact that $\sqrt{x^{2}}=|x|$.Solution (a). As $x \rightarrow+\infty$, the values of $x$ under consideration are positive, so we can replace $|x|$ by $x$ where helpful. We obtain$$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}{3 x-6} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}{|x|}}{\frac{3 x-6}{|x|}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}{\sqrt{x^{2}}}}{\frac{3 x-6}{x}} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{x^{2}}}}{3-\frac{6}{x}}=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \sqrt{1+\frac{2}{x^{2}}}}{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(3-\frac{6}{x}\right)} \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(1+\frac{2}{x^{2}}\right)}}{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(3-\frac{6}{x}\right)}=\frac{\sqrt{\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 1\right)+\left(2 \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)}}{\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 3\right)-\left(6 \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}\right)} \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{1+(2 \cdot 0)}}{3-(6 \cdot 0)}=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned} $$Solution (b). As $x \rightarrow-\infty$, the values of $x$ under consideration are negative, so we can replace $|x|$ by $-x$ where helpful. We obtain$$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}{3 x-6} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}{|x|}}{\frac{3 x-6}{|x|}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}{\sqrt{x^{2}}}}{\frac{3 x-6}{(-x)}} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{x^{2}}}}{-3+\frac{6}{x}}=-\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned} $$

item_thm_1_3_limits_of_polynomials.title: Limits of Polynomials as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

item_thm_1_3_limits_of_polynomials.prompt_md: There is a useful principle about polynomials which, expressed informally, states: The end behavior of a polynomial matches the end behavior of its highest degree term. More precisely, if $c_{n} \neq 0$, then $$\begin{align*}\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} c_{n} x^{n} \tag{17}\\ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} c_{n} x^{n} \tag{18}\end{align*}$$
item_thm_1_3_limits_of_polynomials.proof_md: We can motivate these results by factoring out the highest power of $x$ from the polynomial and examining the limit of the factored expression. Thus, $$c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}=x^{n}\left(\frac{c_{0}}{x^{n}}+\frac{c_{1}}{x^{n-1}}+\cdots+c_{n}\right)$$ As $x \rightarrow-\infty$ or $x \rightarrow+\infty$, it follows from Example 4(a) that all of the terms with positive powers of $x$ in the denominator approach 0 , so (17) and (18) are certainly plausible.

ex_1_4_1_prove_3x_minus_5.title: Example 1: Prove lim (3x-5) = 1 as x approaches 2
ex_1_4_1_prove_3x_minus_5.prompt_md: Use Definition 1.4.1 to prove that $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}(3 x-5)=1$.
ex_1_4_1_prove_3x_minus_5.solution_md: Solution. We must show that given any positive number $\epsilon$, we can find a positive number $\delta$ such that$$|\underbrace{(3 x-5)}_{f(x)}-\underbrace{1}_{L}|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-\underbrace{2}_{a}|<\delta \tag{2}$$There are two things to do. First, we must discover a value of $\delta$ for which this statement holds, and then we must prove that the statement holds for that $\delta$. For the discovery part we begin by simplifying (2) and writing it as$$|3 x-6|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-2|<\delta$$Next we will rewrite this statement in a form that will facilitate the discovery of an appropriate $\delta$ :$$\begin{array}{lll}3|x-2|<\epsilon & \text { if } & 0<|x-2|<\delta \\|x-2|<\epsilon / 3 & \text { if } & 0<|x-2|<\delta \tag{3}\end{array}$$It should be self-evident that this last statement holds if $\delta=\epsilon / 3$, which completes the discovery portion of our work. Now we need to prove that (2) holds for this choice of $\delta$. However, statement (2) is equivalent to (3), and (3) holds with $\delta=\epsilon / 3$, so (2) also holds with $\delta=\epsilon / 3$. This proves that $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}(3 x-5)=1$.

ex_1_5_1_continuity_at_x_2.title: Continuity at x=2
ex_1_5_1_continuity_at_x_2.prompt_md: Determine whether the following functions are continuous at $x=2$. $$f(x)=\frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}, \quad g(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}, & x \neq 2 \\ 3, & x=2, \end{array}\right. \quad h(x)= \begin{cases}\frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}, & x \neq 2 \\ 4, & x=2\end{cases}$$
ex_1_5_1_continuity_at_x_2.solution_md: Solution. In each case we must determine whether the limit of the function as $x \rightarrow 2$ is the same as the value of the function at $x=2$. In all three cases the functions are identical, except at $x=2$, and hence all three have the same limit at $x=2$, namely, $$\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} g(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} h(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} \frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}(x+2)=4$$ The function $f$ is undefined at $x=2$, and hence is not continuous at $x=2$ (Figure 1.5.2a). The function $g$ is defined at $x=2$, but its value there is $g(2)=3$, which is not the same as the limit as $x$ approaches 2 ; hence, $g$ is also not continuous at $x=2$ (Figure 1.5.2b). The value of the function $h$ at $x=2$ is $h(2)=4$, which is the same as the limit as $x$ approaches 2 ; hence, $h$ is continuous at $x=2$ (Figure 1.5.2c). (Note that the function $h$ could have been written more simply as $h(x)=x+2$, but we wrote it in piecewise form to emphasize its relationship to $f$ and $g$.)

ex_1_5_2_continuity_sqrt_9_minus_x_squar.title: Continuity of sqrt(9-x^2)
ex_1_5_2_continuity_sqrt_9_minus_x_squar.prompt_md: What can you say about the continuity of the function $f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^{2}}$ ?
ex_1_5_2_continuity_sqrt_9_minus_x_squar.solution_md: Because the natural domain of this function is the closed interval [ $-3,3$ ], we will need to investigate the continuity of $f$ on the open interval $(-3,3)$ and at the two endpoints. If $c$ is any point in the interval $(-3,3)$, then it follows from Theorem 1.2.2(e) that$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sqrt{9-x^{2}}=\sqrt{\lim _{x \rightarrow c}\left(9-x^{2}\right)}=\sqrt{9-c^{2}}=f(c) $$which proves $f$ is continuous at each point in the interval $(-3,3)$. The function $f$ is also continuous at the endpoints since$$ \begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{-}} \sqrt{9-x^{2}}=\sqrt{\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{-}}\left(9-x^{2}\right)}=0=f(3) \\ & \lim _{x \rightarrow-3^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow-3^{+}} \sqrt{9-x^{2}}=\sqrt{\lim _{x \rightarrow-3^{+}}\left(9-x^{2}\right)}=0=f(-3) \end{aligned} $$Thus, $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[-3,3]$ (Figure 1.5.5).

item_thm_1_5_3.title: Properties of continuous functions
item_thm_1_5_3.prompt_md: If the functions $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $c$, then(a) $f+g$ is continuous at $c$.(b) $f-g$ is continuous at $c$.(c) $f g$ is continuous at $c$.(d) $f / g$ is continuous at $c$ if $g(c) \neq 0$ and has a discontinuity at $c$ if $g(c)=0$.
item_thm_1_5_3.proof_md: First, consider the case where $g(c)=0$. In this case $f(c) / g(c)$ is undefined, so the function $f / g$ has a discontinuity at $c$.Next, consider the case where $g(c) \neq 0$. To prove that $f / g$ is continuous at $c$, we must show that$$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{f(c)}{g(c)} \tag{1} \end{equation*} $$Since $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $c$,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=f(c) \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=g(c) $$Thus, by Theorem 1.2.2(d)$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)}=\frac{f(c)}{g(c)} $$which proves (1).

ex_1_5_4_continuity_absolute_value.title: Continuity of absolute value function
ex_1_5_4_continuity_absolute_value.solution_md: We can write $|x|$ as $$|x|=\left\{\begin{array}{rll}x & \text { if } & x>0 \\ 0 & \text { if } & x=0 \\ -x & \text { if } & x<0\end{array}\right.$$ so $|x|$ is the same as the polynomial $x$ on the interval ( $0,+\infty$ ) and is the same as the polynomial $-x$ on the interval $(-\infty, 0)$. But polynomials are continuous everywhere, so $x=0$ is the only possible discontinuity for $|x|$. Since $|0|=0$, to prove the continuity at $x=0$ we must show that $$\begin{equation*}\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}|x|=0 \tag{2}\end{equation*}$$ Because the piecewise formula for $|x|$ changes at 0 , it will be helpful to consider the onesided limits at 0 rather than the two-sided limit. We obtain $$\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}|x|=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} x=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}}|x|=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}}(-x)=0$$ Thus, (2) holds and $|x|$ is continuous at $x=0$.

item_thm_1_5_5.title: Limit of a composite function
item_thm_1_5_5.prompt_md:
If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and if the function $f$ is continuous at $L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f(L)$. That is,
$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)\right) $$
This equality remains valid if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c}$ is replaced everywhere by one of $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}}$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}}, \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}$, or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}$.

ex_1_5_5_approx_root_x_cubed_minus_x_min.title: Approximating root of x^3 - x - 1
ex_1_5_5_approx_root_x_cubed_minus_x_min.prompt_md:
The equation

$$
x^{3}-x-1=0
$$

cannot be solved algebraically very easily because the left side has no simple factors. However, if we graph $p(x)=x^{3}-x-1$ with a graphing utility (Figure 1.5.10), then we are led to conjecture that there is one real root and that this root lies inside the interval $[1,2]$. The existence of a root in this interval is also confirmed by Theorem 1.5.8, since $p(1)=-1$ and $p(2)=5$ have opposite signs. Approximate this root to two decimal-place accuracy.
ex_1_5_5_approx_root_x_cubed_minus_x_min.solution_md:
Solution. Our objective is to approximate the unknown root $x_{0}$ with an error of at most 0.005 . It follows that if we can find an interval of length 0.01 that contains the root, then the midpoint of that interval will approximate the root with an error of at most $\frac{1}{2}(0.01)=0.005$, which will achieve the desired accuracy.

We know that the root $x_{0}$ lies in the interval $[1,2]$. However, this interval has length 1 , which is too large. We can pinpoint the location of the root more precisely by dividing the interval $[1,2]$ into 10 equal parts and evaluating $p$ at the points of subdivision using a calculating utility (Table 1.5.2). In this table $p(1.3)$ and $p(1.4)$ have opposite signs, so we know that the root lies in the interval [1.3,1.4]. This interval has length 0.1 , which is still too large, so we repeat the process by dividing the interval [1.3,1.4] into 10 parts and evaluating $p$ at the points of subdivision; this yields Table 1.5.3, which tells us that the root is inside the interval [1.32, 1.33] (Figure 1.5.11). Since this interval has length 0.01, its midpoint 1.325 will approximate the root with an error of at most 0.005 . Thus, $x_{0} \approx 1.325$ to two decimal-place accuracy.

item_thm_1_6_1.prompt_md:
If $c$ is any number in the natural domain of the stated trigonometric function, then

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \tan x=\tan c \\
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \csc x=\csc c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sec x=\sec c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cot x=\cot c

$$

ex_1_6_1.title: Example 1

ex_1_6_1.solution_md:
Since the cosine function is continuous everywhere, it follows from Theorem 1.5.5 that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \cos (g(x))=\cos \left(\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} g(x)\right)
$$

provided $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} g(x)$ exists. Thus,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \cos \left(\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1}\right)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \cos (x+1)=\cos \left(\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}(x+1)\right)=\cos 2
$$

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

ex_1_6_4.solution_md:
Solution (a).
$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\tan x}{x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos x}\right)=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\cos x}\right)=(1)(1)=1 $$
Solution (b). The trick is to multiply and divide by 2 , which will make the denominator the same as the argument of the sine function [just as in Theorem 1.6.5(a)]:
$$ \lim _{\theta \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin 2 \theta}{\theta}=\lim _{\theta \rightarrow 0} 2 \cdot \frac{\sin 2 \theta}{2 \theta}=2 \lim _{\theta \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin 2 \theta}{2 \theta} $$
Now make the substitution $x=2 \theta$, and use the fact that $x \rightarrow 0$ as $\theta \rightarrow 0$. This yields
$$ \lim _{\theta \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin 2 \theta}{\theta}=2 \lim _{\theta \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin 2 \theta}{2 \theta}=2 \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=2(1)=2 $$
Solution (c).
$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin 3 x}{\sin 5 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{\sin 3 x}{x}}{\frac{\sin 5 x}{x}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{3 \cdot \frac{\sin 3 x}{3 x}}{5 \cdot \frac{\sin 5 x}{5 x}}=\frac{3 \cdot 1}{5 \cdot 1}=\frac{3}{5} $$

ex_1_6_5.title: Example 5

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

ex_1_6_5.solution_md:
Solution (a). Let us view $1 / x$ as an angle in radian measure. As $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$, the angle $1 / x$ approaches $+\infty$, so the values of $\sin (1 / x)$ keep oscillating between -1 and 1 without approaching a limit. Similarly, as $x \rightarrow 0^{-}$, the angle $1 / x$ approaches $-\infty$, so again the values of $\sin (1 / x)$ keep oscillating between -1 and 1 without approaching a limit. These conclusions are consistent with the graph shown in Figure 1.6.5. Note that the oscillations become more and more rapid as $x \rightarrow 0$ because $1 / x$ increases (or decreases) more and more rapidly as $x$ approaches 0 .

Confirm (4) by considering the cases $x>0$ and $x<0$ separately.

[FIGURE:1e558a457211b8d7 | A graph on an x-y coordinate system displays three functions. The function $y = x \sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$ is an oscillating curve that approaches the origin from both positive and negative...]
Figure 1.6.6

Solution (b). Since

$$ -1 \leq \sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \leq 1 $$

it follows that if $x \neq 0$, then

$$ \begin{equation*} -|x| \leq x \sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \leq|x| \tag{4} \end{equation*} $$

Since $|x| \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow 0$, the inequalities in (4) and the Squeezing Theorem imply that

$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} x \sin \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)=0 $$

This is consistent with the graph shown in Figure 1.6.6. $\square$

ex_1_6_3.prompt_md: Where is the function $f(x)=\frac{\tan ^{-1} x+\ln x}{x^{2}-4}$ continuous?
ex_1_6_3.solution_md: The fraction will be continuous at all points where the numerator and denominator are both continuous and the denominator is nonzero. Since $\tan ^{-1} x$ is continuous everywhere and $\ln x$ is continuous if $x>0$, the numerator is continuous if $x>0$. The denominator, being a polynomial, is continuous everywhere, so the fraction will be continuous at all points where $x>0$ and the denominator is nonzero. Thus, $f$ is continuous on the intervals $(0,2)$ and $(2,+\infty)$.
ex_1_6_3.answer: f is continuous on the intervals $(0,2)$ and $(2,+\infty)$

item_thm_1_6_4.prompt_md: ### 1.6.4 THEOREM (The Squeezing Theorem) Let $f, g$, and $h$ be functions satisfying$$g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)$$for all $x$ in some open interval containing the number $c$, with the possible exception that the inequalities need not hold at $c$. If $g$ and $h$ have the same limit as $x$ approaches $c$, say$$\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow c} h(x)=L$$then $f$ also has this limit as $x$ approaches $c$, that is,$$\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=L$$

item_thm_1_6_5.proof_md: PROOF (a) In this proof we will interpret $x$ as an angle in radian measure, and we will assume to start that $0<x<\pi / 2$. As illustrated in Figure 1.6.4, the area of a sector with central angle $x$ and radius 1 lies between the areas of two triangles, one with area $\frac{1}{2} \tan x$ and the other with area $\frac{1}{2} \sin x$. Since the sector has area $\frac{1}{2} x$ (see marginal note), it follows that$$\frac{1}{2} \tan x \geq \frac{1}{2} x \geq \frac{1}{2} \sin x$$Multiplying through by $2 /(\sin x)$ and using the fact that $\sin x>0$ for $0<x<\pi / 2$, we obtain$$\frac{1}{\cos x} \geq \frac{x}{\sin x} \geq 1$$Next, taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities, so we obtain$$\begin{equation*}\cos x \leq \frac{\sin x}{x} \leq 1 \tag{3}\end{equation*}$$which squeezes the function $(\sin x) / x$ between the functions $\cos x$ and 1 . Although we derived these inequalities by assuming that $0<x<\pi / 2$, they also hold for $-\pi / 2<x<0$ [since replacing $x$ by $-x$ and using the identities $\sin (-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos (-x)=\cos x$[FIGURE:9a41814575a8e0aa | The figure provides a geometric proof for the inequality $\frac{1}{2} \tan x \geq \frac{1}{2} x \geq \frac{1}{2} \sin x$ for $0 < x < \frac{\pi}{2}$. A unit circle in the first quadrant shows an...]Recall that the area $A$ of a sector of radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$ is$$A=\frac{1}{2} r^{2} \theta$$This can be derived from the relationship$$\frac{A}{\pi r^{2}}=\frac{\theta}{2 \pi}$$which states that the area of the sector is to the area of the circle as the central angle of the sector is to the central angle of the circle.[FIGURE:04e69d8174d99d9f | A circle is shown with a sector highlighted in light blue. The sector is defined by two radii and the arc between them. The central angle of the sector is labeled $\theta$, and the radius is labeled...]## TECHNOLOGY MASTERYUse a graphing utility to confirm the limits in Example 4, and if you have a CAS, use it to obtain the limits.[FIGURE:7ffa67a5739be0e3 | A graph displays the function $y = \sin(\frac{1}{x})$ on an $xy$-plane. The curve oscillates between $y=-1$ and $y=1$, with the oscillations becoming infinitely dense as $x$ approaches $0$, a region...]- Figure 1.6.5leaves (3) unchanged]. Finally, since$$\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \cos x=1 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} 1=1$$the Squeezing Theorem implies that$$\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$$proof (b) For this proof we will use the limit in part (a), the continuity of the sine function, and the trigonometric identity $\sin ^{2} x=1-\cos ^{2} x$. We obtain$$\begin{aligned}\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left[\frac{1-\cos x}{x} \cdot \frac{1+\cos x}{1+\cos x}\right]=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin ^{2} x}{(1+\cos x) x} \\& =\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}\right)=(1)\left(\frac{0}{1+1}\right)=0\end{aligned}$$

ex_2_1_1.title: Example 1: Tangent line to y=x^2

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

ex_2_1_1.prompt_md: Use Definition 2.1.1 to find an equation for the tangent line to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ at the point $P(1,1)$, and confirm the result agrees with that obtained in Example 1 of Section 1.1.
ex_2_1_1.solution_md: Applying Formula (1) with $f(x)=x^{2}$ and $x_{0}=1$, we have$$ \begin{aligned} m_{\tan } & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{f(x)-f(1)}{x-1} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}(x+1)=2 \end{aligned} $$Thus, the tangent line to $y=x^{2}$ at $(1,1)$ has equation$$ y-1=2(x-1) \quad \text { or equivalently } \quad y=2 x-1 $$which agrees with Example 1 of Section 1.1.

ex_2_1_2.title: Example 2: Compute slope using Formula (2)

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

ex_2_1_2.prompt_md: Compute the slope in Example 1 using Formula (2).
ex_2_1_2.solution_md: Applying Formula (2) with $f(x)=x^{2}$ and $x_{0}=1$, we obtain$$m_{	an } =\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{(1+h)^{2}-1^{2}}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{1+2 h+h^{2}-1}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0}(2+h)=2$$which agrees with the slope found in Example 1.

ex_2_1_3.title: Example 3: Tangent line to y=2/x

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

ex_2_1_3.prompt_md: Find an equation for the tangent line to the curve $y=2 / x$ at the point $(2,1)$ on this curve.
ex_2_1_3.solution_md: First, we will find the slope of the tangent line by applying Formula (2) with $f(x)=2 / x$ and $x_{0}=2$. This yields$$m_{	an } =\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{\\frac{2}{2+h}-1}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{\\left(\\frac{2-(2+h)}{2+h}\\right)}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{-h}{h(2+h)}=-\\left(\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{1}{2+h}\\right)=-\\frac{1}{2}$$Thus, an equation of the tangent line at $(2,1)$ is$$y-1=-\\frac{1}{2}(x-2) \\quad \\text { or equivalently } \\quad y=-\\frac{1}{2} x+2$$

ex_2_1_4.title: Example 4: Tangent slopes to y=sqrt(x)

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

ex_2_1_4.prompt_md: Find the slopes of the tangent lines to the curve $y=\\sqrt{x}$ at $x_{0}=1, x_{0}=4$, and $x_{0}=9$.
ex_2_1_4.solution_md: We could compute each of these slopes separately, but it will be more efficient to find the slope for a general value of $x_{0}$ and then substitute the specific numerical values. Proceeding in this way we obtain$$m_{\\tan } =\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{f\\left(x_{0}+h\\right)-f\\left(x_{0}\\right)}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{\\sqrt{x_{0}+h}-\\sqrt{x_{0}}}{h}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{\\sqrt{x_{0}+h}-\\sqrt{x_{0}}}{h} \\cdot \\frac{\\sqrt{x_{0}+h}+\\sqrt{x_{0}}}{\\sqrt{x_{0}+h}+\\sqrt{x_{0}}} \\quad \\begin{array}{l} \\text { Rationalize the numerator to } \\text { help eliminate the indeterminate } \\text { form of the limit. } \\end{array}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{x_{0}+h-x_{0}}{h\\left(\\sqrt{x_{0}+h}+\\sqrt{x_{0}}\\right)}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{h}{h\\left(\\sqrt{x_{0}+h}+\\sqrt{x_{0}}\\right)}=\\lim _{h \\rightarrow 0} \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{x_{0}+h}+\\sqrt{x_{0}}}=\\frac{1}{2 \\sqrt{x_{0}}}$$The slopes at $x_{0}=1,4$, and 9 can now be obtained by substituting these values into our general formula for $m_{\\tan }$. Thus,$$ \\text { slope at } x_{0}=1: \\frac{1}{2 \\sqrt{1}}=\\frac{1}{2} \\text { slope at } x_{0}=4: \\frac{1}{2 \\sqrt{4}}=\\frac{1}{4} \\text { slope at } x_{0}=9: \\frac{1}{2 \\sqrt{9}}=\\frac{1}{6} $$
